United States Oṃ, salutations to Śaṅkara, whose body is the nature of glorious consciousness.
Now,
The Spandakārikās, accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Kallaṭa.
Om! Salutation to Śambhu, whose form is the self-awareness of one’s own vibration.
Now,
the Spandakārikās,
accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Rāmakaṇṭha.
The first outflow:
the Vivṛti [states]:
"Of the one whose body is the light of consciousness, unmeasured by the ten directions, time, and so forth..."

Victorious in this world is that supreme Śākta-tattva known as Spanda— the innate attribute of Śambhu, overflowing with the rasa of incomparable wonder— which eternally flashes forth as the one who experiences its own self in such a manner.

(footnote 1) The functions [of the senses] such as the direction (dig) and so forth, because their expansion has not yet emerged within the power (śakti), are incapable of appearing as distinct from it through their own specific characteristics (svālakṣaṇya); the power (śakti) itself, moreover, because of its orientation toward the possessor of power (śaktimat), remains as nothing but that [power].
They are said to consist essentially in embracing the manifestation of the nature of the pure experiencer (gh:
the word "te" also follows the word "iti"). || 27 ||
Commentary: The intended meaning here is this:

Śiva-Śakti alone assumes forms such as the arrangement of mantras, because she is non-different from Śiva during both the states of emergence and dissolution; wherever there is non-difference from Śiva, there [it is Śiva-Śakti].
The nature of Śakti is like that in mental constructs, dreams, cities [of the imagination], and so forth; thus, through such pervasion (vyāpti) and other means, there arises a very firm realization.
For one who is ignorant of the potency of mantra, this results in the delusion of duality, which culminates in fixed notions of means and ends;
however, for the awakened one, mantras [function as the power of Śakti].
They become authorized for the accomplishment of all aims; not only mantras,
but even mere worldly speech attains the status of an unfailing mantra—
by this [it is shown that] the object of action is the knowledge of ritual activity, or the object to be known.
It is characterized as being solely the practice of the Śiva-dharma. || 27 ||

Commentary (p. 80): By this reason, namely, the present exposition, these mantras—consisting of the arrangement of phonemes and so forth that denote the deity to be propitiated—are "possessors of the nature of Śiva" (*śivadharmiṇaḥ*), meaning they possess qualities such as omniscience that belong exclusively to Śiva, the Supreme Lord, and are not shared by any other.
Those for whom that *dharma* exists are "those who are such," meaning they possess a nature non-different from Śiva.
For what reason? Because, having ascended upon the power—the capacity or energy—belonging to that Śiva whose nature was just explained immediately prior.
In the state of desiring to utter [the mantra], having accepted it through the logical proof of its non-difference [from the Self],
they proceed toward their respective offices of authority, praising by means of the power (*bala*) or energy (*śakti*) of Śiva, who is omniscient and endowed with the strength of omniscience.
They proceed toward their own capacity for accomplishing specific effects [—toward their mastery].
For these, having not yet attained the state of non-difference from the Supreme Lord, consist merely of phonemes characterized by the properties of arising and perishing; even a blade of grass...

They are unable to bend [the disciple]. However, by means of the previously mentioned forceful penetration (*balākrāmaṇa*), they become possessed of unimpeded power through the performance of their respective successive and final tasks—beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ending with the extraction of the venom of the scorpion—aided by the necessary procedures (*itikartavyatā*). If this is so...
Since all mantras possess an equal vigor characterized by the power to overcome [obstacles] as previously described,
how can there be a difference in their respective scopes of authority? Why should they not all be authorized to accomplish every purpose?— to this [question]:

To establish that the very cause is being constrained by *niyati* (the principle of necessity) fashioned by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), he provides an analogy: "How do these mantras function for the sake of the restricted office of practitioners?—just like the instruments of embodied beings. Indeed, as follows:

The instruments— the sense organs— of all embodied beings, who possess the conceit of self-identity fixed upon impermanent things such as the body alone, proceed from the Supreme Lord himself, according to the reasoning established here in the verse beginning with "this group of instruments."
Even though there is equality in their acquisition of activity, causality, and so forth for the purpose of bringing about consciousness, the instruments (karaṇas),
by the power of that imagined capacity of necessity (niyati-śakti),
have their capacities restricted solely to the illumination of objects such as sound, each according to its own nature.

Do they not function for distinct, separate offices, rather than all [mantras] functioning for every [purpose]? In the same way, these mantras function for the practitioners who have accepted the realization of the "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) of the supreme nature, according to their specifically assigned offices; therefore, they are like instruments.

Even mantras endowed with the power of omniscience have only restricted domains of authority. Consequently, those mantras possessing the nature of Śiva, having been granted their specific authority, become stainless (*nirañjana*)— that is, free from *añjana*,
which consists either of the impurity (*mala*) in the form of the coloring of the denotable object, or of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) in the form of the phonemes and so forth.

They have emerged; therefore, being of peaceful form— because their nature is peaceful and pure due to the fact that only pure consciousness remains— they are such that their self is a changeless form, and thus they abide right there in Śiva, the supreme cause, which is their own essential nature.

They completely dissolve; that is, they attain oneness with what? With the mind of the worshipper—that is, together with the practitioner’s own mind. For in that state, because of the absence of the limiting condition of intentional thought (abhisaṃdhi), there remains only the natural state.

The practitioner’s mind is together with that [mantra]. What is established by this? It is this: there is non-difference between the mantra and the consciousness during their states of arising and ceasing, due to their ultimate cause, Śiva. Thus it is.
As the very Śiva-Śakti, assuming the form of phonemes, mental constructs, and so forth, by virtue of being the essence of mantra and the essence of the practitioner's mind, she has arisen; now,
for practitioners who have not yet attained the realization of the touch of the power of their own true nature—
Producing the delusion of duality, it culminates in the authority for accomplishing a fixed purpose.
However, for one who possesses a very firm self-realization within their own nature exactly as it has been explained,
and who knows its rising and setting, all mantras become authorized for the accomplishment of all purposes.
They become effective even without depending on the necessity of association with various specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*) and so forth;
or, let alone the ritual mantras (*mantra*), whatever statement one utters with whatever intention,
that very thing attains the status of an infallible mantra— this occurs precisely through the force of its own inherent nature.

The essential meaning is this: the yogin must realize that the potency of mantras is established by its very nature through the penetration of the power of intrinsic being (*svabhāvabala*). This should be understood as an illustrative indication; for, according to the reasoning already stated, it is not only mantras that possess the nature of Śiva.
As long as no action, cognition, effect, or object of knowledge exists that—having attained its nature through non-difference from the supreme reality—is not essentially Śiva;
this he will state immediately hereafter. This has been explained in the Vṛtti.
"By the power of that which is the nature of unobscured consciousness," and so forth. (11)
Thus ends the second outflow, titled "The Perception of a Distinct Nature," in the Spandavivṛti composed by Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. 2.
Now begins the third natural outflow, titled "The Establishment of the Power of the Universal Nature."

Now, by way of introducing an alternative position, it is the occasion to discuss the fact that Śiva, who is indeed one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), possesses the inherent character of manifesting as the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) consisting of the manifestation of the universe— a point promised in the second half of the opening verse of this treatise.
He speaks three verses in order to establish [this] through both logical reasoning and scriptural authority:

"Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being; because it takes on the form of their perception, and because it realizes identity with them. (3.1, 28)
Commentary: This self is indeed of the nature of all things by way of being the source for the arising of all entities. [The phrase "this" (*ayam*) has been introduced from manuscript *gh*.
Because there is cognition only of that which is being experienced, it is precisely the external object that is being experienced.
One perceives it as a body, but not as a single body characterized by the head, hands, and so forth. || 28 ||

Note: Every object being perceived is, in reality, like one's own limb for the conscious individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, his body consists not only of the elements (*bhūta*), but also of objective existents (*bhāva*). For the perception of an existent, such as a jar or pleasure, is...
Origination is simply the state of being experienced;

for that which is not being experienced cannot attain self-establishment. Therefore, the emergence of all things occurs even from the individual soul (*jīva*). Consequently, that too is composed of the universe. [The limited "I"—]

The term "product" (kṛti) refers to the body, which possesses a head, hands, and so forth, and consists of the elements; however, that which consists of dispositions (bhāva) is that which is cognized through objects such as sound and the rest. || 28 ||
Therefore, among all reflections upon the meaning of words, there is no state that is not Śiva;
for the enjoyer alone always abides everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment. (3/2, 29)
(* Vivṛti: [The commentary] says:
By means of that such-like nature which consists of all things, there is no state in the reflections upon word and meaning that does not manifest the nature of Śiva (or: does not manifest Śiva).
Because it manifests [everything], the enjoyer alone indeed exists everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment; there is no other object of enjoyment whatsoever. || 29 ||

Note: Through the realization that all things consist of the universe as previously described, whatever stream of consciousness exists within the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) consisting of the denotable and the denotative is composed solely of Śiva, whose nature is supreme light; therefore, the subject is the Supreme Lord.
Through the dispatching of the wheels of will (*icchā*) and the rest,
one is intent upon the wondrous manifestation of the objects to be ruled, the self, the knowable, and the effects; by achieving identity with that [universal consciousness],
there is a state of perpetual, all-pervasive presence— thus, the very nature of the Self is the unfolding of the universe.
The nature of the manifestation of power has been fully accomplished. || 29 ||
Or, he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play—seeing thus and being constantly disciplined, he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (3/3, 30)

Commentary: He whose mind is of such a nature—that is, [one who perceives] "the entire world is composed of me alone"—seeing everything as play, is liberated even while living like a Lord because of his constant union [with the Absolute]; for him, the body and so forth do not function as a cause of bondage. || 30 ||
Note: According to the principle indicated in the immediately preceding verse, for the yogin who has cultivated uninterrupted attention and discernment,
there arises the realization of the full state of "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva) as the independent, conscious Bhairava, the Lord of All.
Having perceived this entire universe as merely a plaything fashioned for His own sport,
He is not tainted even in the slightest by the constraints of doubt, fear, or the stain of anxiety, despite being colored by joy, sorrow, and the like produced by His own pastimes.
The meaning is that liberation occurs even while one is still living, due to being a knower of reality as it truly is. || 30 ||
Commentary (p. 86): The connection is that he who possesses such consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*).

Thus, according to the manner just explained, for whichever supreme practitioner (*sādhakottama*) there is consciousness—that is, perfect knowledge—he [remains] constantly, without interruption, in all states.
Disciplined and concentrated, through the perspective of the teachings already stated and those yet to be stated, he—

cultivating the power of his own nature with an undistracted and one-pointed mind— is liberated even while living, while still maintaining the vital breaths that have their locus in the determined body.

Through the firm realization of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as the all-pervasive, the essence of all, the Lord of all, and the independent self-nature, one has emerged beyond birth and other such states; that one has become none other than the Supreme Lord— of this there is neither doubt nor delusion.

Because this matter is unshakable due to its being self-evident, logically established, and perceived [by him], what does the one liberated while living do? He regards the entire, complete, and infinitely diverse world—
the manifestation of endless entities— as a mere play, consisting only of the sport of the moving and unmoving beings created by himself, like toys fashioned for his own amusement.
Beholding and contemplating [this]: for every person,
lacking the vision of pure consciousness capable of perceiving their own unmanifested true nature,
perceives this entire collection of phenomena as distinct from themselves and from one another.
Constantly imagining that [the self] has arisen from some other cause,

and experiencing the transformations of joy, sorrow, fear, and so forth produced by that state of being, one repeatedly becomes a vessel for the bonds of birth and so on upon the path of existence. But he who...
The manifestation of the supreme consciousness that has arisen occurs by way of the mode of what is to be established; it is, for example,
like someone intent on play who plays with imitations of objects— such as those serving as causes for fear, anger, and so forth— which have been imagined by himself.
Because he knows things as they truly are, he does not undergo even the slightest turbidity of transformation such as fear;
likewise, knowing things as they truly are—since they are merely the manifestation of their own inherent nature and power—he does not undergo even the slightest distortion. Thus, everything...

Seeing [all things] as mere play, one is liberated even while living. To the question, "How is his consciousness?"—the author explains this with the verse beginning with "by that" (*tena*); by that reason which is about to be stated, there is no state whatsoever among the reflections on words and their meanings that is not Śiva—for him.
"He who possesses such consciousness is liberated while living. A word (*śabda*) is a collection of words that conveys meaning;

the meaning (*artha*) is the multitude of entities to be expressed, which is manifold due to distinctions such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Reflection upon these two consists of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpanā*) corresponding to each [object], arising from the coloring by infinite objects of thought.
Regarding these cognitions, which constitute worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) within these reflections on words and meanings—
there is no such state or condition whatsoever, whether in the form of reflection on words or reflection on meanings,
that does not directly become Śiva himself. Since this is so, at that time, the enjoyer is indeed the experiencer alone.
The Lord is eternally and always present everywhere, in all states, as the very essence of the object to be experienced—that which is to be enjoyed.
There is no such thing as an "object of enjoyment" existing separately;
this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is merely a manifestation of the failure to discern the ultimate reality.

"For what reason is there no state that is not auspicious? To this he says: because the living soul (*jīva*), which is the Self (*ātman*), consists of all things and is the form of the universe, its cognition is such that [subject and object] are not mutually distinct;
even the empirical activity (*vyavahāra*) of the living soul is established only on the basis of the non-difference between the known (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).
This is the meaning. Why is this so? Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since all things arise through the realization of identity with the nature of that consciousness.
Regarding "the nature of the consciousness of some object of cognition"—such as a jar, pleasure, or the like—that which is the consciousness is the knowledge; its "nature" is its essential form.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); by that cause, the realization of identity is the consciousness of non-difference;
from that cause arises the emergence of all entities, the production of all things; therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything. What is meant?

When this empirical activity of the individual soul (jīva) is investigated, it establishes the true nature of reality. For instance, it brings forth and creates its own object only by being conscious of it; indeed, an object exists only as it is being experienced.
It attains its own nature, but not as something unperceived; and being perceived is nothing other than appearing in this or that form.
And appearing is non-different from light (*prakāśa*); it is nothing else at all. As the proponent of Nyāya has said:
"And because [the soul] experiences through volition, and because it does not experience that which is not of its own nature.
Thus, whatever this living being perceives, each of those things becomes his very body;
it is not restricted solely to a specific arrangement of parts such as a head and hands.

For even that [the body] becomes his "embodied" state only during the condition of being perceived; at other times, however, it is merely an external object. And thus, because of the commonality of being perceived, the knowers of reality have recorded two kinds of bodies for him: the material (bhūtātmaka) and the mental (bhāvātmaka).

In this context, the first quarter of the verse— “the body which is pure consciousness, unmeasured by the reckoning of directions and so forth, because it has been made to forget its true nature through the power of the majesty of *māyā*”— refers to the Possessor of Power (*śaktimān*). By means of the remaining portion, [the author] reveals the meaningfulness of the word *spanda*.

The manifestation of Śakti, which is inherent in that [Śaktimat], is perceived as the unfolding of Śakti, synonymous with the bliss of Brahman and so forth. Through the word "conquers" (*jayati*), it is understood that the principle of Śakti possesses supremacy over all things. And therefore—

For those devoted ones who immerse themselves in the enjoyment of the aesthetic flavor of that absorption, it is suggested that they become vessels for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and that they become desired by the entire universe.
Let some wander by themselves in the naturally dense and treacherous wilderness, having entered it without the directions shown by those who know it;
for by that very path, they may lead others astray.
They are preparing to depart; this is a great delusion.

[Note 2: For those who plunge into the naturally profound ocean of the Śaiva Āgamas without the guidance of the true tradition taught by the wise, their consciousness is enveloped by the power known as Vāmā; thus, [they proceed] on the basis of their own arbitrary inventions.

For those possessed of high expectations, there is, in reality, a state of being almost submerged in the middle without reaching the further shore; alas, as for that exhortation intended to show the other shore to their followers who are wandering on its wrong path— how tragic!
"The opening of the eyes is like falling into a blind well; therefore, this effort of mine is intended to carry such people across to the further shore.
[Thus, amidst the fierce mutual collisions caused by the incessant impact of the winds of various doctrines—]

Those who, by producing continuous streams of powerful sounds that pierce the ears and split the temples, agitate the ocean of the scriptures with the impetuosity of their commentaries; and by whom seekers whose minds were distressed and deprived of the raft of the meaning of the scriptures—lost amidst the confusion of rising whirlpools of intellect—have been rescued: by them [this work] is offered. (3)
One person, having diverse tastes, even while knowing the supreme reality, falls into error;
another, whose intellect is opposed by the darkness of hatred, does so by nature; and yet another is simply dull-witted.
Thus, a compendium of words that captures the hearts of all is truly difficult to find.
However, there are now some discerning people here who are worthy recipients for the virtuous.

Having unified this *Spandārthasūtrāvalī*, which was composed by someone else with the intent of expanding [the teaching], while others had reduced it to two threads, I have arranged it here according to the tradition.
I place this pair [of works] into the rubies of the minds of the wise—pierced by the diamond-point of the power of the Lord’s grace—in order to make them successful. (5)

[(Footnote 3) First, the *Sūtrāvalī* was composed by the venerable Vasuguptapāda. Subsequently, it was refined by the perfected masters (*siddhas*) such as Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa through commentaries that clarify its concealed meaning. Now, however, [this work consists of] the composition of the *sūtras* and their refinement.]

In order to bring to fruition the two previously established tasks, this very *Spandārthasūtrāvalī* has been compiled and joined together, incorporating an explanatory commentary on the meanings that are in agreement with the *Vṛtti*.

Endowed with a sublime composition that determines the ultimate truth as handed down in the scriptures, it is inlaid within the pure jewel-like hearts of the sensitive, which have been permeated by the crest-jewel of the magnet-stone known as the descent of supreme power (*parāśaktipāta*). Through the contemplation of its fragrance, beauty, and other qualities— [The text continues: ...it is said that even those who are dull-witted, having become intoxicated by the wine of the nectar of this [work], attain the state of being a *khecara* (sky-farer). Furthermore, by means of the *yogapīṭha* (seat of yoga) described here, one attains the supreme state. Thus ends the *Yogapīṭhamālāstotra*, composed by Śrī Śambhunātha. May the venerable Vimala, who is the very essence of the *Trika*, grant me his grace. May the venerable Bhūtirāja, who is the very soul of the *Śiva-sūtra*, protect me. May the venerable Utpala, who is the very heart of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, grant me his favor. May the venerable Abhinavagupta, who is the very essence of the *Tantrāloka*, protect me. May the venerable Kṣemarāja, who is the very life of
Having ascended into the midst of the Lord’s palace made of nectar,
one experiences unsurpassed bliss through the unimpeded expansion of one's mental state;
for by its opening and closing, the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.
We praise that Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra).

Commentary: By this [verse], it is shown that the very nature of one's own self, which is of the essence of Śiva, is the cause of the creation and dissolution of the universe through mere volition, [and] that [the Lord] consists of a body of consciousness (vijñānadeha).
The fact that [the Lord] is the cause of the arising of sovereignty over the wheels of power (śakticakra) is established by means of a salutation.
Commentary:
May this collection of synonyms, which illuminates the meaning of the functions of *spanda*, always lead to the realization of the true nature of the non-duality of Śiva.

For just as an object intended for attainment at the initial stage of the desire to bring it about is non-different from the seeker, so too here, in the state of Śiva, the reality— which is variegated by the uninterrupted manifestation [of all things]—
is [non-different from Him] due to its nature as the unfolding of Being.

At the moment of perceiving an object, this individual soul (jīva), its capacity being contracted due to the non-recognition of its own true nature, perceives itself as having a head, hands, and so forth, by virtue of being the locus of a limited ego-sense; because that [perception] consists of the process of manifestation and so on, it is said to be "of the nature of the elements" (bhūtātmaka).
That which it refers to as an external object, such as sound and so forth, consists of existence;
yet when the ultimate reality is investigated, both [existence and non-existence] are its body, since there is no difference in their being objects of consciousness. Thus...
In the state of association with objective entities characterized by being perceived, the individual soul (jīva),
although existing as all-pervading and universal in form due to its non-difference from the objects of perception,
[remains as such] because of the non-emergence of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the reality of perceiving those objects; thus, this entire [world]...
By distinguishing the self from other causes external to itself and from other selves through their mutual distinctness,
and by identifying the self with the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) toward impermanent entities such as the body, one becomes subject to the bondage of birth and so forth.
He is designated as a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī jīva*). But when,
through the awakening produced by the falling rays of the power of Śiva, the sun, his clear vision dawns,
he perceives the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body and other such things, which is manifesting with extreme clarity.
When one who is firmly established in self-realization becomes manifest through the powers of perceiving and reflecting upon things as they truly exist,
then that very person becomes a wheel of powers consisting of the diverse manifestations of the universe, inscribed by mere volition.

Śiva is attained. Therefore it has been said: by the power of the nature of the cognition of each respective object, there arises the realization of identity through the consciousness of non-difference from the object being experienced; from that, the emergence of all things occurs. Consequently, the individual soul (jīva) is composed of everything; and by that, his...

By the reason characterized as the realization of being composed of all things (*sarvamayatva*), there is no state that does not consist of Śiva; and therefore, the enjoyer alone, as the Lord, exists eternally and everywhere in the form of the objects of enjoyment and the entities to be governed. Thus, for whomsoever...

This has been repeated for the purpose of synthesizing the meaning of the statement, "That consciousness is the one liberated while living" (p. 92). By these three verses, the existence of the Self alone as the universal form is established, since no other cause for the phenomenal world (*viśvaprapañca*) is logically possible. As it has been said:
The divine Self, by its own power of illusion, fashions itself as the self through itself;
it is that very same [Self] which perceives through differentiation— this is the certainty of the Vedānta.
Thus it is said. Likewise, it has been stated by another through the medium of praise:
the entire collection of entities, from Śiva down to the earth, exists as non-different [from Him];
that very same [collection] is designated by the term "power" (śakti) within Śiva, whose nature is eternal, invariable, and one.

These two are conjoined because their non-difference has been accepted. In reality, however, the supreme Śakti is one alone, as it possesses the reflective awareness of the perfect "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa). Within the supreme sovereignty that flashes forth through the manifestation of most wondrous powers, there exist the manifestations of entities characterized by infinite variety, brought forth by the power of Māyā.

However, because the multitude of entities— which arises merely through the inclination toward the grasping of lower levels and which has attained the state of primary and secondary divisions— is manifested, there are many designations that convey the intention of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power. This is the meaning:

The universe has been manifested by the will of Śaṅkara alone within His own Self; though it possesses a stable existence, it is merely the unfolding of His power (*śakti*). Yet, through the power of *māyā*, it appears as manifold.
Thus, by means of praise to Him, the attainment of identity with Him is prayed for.

Commentary: We praise—that is, we extol—that Śaṅkara, the creator of ultimate bliss. Who is he? He, by whose opening and closing—that is, by the expansion and dissolution of his power—the destruction and emergence of the universe, the world, occur.

Destruction and manifestation. We shall explain later that the correspondence [of these terms] to the respective order is not intended here. Of what nature is that [reality]? It is "the source of the power of the wheel of energies" (*śakticakravibhavaprabhava*).
The "wheel of energies" (*śakticakra*) is the collection (*samūha*) of the energies whose essential natures will be described below. That—

The construction of the words as "the origin (prabhava) of that manifestation (vibhava), which is sovereignty (aiśvarya)" is indeed easily understood. However, it remains to be considered how this accords with the actual nature of things. Śaṅkara, for his part, is eternal, of a single unchanging nature, and truly one.

The intended meaning of this treatise is that "the category (padārtha) exists in the ultimate sense" (paramārthasat), because it is established in that manner. However, how can its two mutually contradictory, impermanent, and specific states—consisting of closing and opening [of the eyes]—be presented as being related to it? For [they are presented] through the manifestation of an agent.
By this very [statement], it is established that Śaṅkara "opens his eyes and closes them.
And thus, the possession of impermanent states is untenable in the case of the eternal Lord; so how can it be said, "by whose opening and closing of the eyes"?

To this it is replied: by the two terms "unmeṣa" (opening) and "nimeṣa" (closing), which function metaphorically, only the single will belonging to Śaṅkara is expressed; and that is His eternal attribute, constitutive of His very nature, which is denoted by the words "unmeṣa" and "nimeṣa."

And duality exists only figuratively; for since the world itself consists of effects manifested by the power of the Supreme Lord's *māyā*, and thus being impermanent, its dissolution and emergence are possible, and consequently, closing and opening [of the eyes] occur in reality. And these two—

These two have as their sole cause the will of the Lord (īśvarecchā). Thus, because it is the cause of the unfolding (unmeṣa) characterized by emergence, the will of the Lord itself is metaphorically designated by the word "unmeṣa"; and because it is the cause of the closing (nimeṣa) characterized by dissolution, it is metaphorically designated by the word "nimeṣa. This is just as [the cause of longevity] is designated by the word "life" (āyus) because it is the cause of life.

Ghee. And that is the power (*śakti*) of Śaṅkara, non-different from him; and the very realization of that is the cause for the attainment characterized by the recognition of the Lordship of the Self (*ātmaiśvaryapratyabhijñā*). And she [the Power], according to the logic to be stated in the verse "as if out of a desire to see all objects" (*didṛkṣayeva sarvārthān*, SpKā 3.11),...

Because it resembles the desire well-known among worldly persons, it is designated by the word "desire" as a means for its comprehension. For just as an object desired by a person during the state of desire exists without being distinct from its own essential nature, so too [is this case].

Within the power of the Blessed One, the world—variegated by the particularity of infinite manifestations—abides as non-different from his own nature, which has not undergone even the slightest modification.
This is that state of Śiva, which is ultimately real, and which is thus praised by those who know it: (p. 6)
Salutations to the Lord, who always finds delight in creation, who always dwells in the bliss of preservation,
and who is eternally satisfied by devouring the three worlds.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"That which is this intuition (*pratibhā*), colored by the succession of various objects, yet whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness—that cognizer is the Great Lord."

Thus, the designations *icchā* (will), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *kriyā* (action) applied to the single supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*) arise solely from the manifestation of the power of *māyā* characterized by "this-ness" (*idantā*); for, setting aside the singular state of Śiva, the power of *māyā* has established its footing everywhere, and by virtue of it—

Within the single Śiva-tattva, which is ultimately real, there are designations for other principles such as Sadāśiva and so forth in the procedural scriptures (*prakriyā-śāstra*). This will be established later, on the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with "the loss of the essence of the supreme nectar" (*parāmṛtarasāpāyaḥ*, *Kārikā* 3.14). That...

The supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śaktiḥ*), characterized in this way, is metaphorically designated as "dual" because it is the cause of the two states of the universe manifested through its own play (*līlā*). Therefore, the intended meaning here in the first half of the opening verse is: [He] by whose mere will the universe...

We praise Him who is both dissolution and emergence. And here, that correspondence of number need not be taken in its primary sense—that emergence occurs through expansion (*unmeṣa*) and dissolution through contraction (*nimeṣa*)—for the numerical correspondence of the meanings is what truly coheres. Furthermore, this expansion and contraction are merely His will.
In order to demonstrate this much of the intended meaning, the commentator Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa himself has explained [it as follows]:
"By mere volition..."

Thus [it is said]. However, according to those who follow the justification of the respective order [of the verses]: at its *unmeṣa* (opening), due to the withdrawal of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), there is the dissolution or destruction of the world as its own nature expands;
at its *nimeṣa* (closing), due to the expansion of the power of action, there is the emergence of the world in the form of the contraction of its own nature.

Explaining [the term] as "emergence" (*udbhava*), they establish the opening and closing (*unmeṣa-nimeṣa*) of Śaṅkara alone as having the nature of ultimate reality; yet, by regarding a merely conceptual object as the ultimate reality, they do not indeed perceive the internal essence of this [true] vision.
"Have they entered?"—homage to them!

But surely, since it has been established that the power (*śakti*) of the Lord—who possesses an eternal, non-deviating, and unitary nature—is likewise of that same nature, because their non-difference is admitted; how then [is this so]?

It has been explained that "the wheel of powers" [is thus]. To this we reply: Indeed, it is precisely this unsurpassed sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) that is intended here, namely, that even though there is no deviation from the mere self-reflective awareness (*svarūpaparāmarśa*) of "I" in all circumstances...

It delineates this painting of the three worlds, inlaid with various manifestations expanding without limit; yet, even while being delineated in this way, when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not differ in the slightest from its own essential nature.
As it has been said:
"O Lord of All, your unprecedented state of supreme lordship triumphs, in that it is devoid of anything to be ruled."
There is yet another [nature] of yours, just like that, by which this world appears; yet it does not appear as it truly is.
Thus it is written elsewhere as well:
"Homage to you, who manifest the wondrous painting of the three worlds, proclaiming the radiance of marvelous intuition."
Salutations to Śambhu, who shines with hundreds of illuminations fashioned by the wick of his own single, subtle, and perfectly pure power.
Thus, this kind of Śaiva sovereignty,

in which the darkness of all māyā has been swallowed up by His grace, is to be personally realized only by the great-souled ones who are perfectly awakened and for whom the ultimate reality has been revealed.

However, for those awakened by the descent of the Lord’s power (*īśvara-śaktipāta*), who practice according to the sequence of instruction from a truly approached authentic Guru, there arises an immediate personal experience. On the other hand, those who are not awakened are simply not fit for instruction. Thus it is said.
This very point will be established here below.

Such being the case regarding the supreme sovereignty of Śaṅkara, these manifestations of existence— which, though divided into two kinds by way of the conscious and the unconscious due to the power of his most wonderful illusory energy (māyā-śakti), are nonetheless infinite due to their internal subdivisions— [arise].

That single, ultimate power is non-different from the very nature of the Supreme Lord; yet, appearing as a multiplicity through the differentiation of various names and forms— which arises solely from the distinction in the reflective awareness of "this"— it manifests as many.

It is designated as the "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*). And when the term "power" (*śakti*) is used to designate individual entities (*bhāvavyakti*), its sole purpose is to demonstrate the non-difference from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). These very [powers] are the manifestations (*vibhava*).
Sovereignty belongs to the Lord, because he possesses the nature of manifesting himself through those very powers.
As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Power and the possessor of power—these two alone are said to be the categories of reality."
The entire universe is his power, and Maheśvara is the possessor of that power.

Thus, this [Lord] is the source— the cause of origination— of this manifestation which constitutes His own power (*svaśakti*), but not of something distinct from His essential nature that has acquired its being from some other source. And for this reason, by the first half of the first verse beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*), [this is established].

Even though Śaṅkara’s status as the cause of the universe has already been established, this latter half of the verse, beginning with "him" (tam), provides a specific qualification intended to convey the particular characteristic of his being the source of the universe that consists of the circle of powers (śakticakra). It is not [merely a restatement].

This has been restated. This very point was explained by the author of the *Vṛtti* as the causality for the arising of the sovereignty of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of the body of consciousness (*vijñānadeha*).
By such [statements] as these: "The body of consciousness" (vijñānadeha) refers to Maheśvara, whose form is pure consciousness alone;

he is the self—the essential nature—of that sovereignty which consists of the wheel of powers (śakticakra). This is indeed the intended meaning of that [term]. Furthermore, he is the one for whom there is no deviation from such attributes.

The Supreme Lord is established here by the word *Śaṃkara*, whose meaning will be explained. And he is none other than the Self—this is indicated by the syntactical construction involving the pronouns *yat* and *tat*; for:

By reflecting upon the meaning of the section elaborated in these fifty verses, it results that the aforementioned qualification applies exclusively to that [Self] alone, without deviation. This very point has been demonstrated by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) through this [verse],
which concerns one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*) consisting of Śiva.

By one who explains thus: "one's own"—that is, of the self (*ātman*)—the state belonging to oneself (*sva-ātmīya-bhāva*), namely its essential nature (*svarūpa*) or its own-being (*svabhāva*); for this is the intended analysis (*vigraha*) of that term. Therefore, this is the intended purport (*tātparya-artha*) of this first verse.

It consists of a formal commitment to the subject matter to be established in this treatise, namely: that the Supreme Lord effects the dissolution and emergence of the universe by His mere will; and that although the universe has obtained its stability, it is the manifestation of His power alone, appearing as manifold only through the influence of *māyā*.

In this context, these two very points are elaborated according to the sequence of demonstrating logical reasoning and empirical perception. And thus: from the very beginning, because the self-reflection of one's own nature does not arise due to the power of *māyā*, [it is distinct] from the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

The distinctness of the Self—which appears as non-different from the body and so forth—is now demonstrated. Therefore, the world, which is an object of cognition, is non-distinct from that cognizer insofar as it exists as its power (*śakti*), since [the cognizer] possesses a truly real nature; thus, it is precisely in this [sense].

Regarding the two meanings, [they are] logical proof and perception; thus, by this verse, the *spandasiddhānta* (the doctrine of vibration) is introduced as having four outflows (*niḥṣyanda*). Its status as a *siddhānta* is because it is the end (*anta*), that is, the finality and certainty, regarding the already established (*siddha*) reality of the Lord (*īśvara-tattva*), and not regarding something yet to be proven (*sādhya*). Alternatively:

This realization of the fourfold path—consisting of knowledge (jñāna), action (kriyā), yoga, and conduct (caryā)—as proclaimed in various philosophical systems, is the cause of success because it brings about purification;
therefore, this alone possesses the status of a definitive doctrine (siddhānta). Furthermore:

The teachers instruct that by this opening verse, which serves the purpose of ensuring the unimpeded completion of the work already begun, the relationship (*saṃbandha*) and other elements are also indicated; and all of that is obtained from the very phrase "we praise Śaṃkara," because it constitutes the definition of the means (*upāya*).

The means (*śāstra*) is primarily of the nature of the highest good (*śreyas*), while the goal (*upeya*) is characterized by the recognition of the sovereignty of the Self (*ātmaiśvaryapratyabhijñā*); both of these are expressed by the word *śam*. Its author is Śaṅkara, a name whose meaning is etymologically consistent with this [work].

[This belongs] to the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is the direct author of this supreme good, which consists of this scripture. Those who have compiled this tradition [of His] have attributed the designation of "author" [to Him]. Thus, between the Lord and the scripture, there exists the relationship of agent and product.

The connection [between the treatise and its subject] is as follows: it is understood from the word "we praise" that the subject matter (*abhidheya*) here is the essential nature of Śaṅkara. For it has been determined by the wise that the purpose of praise is precisely the exposition of the nature of the object to be adopted. Therefore, between the treatise and its subject matter, there is a relationship of the expositor and the exposited...

The relationship [between the treatise and its subject] is characterized by that of the means of exposition (*pratipādaka*) and the object to be exposed (*pratipādya*). Furthermore, the purpose—which consists in the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own sovereignty—is understood from the very word of Śaṅkara.
For it is the Lord (*īśvara*) alone who is explained as the agent of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*); such is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
The relationship between the two purposes is characterized by the nature of means and end (*upāyopeyabhāva*).

Thus, the three [factors] beginning with the relationship have been explained. The designation of this treatise is *Spanda*, as seen in such passages as: "For the sake of discerning the reality of Spanda" (*Sp. Kā. 1.21*), and so forth, within this very work.
This is conventional usage. Furthermore, this term "vibration" (*spanda*) refers to that which is solely the self-reflection of one's own nature—
eternal, the cause for the differentiation of emptiness, consisting of the impetus of that very [nature] alone, and designated by another name as "power" (*śakti*).

Because there is a slight movement (*spanda*) from the supreme Lord’s own nature (*pārameśvara-dharma*), it is designated as "the expressive" (*vācaka*) by virtue of its conformity with the meaning. Since this treatise (*śāstra*) is the cause for the realization of that [nature], it too is denoted by the word "Spanda. Furthermore, the subject matter (*viṣaya*)—here, by the term "subject matter"—is...

The qualified recipient (*adhikārī*) of this instruction is now specified; whereas in other treatises the word "subject matter" (*viṣaya*) is intended to denote the "thing to be expressed" (*abhidheya*), here the "thing to be expressed" has already been explained previously. Of this—

He is awakened because the darkness of all doubt has been dispelled by the light of his own true nature, which is being unveiled by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s supreme power (paraśaktipāta), as indicated by the excellence of his pure faith and devotion; he is one who has properly received the purificatory rites such as initiation (dīkṣā).

The realization of one’s own sovereignty remains as a mere consequence of the impulsion of the Guru’s word; for it is precisely such a person who has been previously accepted here as the one to be instructed. Thus, both the expression and its object are to be understood. And this opening verse has been explained.
This contains within it the introduction to the entire meaning of the treatise. || 1 ||

Now, [one might object]: "Surely, with respect to this manifold of living beings—which is divided by distinctions such as gods, humans, and animals; which possesses a vast array of bodies, instruments, and worlds; and which is differentiated by innumerable intermediate varieties—[there exist] pleasure, pain, hunger, thirst..."
How can that nature— which is perpetually transmigrating, permeated by the duality of old age and death, and characterized by the conceit of being delimited by birth and so forth—
be asserted as non-different from Śaṅkara, who possesses the marvelous sovereignty just described? This [nature] is utterly distinct from him.
By whom was this explained? How can he, whose non-deviation from such established attributes has been thus demonstrated, be Śaṃkara, my very own Self? To this, he says:
"In whom all this [this universe] resides as an effect, and from whom it arises..."
It has emerged; because its nature is unobstructed, there is no cessation anywhere.

Commentary: (p. 3) But how can there be a designation of the transmigrating being, who is indeed [of] his own nature, as Śiva? If this is asked—[if the reading "ity ucyate" is taken as such, though the reading lacking the word "yadi" is also found]—then [it refers to] that in which this world resides and from which it has arisen.
Even in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), because its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is never obscured, there is no cessation whatsoever;
therefore, it is called Śiva-ness. (Note:
This refers to the collection of the principles of reality whose nature consists of various differentiated objects of knowledge.)
It is that very [reality] which, by being the cause of manifestation and persistence and by being the agent, serves as the foundational substratum;

which, because it cannot tolerate contact with objects of knowledge, is of the singular nature of pure consciousness whose majesty is immeasurable and undivided. It is this alone that is intended here.

This is intended as the word for one's own inherent nature (*svasvabhāva*), and not the essential form (*svarūpa*) of the *aṇu* (individual soul) whose consciousness of sovereignty has been stolen by *māyā* and who possesses the conceit of [distinctions between] genus and individual; for that [latter] has its own nature obstructed. || 2 ||

Commentary: Of this reality about to be described, there is no restriction—no limitation, no cause for designation by means of "this-ness" or "quantification," and no property of an object of cognition—at any place, time, form, or particular state; it does not exist [as such].

For what reason? Because its nature is unobscured (*anāvṛtarūpatvāt*). That is to say, it is that whose nature is not obscured or covered by the impurity consisting of the conceit of birth and so forth; such being the case, the state of being so is its reality, and it is for that reason [that it is so]. To demonstrate the logical possibility of its being unobscured, he states a qualification:

"In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged"—here, "this" refers to that which exists as an object of cognition; "all" refers to whatever has been conceived in whichever philosophical system and in whatever manner; "that entire effect," whose existence is dependent upon an agent, [resides] "wherein"—that is, in which.
It abides as one, established as both the knower and the agent, serving as the universal substratum for the entire multitude of objects to be contained;
[it exists] in the form of this or that, such as earth and so forth, or a jar, a cloth, a cow, and so forth.

"Having attained a firm foundation" means that because every object contained within it is manifest, it has acquired its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*). Now, one might object: objects such as jars and cloths contained within the light of the sun and so forth do indeed possess existence, since they are manifest in their respective forms.

It reaches [its destination]; likewise, it has been stated that "all this effect resides therein. Is it by this very manner, or by another way? He says: "And from which it has emerged"—meaning, by the exclusion of other causes such as *pradhāna* and so forth, from which [it emerges]. (p. 17)
"Emerging from," that is, arisen from, a single cause which has become the sole agent.

This is the meaning here: that entity which, for everything comprised within the scope of "this-ness" (idantā) as an object of knowledge (prameya), is collected in the scriptures through various divisions.
He is the foundation because he exists as the sole illuminator of the multitude of principles;
he is the source and cause because he is the agent; and he is so because he himself cannot be touched by the quality of being an object of cognition.

That which is not an object for other illusory subjects, whose majesty is unlimited, and whose sole nature is pure, stainless consciousness— this is what is intended here by the term "one's own essential nature" (svasvabhāva), and not that self which is contracted by the conceit of being limited by genus and so forth.

The nature (*svarūpa*) or essential character (*svasvabhāva*) of the multitude of living beings—who fall within the category of effects and whose consciousness of their own sovereignty has been concealed by the power of *māyā*—is [the Self]. Thus, it is rightly said that "Śaṅkara is indeed the Self. This very point was stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*:
But how, then, can that which transmigrates by its very own nature be designated as Śiva?
Having thus raised this objection:
This has been explained by one who elucidates that in which this world is situated and from which it has arisen;
[this refers] to that [emptiness] in its state as a transmigrating being.

Thus, the mode of being (*vṛtti*) should be understood as follows: for transmigrating beings, there is the state of *māyā*, which consists of the conceit of birth and so forth manifested by that *māyā*; even in that state, there is no real cessation of their own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*). || 2 ||

Now, as for this category of reality called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) thus established, is it to be accepted as "yes" solely on the basis of scriptural authority (āgama), or rather through the two well-founded means of proof: reasoning (upapatti) and perception (upalabdhi)?
In order to sever this doubt— namely, whether it is possible to lead [the object] into the sphere of practice—
he will set forth a logical proof in a subsequent verse; to introduce that,
the following is first stated:

By means of that supreme wisdom which has attained firm establishment in the reality of the meaning expounded throughout this entire treatise, at the moment of reflecting upon one's own true nature, [that nature] is like a mass of frost vanishing when touched by the rays of the sun; but now—

For all subjects who are possessed by the power of *māyā*, which expands through the nature of the great darkness of the delusion of duality, there arises— due to a fall, as it were, from their ultimate nature as the knower— the cognition "I" (*aham*) with respect to the body and so forth, which are merely objects of knowledge, as if they were the knowing subject.

It is the root of the knot of differentiation, which is extremely difficult to break; therefore, for the sake of discerning that essential nature of the self— which consists of the notion of "I"— from those [objects] such as the body,
and for the sake of attaining the non-cessation of all things as promised immediately prior.
Introducing the logical proof based on the authority of one's own experience, he says:
"Even though it expands through the various distinctions of waking and so forth, it remains undivided;
it never departs from its own innate nature as the perceiver. (3)

Commentary: (p. 4) Even when a distinction is manifested through states such as waking and so forth—(in the variant readings kh and gh: "when a distinction occurs")—its essential nature remains veiled; because the state of being the perceiver is common to all three stages, there is no alteration in its essential nature, just as [in the following example].
And [it exists] in the sprouts and so forth of poison (the reading "of a tree" in some versions is not original), as well as in the five aggregates.
Note: By the mention of the word "etcetera" (ādi), the two states known as dreaming and deep sleep are to be understood.

Remembrance, intoxication, fainting, and so forth are included within those two. Among these, that state in which a person—whose sovereign of the senses (karaṇeśvarī) is expanded to grasp external objects through the sense organs [is called waking].

That state in which [the mind] vibrates is the waking state (*jāgarāvasthā*). That state in which, for one whose wheel of external organs has ceased, there is the grasping of the enjoyment of objects provided by the mind alone—which possesses the power of all the organs—is the dreaming state (*svapnāvasthā*). That state in which even the activity of the mind has come to rest...
That state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the non-perception of the objects characterized by the two aforementioned forms.
Memory (*smṛti*) is the non-erasure of an experienced object. Intoxication (*mada*) is a confusion of mental modifications (*citta-vṛtti*) produced by excessive drinking.
Fainting (*mūrchā*) consists of a delusion born from despair and the like. In these [states]...

While these states are manifesting, by means of the valid cognition of one's own experience— which possesses the strength of continuity and unity— the non-difference of the abiding subject from the state of being the perceiver is established. It should be understood that *tad-abhinna* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Commentary (p. 19): Therefore, there is no cessation anywhere of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it does not turn away from its own innate, unconditioned intrinsic nature—that is, from its own essential form—and does not become otherwise; the connection [of the words] is "it does not fall away. From what kind of intrinsic nature?

"From the perceiver" means from the one who perceives, the knower, the experiencer. And when does it not cease? Even as the differentiation of waking and so forth spreads—that is, the differentiation (*vibheda*), the distinction (*vyatireka*), the mutual distinctness of the states—in that [differentiation], it does not cease.
While [the state] is expanding and unfolding; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), the states of dreaming and deep sleep are grasped;

the states of memory and so forth are included within dreaming because they share a similar nature, and the states of intoxication, fainting, and so forth are included within deep sleep. Among these, "waking" refers specifically to the waking state.

It is well-known in the treatises as that state in which a person, having grasped the objects of the senses— such as sound and so forth— through the sense organs such as the ear, moves about with his faculties extended. Dream is the state of sleep, in which [the person], exhausted by his own activities, [remains].
Even when there is withdrawal from the abiding of the ears and other senses, one still perceives objects through the mind alone.

Deep sleep (*suṣuptam*) is a state of pleasant slumber characterized by profound drowsiness; it is that state in which, upon the cessation of even mental activity, there is no perception of external objects for that duration.

The state of memory (*smṛti-avasthā*) consists in the non-forgetting of experienced objects; it is like a dream, because of the similarity in the grasping of objects by the mind alone. Intoxication (*mada*) is a disorder produced by excessive drinking, characterized by the loss of the functioning of the mind and the senses. Fainting (*mūrchā*)...
The self whose nature is delusion, produced by the consumption of poison, dejection, and so forth—

because of the similarity in the absence of the apprehension of such objects of cognition (*vedya*) and others, whatever other states may exist that are equal to deep sleep (*suṣupta*), they are all included within these very [states].

Even though this differentiation proceeds on account of these [states], it does not deviate from its own nature as the perceiver. If this perceiver were merely of the nature of the states themselves, then, like those states, it too would be differentiated. However, while their differentiation spreads forth, this [perceiver] remains [unified] by virtue of its own nature.

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that [the entity] does not cease from being distinct from its states. How do we understand this—that even while it remains the substratum of the states, it does not deviate from its single nature even as those states, possessing different forms, unfold? Here, [the following] contains the reason:

He states the qualification: in what kind of state does that [consciousness] spread? It is in that which is non-different from it—non-different, uniform, and characterized solely by the nature of being a non-distinct perceiver; wherein its own essence, being all-pervasive, is itself experienced.
Even amidst the difference of states, there is no difference in the substrate characterized as the perceiver; (p.

22) in this regard, everyone’s own experience is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, [the experience] "I who slept am now awake" is itself experienced as being bound by the thread of a single unifying subject.

The states beginning with waking proceed in succession; and apart from these, no other state is possible for transmigrating beings, even though they are infinite in number. Therefore, just as in a single body there is one pervasive perceiver whose nature is distinct from the states, so too [is it elsewhere].

He alone is established as the one all-pervading reality even within all bodies; for despite the difference between bodies, there exists no other characteristic for him apart from being the mere perceiver. The notion "I," which arises as distinct for every living being, is illusory and not real. It is precisely for the sake of dispelling that [notion] [that this is taught].

The commencement of the treatise: Furthermore, that very single specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is nothing other than the mere state of being the perceiver, never deviates from its own nature—this is Śaṅkara’s own essential being. This has been correctly established for those awakened ones who do not deny their own experience. By means of these very states...

It should be understood that its non-differentiation is established even within the states well-known in the Yogaśāstra, such as waking and so forth; for even in those states, it persists as the pervasive perceiver. These states are now briefly defined: therein, with the mind [fixed] upon the object of meditation...
The waking state is merely the immediate onset [of consciousness], which is well-known in some traditions as *dhāraṇā*.
Within that very state, the continuous flow of a single stream of similar cognitions, through the exclusion of dissimilar cognitions, is the dreaming state.

That which they call "meditation" (dhyāna) is the state of consciousness during dreamless sleep accompanied by sensation— a state in which the mind, through a gradual intensification of one-pointedness, possesses only the subtle appearance of the object of meditation unmixed with other cognitions. This is what [they call meditation].

They describe a specific state of cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration, characterized by the successive following of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*), as being that which is followed only by bliss and the sense of self.
As for that which...

The asamprajñāta samādhi, whose definition has been established as "preceded by the practice of the causal sign of cessation, wherein only residual impressions remain" (Yoga Sūtra 1.18), is that deep sleep in which there is no object of cognition.
And in all these states, there exists a single, pervasive, essential nature in the form of the experiencer.

Existence (*sattā*) remains established. For, first, in a concentration (*samādhi*) that possesses an object (*sālambana*), because of the existence of a distinct object of cognition, the existence of the cognizer—the perceiver—is quite evident, just as in the worldly state. However, where there is an absence of form due to being without an object (*nirālambanatva*), there [the existence of the cognizer is not evident].
At that very moment, there is merely the non-perception of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), but not the absence of the knower’s (*vedaka*) nature of knowing,
as is the case in deep sleep and similar states; for one who has emerged from that state,
that condition becomes an object of knowledge through the necessity of being remembered, thereby manifesting the existence of the all-pervasive [Self].
It indeed manifests [itself]. Furthermore, those who—
deluded by the mere absence of the capacity for the cognition of an object—
regard the perceiving Self itself as unreal, [we shall address] them later.
He will cause [the self] to awaken. All this has been stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*:
even while distinctions such as waking and so forth are occurring, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that [self] is not obscured.
Having indicated this with such a passage, it is established by means of the analogy of the potency of poison:

"But surely, in specific states such as waking and so forth, this [nature] does not cease from the perceiver by its very nature, because of the existence of the knowledge that perceives one's own self" (p. 25).

How is it that which was established—that [the Self] exists as a single form by virtue of being the nature of one's own experience—is so established? Because in those various states, such cognitions arise for the experiencer himself, namely: "I am a human," "I am a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth.

"I am Devadatta," "I am young," "I am old," "I am thin," "I am fat"—these and others have the body as their basis; "I am happy," "I am miserable"—these and others have the intellect as their basis; "I am hungry," "I am thirsty"—these and others [have the vital functions as their basis].

These have the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as their support. Furthermore, the cognition of the subject as emptiness (*śūnyatā-pramātṛ-pratyaya*), which is to be known through the reflective awareness—“I was not conscious of anything”—arises for one who has awakened from states such as deep sleep, having emptiness as its object. All these, beginning with the body...
Since these [faculties] are impermanent, the notion of "I" which has them as its object is likewise impermanent.
To the question, "In that case, how can it be said that this [notion] does not cease from the nature of the perceiver? he says:
"The cognitions 'I am happy,' 'I am suffering,' 'I am attached,' and so forth..."
These [mental states] clearly exist elsewhere as well, being permeated by conditions such as pleasure and so forth. (4)

Commentary: And that [Self] is indeed continuous throughout all states, because—as in the thought "I who was happy am the very same I who am now suffering," or "I who was previously impassioned am the same one standing here later"—it exists as a continuity; not otherwise, that is, apart from the states themselves. As the scripture says:
"...that is considered the supreme nature.

Regarding this, the marginal note (*ṭippaṇī*) states: "Of consciousnesses" (*saṃvidām*); the plural number [indicates that] it is precisely the stream of cognitions (*jñānasaṃtāna*)—momentary and independent—which, by way of memory, imagination, and so forth, spreads out to a very great distance.

The intended meaning is that [the self], though branching out in many ways through its notions of "I" and so forth, takes as its objective support only the intellect (*buddhi*) and other such factors; it does not take as its objective support a relationship with anything else that is considered to be the rememberer or the seer. Such being the case:

In order to avoid all these consequences— that there would be no synthesis of memory, recognition, and so forth, and that in the absence of such synthesis, the cessation of all worldly activity would follow—
it is specified "elsewhere" [in the verse], meaning [the self] proceeds by way of a continuum of cognitions such as those of happiness and the like.

Śaṃkara, whose nature is that of a single substratum for the synthesizer who is free from cessation— established by the self-experience of every cognizer as the pervader of the prior and posterior states of all objects— is perfectly manifest. 4.

Commentary (p. 26): The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: those cognitions such as "I am happy" and so forth exist elsewhere; therefore, that [consciousness] does not cease from its single nature.
Because they are internal, the primary cognitions based on the intellect (*buddhi*) are indicated here.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), however, those [cognitions] having the body and so forth as their objective supports are included; and these have been explained previously. Therefore, all these cognitions [occur] elsewhere, distinct from the states such as pleasure and so forth that have already been explained.

They abide in the perceiver of pleasure and so forth; like rivers in the ocean, they remain there with their mutual distinctions dissolved, existing in unity—meaning they attain identity with it. And this is clearly evident, as it is perceivable through one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*). Therefore, consciousness is indeed one.
The "I," which flashes forth as the nature of the perceiver, is ultimately real; yet,
due to the absence of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of such a true nature produced by the power of *māyā*,
it experiences impermanent things such as pleasure and so forth, [thinking], "I am happy" and "I am suffering."

By such statements as these, [consciousness] is indicated by the plural form "saṃvidaḥ" (consciousnesses) because it is admitted to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with states such as cognition (*buddhi*). Furthermore, if—
due to its connection with objects of experience such as pleasure and so forth— consciousness were also [designated] as "I," just like pleasure and the rest...

If, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the forms of cognitions were indeed many, then there would be no synthesis such as memory, recognition, and so forth; and in the absence of that synthesis, the cessation of all worldly transactional activity would follow, which is not desired; therefore, [the cognition] is "elsewhere."
He states a qualification of the meaning already indicated: in what other way do these cognitions exist?
[They exist] in all particular states consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion—namely, in all [states of] pleasure and so forth that are permeated by the condition of pleasure and so forth.

Because they possess the nature of arising and perishing, [the internal organs] are impermanent; because they share the common quality of being objects of cognition, they function similarly to objects such as sound and so forth; yet, they abide as a pervasive entity in the form of a single cognizer characterized by "I," since in instances such as "I am happy" or "I am suffering," and so on, [this "I" persists].

When the conditions arise, two meanings manifest: one is of the nature of pleasure and so forth, consisting of the object of cognition (*vedya*); by virtue of being an object of cognition, it is understood—as with a jar or other objects—to be impermanent and manifold. The other is "I," consisting of the subject of cognition (*vedaka*). And that...

Pervading the preceding and succeeding states, it is well-known to all cognizers as the agent of synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), which is the cause of all worldly transactions; being eternal because its nature is that of pure perception alone, it shines forth as one. Thus, in this way—just as:
Even though differentiation spreads through causes such as waking and so forth, this [Self] remains one and possesses an undifferentiated specific characteristic (*abhinnasvalakṣaṇa*);

likewise, even though differentiation proceeds through the cause of the continuum of cognitions such as happiness contained within states like waking, it remains one and possesses an undifferentiated specific characteristic; for here too—
"I who was happy have now become unhappy or remain impassioned"— in this way,
the various states are perceived as being bound together by a single unifying subject. Therefore,
even with respect to all the particular states existing within the infinite streams of sentient beings, not even the slightest...
The alteration of the nature of the mere perceiver—which has not been produced [by causes]—is self-established;
because its form is eternally unobscured, it is unceasing everywhere, real, and Śaṅkara is indeed its own intrinsic nature. This is that.
Having explained that "it is indeed continuous throughout all states," and so forth, [the text concludes]:
"That is remembered as the supreme intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
Thus it was established as the final conclusion by the author of the Vṛtti. || 4 ||
Having thus established that it is logical to designate one's own essential nature as Śiva,
he now states its definition in brief and speaks in order to demonstrate its ultimate reality:
Where there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped nor the grasper,
and even no state of delusion— that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality.

(* Vivṛti: the object of apprehension) The *Vṛtti* states: And its intrinsic nature is this—that it is untouched by the states of pleasure, pain, the apprehended, the apprehender, delusion, and so forth; and that alone exists from the perspective of ultimate reality.

The ultimate reality exists because it is eternal; pleasure and the like, however, arise from conceptual construction, are momentary and transitory, are external to the nature of the Self, and are equivalent to objects such as sound. Furthermore, when [the Self] does not possess the nature of pleasure and so forth, it is then exactly like a stone. || 5 ||

Note: By negating the nature of pleasure and so forth, the twofold state of being an object of cognition—both external and internal—is negated. By the word "grāhaka" (the subject), the state of the illusory cognizer (*māyīya-pramātṛ*) consisting of the body and so forth is rejected.

Even the state of the object of cognition, the act of cognizing, and volition, because they are recalled at a later time, are indeed dependent upon the ground of the cognizable; thus, since the status of being a real entity within the sphere of knowledge is denied, he says "that exists" in order to refute mere non-existence.

That [consciousness], whose sole nature is an ever-arisen and undeluded perception, is established as the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*), because the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*) are mutually distinct in nature;
for the object of cognition is unreal by nature and subject to momentary destruction, whereas the cognizer alone is the ultimate reality. || 5 ||

Commentary: (p. 29) That entity, characterized by the qualifiers to be mentioned, which is expressible by the term "own-nature," exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) and in reality (*tattvataḥ*); the meaning is that everything other than that is of an unreal nature (*asatyasadbhāva*). What is that? It is that wherein there is no suffering, nor...

It is bliss, neither the grasped nor the grasper, nor even is there a state of delusion. By this negation of its being of the nature of bliss and so forth, its state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is negated. For the object of cognition is of two kinds: external and internal. Of these, [it is neither].

The internal [objects], such as pleasure and so forth, are to be known by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); that [internal nature] does not exist in Him, because He has been established as having the singular nature of being a distinct knower. External objects, however, are sound and so forth, which are the objects of cognition; they are designated by the term "the graspable" (*grāhya*), for they are apprehended by the external senses, such as the ear.

That [object] is experienced by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as consisting of pleasure and so forth; yet even that does not exist there [in ultimate reality]. For its form does not become an object of perception by way of having sound and other sense-objects as its nature.
Furthermore, the "grasper" intended here is the subject (*pramātṛ*) belonging to *māyā*, and not the ultimate (*tāttvika*) one.

It has the nature of being merely the perceiver, because it is established as being thus eternally existent. Likewise, even the subject—the ego consisting of the body and so forth belonging to Māyā—is not present there.
As for the reading "grāhakam," they explain it as "the sense organ"; that too is absent where [it is said to be].
It does not exist. Thus, that reality which is of the nature of a mere grasper, distinct from the essential nature of the grasped and the act of grasping—that exists.
But if this is so, is this not merely a state of delusion?
Thus it has been established, for in that [state] there is an absence of the nature of pleasure and so forth.

To refute this, he says: "Nor even is there a state of delusion"—the state of one who is deluded is "delusion-ness," which is the absence of the capacity to perceive and be perceived; where even that does not exist, [it is not so].

It exists; for even that [state] is established as being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*), since it is later recollected in another state as "I was deluded," its non-perception at that time being merely incidental. And given the existence of this objectivity in the state of delusion—
How could there be the nature of a reality consisting of a single essence of the knower? If, in this way,
even the state of being deluded does not exist therein—
because of the negation of the nature of all knowable objects that constitute the domain of its cognition— then it would be a mere non-existence.

That [objection] would thus have been established. To refute that, he says: "That exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ). That very entity which has been explained as being characterized in such a way exists from the perspective of ultimate reality, because its essential nature (svabhāva) is defined by the constant, unimpaired characteristic of being the mere perceiver.

Furthermore, that which consists of pleasure and so forth has its nature obtained through mere conceptual construction; it is momentary, always an object of cognition (*vedya*), and is utterly distinct from the Self (*ātman*) because the latter has the sole nature of being the cognizer (*vedaka*). Therefore, whatever exists within the sphere of the cognizable is all unreal, because it is impermanent. But that which...

The knower is one and only that which exists in the ultimate sense; this is the meaning. This has been explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) in the passage beginning with "that" and "this is its intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). || 5 ||
