Now, in order to demonstrate that this very Self, Śiva— who exists in the ultimate sense— is the most worthy of being accepted by first establishing His independent power to accomplish all things, he speaks a pair of verses.
For this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts like one who is undeluded,
performing the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal along with the internal wheel.
One obtains it; therefore, that reality must be examined with effort and respect, because its independence is everywhere uncreated.
(Yugalakaṃ) Commentary: (p.

7) Since [the group of instruments], together with the internal wheel, [is of the nature of consciousness]—(Note: Following "yataḥ," there is also an additional reading, "caitanyasvabhāvāt.")—of the group of instruments, including the internal wheel.
Even for that which is deluded, there are arising, abiding, and cessation as if it were undeluded;

since it is capable of imparting consciousness to others, how could it be devoid of intrinsic nature? Therefore, that reality must be examined with effort by the yogi, in order to understand how it bestows consciousness upon the instruments and other faculties.

Likewise, autonomy is possible even in relation to the bodies of others and so forth; for autonomy, which constitutes one's own essential nature, is manifested through practice everywhere, since it is uncreated. (6–7)

Note: *Utpatti* (emergence) is the state in which [consciousness] begins to manifest itself by looking toward the object it desires to know. *Sthiti* (stasis) is the state of resting in the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) of the colored object. *Nirodha* (cessation) is the state of making the object one's own through the fulfillment of its purpose.

The states consisting of the cessation of their own respective functions and the absorption [of the organs] into the Self— these are perceived through the power of contact with that which is the ultimate reality,
the nature of the Self, by the thirteen instruments (karaṇas) which are considered to be insentient.
Just as the attainment of independence in the instruments [of action] has been understood, so too,
upon the ripening of the state of excellence in practice, it leads to the acquisition of independence over all objects for the common good;
its characteristic is that of being the creator of everything dependent solely upon one's own will.

Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is spontaneously established within the body and its particular states when they are endowed with the perfection of immersion (*samāveśa*); it is independent of causes such as material or auxiliary factors, because even in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), worldly activity is accomplished solely through its majesty, [despite] the pervasion of *māyā*.

However, when there is an absence of self-reflection due solely to the power of delusion (*moha*), the establishment of an entity occurs in dependence upon external causes; this is what constitutes the conventional usage of "dependence.
Since independence is established in this context, its excellence as that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*) is emphasized. || 6-7 ||

Commentary: That reality, the entity known as one's own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which exists by way of ultimate existence (*paramārthasattva*), should be examined with effort— that is, with supreme exertion (*yatna*) that is constant and uninterrupted, and with reverence— that is, through an excess of faith (*śraddhā*)— in all states of experience.

In accordance with the instructions to be taught hereafter, one should gradually clarify [the Self] as the nature of the subject through the reflective awareness of the subject's own essence, by means of its intentness upon the differentiation of the two groups characterized as the object and the subject; for this [consciousness] belongs to it.
The independence that has just been introduced—

the capacity to perform all actions solely by one's own will— is entirely natural and innate for one who abides everywhere, in every body or in every particular state; it is not, however, [something acquired].

[The world] depends on other causes such as the cooperation of the *upādāna* (material cause) and so forth; for even among transmigrating beings, the accomplishment of all worldly transactions occurs solely through the majesty of His sovereignty (*svātantrya*). However, due to the delusion of *māyā*, because of the absence of awareness of the true nature [of reality], everyone [is bound].
The transmigrating being acts as if dependent in all activities,
because the accomplishment of every purpose depends upon external causes; therefore,
that reality (tattva) must be investigated in order to attain innate sovereignty, and not otherwise.

It has been taught that because pleasure, pain, delusion, and the forms of the grasped and the grasper are negated, it must be understood as being without substantial reality. Now, in order to demonstrate the independence indicated by the word "this" (*iyam*), there is a qualification characterized by the relative pronoun *yat*.

It is explained as follows: What is that reality (*tattva*) to be examined? Because from it [proceeds] this group of instruments—the group of external instruments such as the ear and so forth, and of internal sense-faculties (*indriya*) such as the mind and so forth.

The aggregate of the thirteen instruments undergoes activity (*pravṛtti*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*). Activity is the state in which there arises an orientation toward the object intended to be grasped;
maintenance is the state of resting upon the object already grasped; and withdrawal occurs because the purpose has been accomplished.

Upon the abandonment of external objects, there occurs the cessation of its own activity, which is the state of dissolution; he attains or reaches these. Of what nature is the group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*)? It is "deluded," being for the most part well-known as being merely inert. How does it attain this? "Like one who is not deluded," that is, like a conscious being. This is the meaning.

What is meant is this: even though this wheel of external and internal senses is by nature insentient, it becomes capable of conscious activities such as functioning through the power of contact with that [reality];
that reality, when made manifest as the Self, possesses the sovereignty that bestows consciousness upon the senses.

It is indeed capable of securing mastery over all objects; therefore, it must be examined so that, while mastery is being manifested even at the stage of practice, such play as entering the bodies of others becomes possible. This is as follows:
And since it is not of the nature of pleasure and so forth— as expressed by the words "when it is not that," and so on—
therefore, that reality must be examined with effort.
And this has been explained separately in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of such passages as "ityādi" [and so forth]. || 7 ||
Now, why is this said—that there is some reality (*tattva*) to be examined, by virtue of which the sense organs become conscious? Indeed, worldly convention is established thus:
every conscious cognizer (*pramātṛ*), through the connection with merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), [acts] by means of that which is called desire (*icchā*).
Being joined with the quality [of desire], and becoming possessed of effort toward an object— whether it be something to be rejected or something to be accepted—

that very quality called desire impels the collection of insentient organs toward the rejection or acquisition of those respective objects; and that [collection of organs], being thus impelled, remains indeed insentient.

It performs its own function like a giver and so forth. How then was it said that "one obtains activity and so on through the engagement of a cause that is as if non-deluded"? And it has been explained:
by the very power of contact with that cause.
Anticipating the question, "How does [the Self] become capable of accomplishing the operations of consciousness, such as engagement in activity?
he says the following in order to clarify, by demonstrating the worldly transactions of the transmigrating person (*saṃsāri-puruṣa*), how this aggregate of instruments becomes conscious.
For this [mantra] does not function as an impeller by means of its own desire or command;
rather, through contact with the power of the Self, the person becomes equal to it.

Commentary: Nor does he impel the instruments by means of the impulse of his will (there is also a variant reading: *icchāpreraṇena karaṇāni prerayati*); rather, abiding in his own essential nature, he acts only in accordance with whatever kind of will arises within him.
It produces both external and internal effects; therefore, its capacity is not restricted solely to instruments, but extends everywhere. || 8 ||
Commentary: The intention here is as follows— just as the Supreme Lord,

by means of His powers of perfect knowledge and agency, imparts activities such as the process of manifestation to the worlds and thereby ascends into the state of possessing knowledge and action throughout the universe.
In this way, through contact with that unsurpassed power alone, the capacity for being a knower and so forth arises in the yogi; yet, by virtue of *māyā*,
the powers of knowledge and action also become contracted, turning toward limitation and becoming restricted as internal and external faculties.

Since [the senses] are able to operate within their respective fixed domains when extended outward, even the *aṇu* (individual soul), abiding in its own nature, is independent in the impelling of the circle of instruments (*karaṇacakra*) and so forth; it is not, however,
[dependent] on the impelling of the quality called desire (*icchā*), which is bound by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
Its agency is metaphorical, like that of a sickle or other tools impelled by an agent. || 8 ||

Commentary: Indeed, it is not the case that desire alone is the "impelling" (*nodana*). For "impelling" refers to an instrument (*karaṇa*), such as a goad, by which one is driven. It is as a prompter—that is, as the impeller toward the group of sense organs—that this transmigrating person, the cognizing subject (*pramātā*), exists and remains active. Just as...

Just as someone like Devadatta impels an insentient object such as a goad by means of an instrument such as his hand, this internal person does not, in the same way, set the insentient group of instruments into activity toward their respective objects through mere will; rather, it is through the touch of the power of the Self— that is, the Supreme Self.

The power or capacity belonging to the cognizer, the Lord who is the creator of all— which is the inherent nature itself, consisting in the ability to bring about all things independently of other causes—
by contact with that, by association with that, one would become equal to Him, to that Supreme Being denoted by the word "Self."

He becomes equal to the agent. This is the intended meaning here: precisely where the Supreme Lord—designated by the word "Self"—abiding in His own essential nature, is autonomous to bring about the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of this universe according to His will, it is in that very [nature]...

It has been stated that even this transmigrating person (saṃsārī), while remaining [as a limited subject], is independent in causing the group of instruments to engage with their respective objects; therefore, he would be equal to Him. Consequently, just as the Lord [is independent] through His two all-pervasive powers called knowledge and action, so too is the universe...
Just as [the intellect] brings about all activity and so forth, knowing and acting, so too the Puruṣa—
merely through contact with its power— possesses the capacities of knowledge and agency that have arisen, and by virtue of Māyā,
[acts] through the powers of knowledge and action which have specific objects.
Through the two [faculties] that have issued forth as the internal and external groups of instruments, he knows and acts upon his own objects; thus his similarity to them has been stated,
yet he does not impel the instruments by means of the impulse of desire.
This and so forth has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*). || 8 ||

But surely, by setting the group of instruments into operation within its own function, the Person (puruṣa) attains a sovereignty similar to that [of the Lord] through reaching the state of being the Lord; thus, would it not be established that there is indeed no difference between those two, the Lord and the Person? How [is this so]?
Has the similarity of the *puruṣa* to Īśvara, which is based on [their] difference, been established in that state? To this he says:
"Of one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desirous of his duties..."
When agitation is completely dissolved, then there shall be the supreme state.

Commentary: Furthermore, this contact with one’s own power (*ātmabala*) does not occur for one who, though desiring to act, is pervaded by innate impurity; rather, it occurs when the agitation [expressed as] "I am [the body, etc. (*ahamiti*) dissolves.
(Note: *gh* reads *kṣobho dehādyahamiti* as the corrected reading, and there is also a reading *pralīyate*.)
When that which has the nature of the state of being a condition dissolves for him, then he attains firm establishment in the supreme state. || 9 ||
Note: Although there is non-difference between the Lord and the individual soul due to the attainment of equality with the Supreme Lord,

the individual soul alone is characterized by impermanent and incomplete satisfaction because it is afflicted by impurities rooted in passion and the like, whereby it is rendered incapable of acquiring the means for attaining its goals.
The poverty of power is precisely what constitutes the semblance of equality with the Lord based on duality;
when there is the dissolution of the afflictions of Māyā, the state of identity with consciousness—which is non-figurative in its manifestation—is itself supreme purity. || 9 ||
Commentary: (p. 38) It is true that there is non-difference between these two in that state;
however, this person, by reason of his own innate impurity—the stain consisting of passion and so forth rooted in the identification of the self with the body and so on—[is not liberated].

He is full of longing, covetous for a mere fragment of momentary pleasure; yet, being poor in power and thus incapable of performing the necessary actions that serve as the means for attaining those very objects of desire— therefore, even though he wishes for it, he does not obtain what he desires— for such a person as this...
When, at that time, the agitation—

the illusory affliction consisting of the notion of "I" which takes as its object a specific body and so forth— is dissolved, [there arises] the sun of the natural notion of "I," which transcends artificial objects of perception.
Through contact with light, it would dissolve and perish like a mass of frost;
then the supreme, unsurpassed state (pada) or station would exist, manifesting as true being— namely,
the non-duality of the two consciousnesses, the higher and the lower, denoted by the terms "Self" (ātman) and "Person" (puruṣa), within that very [state].

The meaning is that [the Self] would manifest as something perceivable during its state of manifestation. This very point—that this [Self] is established in its own essential nature—is demonstrated by this verse.
Granted, in other philosophical systems, the impurity of this person may be established through various modes; however, here—

This [self] is precisely this much: that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) arises, established upon objects distinct from those [bodies and so forth], which are insentient by nature, non-eternal, and dependent;
for all conceptions of being a transmigrating being (saṃsāritva) have their basis solely in that [notion]. In that very [notion]...
When [all dualities] have dissolved, there is supreme purity, characterized by the manifestation of one's own true nature. As it has been said:
"When the island of the notion of a body has collapsed and unity is attained within the stainless ocean of consciousness..."
Without ever withdrawing the collection of your senses,
you, the inner Self of all, shine eternally as the one.
Likewise,
even though it were not dependent on a self, no one would be able to employ the universe at will, as one employs one's own hands and other limbs.
Like a child, [the world] fails to recognize its own power because you, who possess all power, abide within it; yet everyone is indeed omnipotent when you are within.
Thus, this has already been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words "And that [is] his," and so forth. (9)
But surely, the Self itself— whose agitation characterized by the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth has dissolved,
and which remains in a state of perfect tranquility like a windless ocean—
is what is designated by the term "supreme state"; so how can a person [be affected] by contact with its power?

One would encounter a property that is distinct from that [state] and consists precisely of agitation (*kṣobha*), by being joined with which the group of sense-faculties attains activity and so forth, and perceiving its own objects— thinking "I act" and "I know"— becomes truly agitated? Thus [it is asked].
In order to shatter the confusion of mind among those who do not know the self, he said:
"Then its dharma— characterized by knowledge and agency— would be uncreated."
For he knows and accomplishes everything that is desired by him. || 10 ||
Commentary: Because, at that time which consists of the dissolution of all agitation, there exists an uncreated, innate quality (*dharma*) whose nature is the state of being a knower and an agent;
therefore, at that very time when one has attained the self of yoga, whatever one desires to know, that very thing [is known].
He both knows and acts [at that time], and not otherwise during the state of transmigration. || 10 ||

Note: The single, non-deviating quality of the Self known as its status as the perceiver (*upalabdṛtva*) is an inseparable attribute (*ayutasiddha-guṇa*) consisting of the reflective awareness of its own nature; it is precisely this that is traditionally taught in a dual form as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "action" (*kriyā*), according to whether it has objects of knowledge or effects as its domain.
The unimpeded manifestation of the greatness of the attribute [of consciousness] is to be personally realized;

it is found solely in that locus characterized as the perceiver, wherein the powers of omniscience and omnipotence are fully unfolded, and which is untainted by the defilement of conceptual construction. For, therein—
Unrestrained sovereignty consists in the freedom [of consciousness] with respect to objects of knowledge, effects, and reflective awareness; however, that which—

in the state of transmigratory existence— consists of the notions of "knowing," "acting," and "I" regarding objects of cognition due to being deluded by non-recognition (akhyāti), is artificial and limited.

Because it possesses a state in which its autonomy is regulated, the attribute characterized by knowledge and agency is indeed its very nature (*svabhāva*) and not a state of agitation. Therefore, for that [nature] which is being conjoined with the functioning of effects— such as the activation of the wheel of instruments (*karaṇacakra*)— through the contact with its own power:
The perception of its similarity [to that]. || 10 ||

Commentary: (p. 41) At that time—meaning, at the time characterized by the aforementioned complete exhaustion of agitation—the attribute (*dharma*) consisting of the characteristics of knowledge and agency, which is uncreated, spontaneously established, and eternally non-distinct from this Self, certainly exists; this is the implied sense (*śeṣa*). For [it is] because...
From that unerring quality which serves as the cause, all desired objects—

whether as things to be known (*jñeya*) or as effects to be attained (*kārya*)— are obtained; at that time, in that state characterized by the union consisting of the connection with the nature of reality, that person [attains them], and not otherwise.

At other times—that is, during the state of the transmigrating person whose essence consists in the cognition of "I" supported by the body and so forth—he both knows and acts. What is meant? Knowledge, which is to say the status of being a perceiver (*upalabdhr̥tva*), is a quality of this Self that is non-distinct from it; and that [quality] belongs to an object determined as "this" (*idantā*). (p. 42)

Because it is twofold—consisting of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the effect (*kārya*)—it is figuratively designated as dual. In reality, however, there is only one power of the Lord, which consists of the reflective awareness of His own nature;
because it is of the nature of pure consciousness, it is expressed by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Because it consists solely of such intensity (*saṃrambha*), it is designated by the term "action" (*kriyā*). And this very nature (*dharma*) belongs to him who abides in a self-nature characterized solely as the knower (*vedaka*), untouched by the disturbance of the perception of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*); [this nature] exists through his omniscience and his omnipotence.

It unfolds. Furthermore, because there is an absence of such a reflective awareness of one's own nature, that which consists of the state of being a knower and an agent—based on the notion of a knower with respect to the body and other objects of knowledge—is artificial and limited in its scope. Therefore, [this is not the true nature] of the Self.

The state of being characterized by knowledge and agency, inseparable from its essential nature (*svabhāva*), is indeed the [true] nature itself, and not the state of agitation (*kṣobha*). And the transmigrating person, touching such innate power (*ātmabala*),
[acts] through the activation of the group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) and so forth, by means of knowledge and agency with respect to his own objects.
"What is stated—that one who is engaged [in yoga] becomes equal to that—is precisely what is established.
This very point the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) explains with the words beginning: "In that time which consists of the dissolution of agitation," and so forth. (10)
Having thus established the nature of the self through reasoning,
he says the following to demonstrate the fruit of its realization: "Beholding that very nature as the presiding subject..."
How could such a crooked path belong to one who remains as if smiling? || 11 ||

Commentary: Thus, since the nature of the Self is that which is woven through all things and endowed with all powers, therefore, for one who stands as if possessed by wonder while perceiving that very nature as the presiding principle and as all-pervasive, there is a miserable course of rebirth.
It does not become a refuge. || 11 ||

Note: For one who recognizes the presiding subjectivity— which, as the nature of Śiva established by logical proof, manifests through an uninterrupted continuity of time as a state of perpetual arising both internally and externally— [the following applies].
For one who reflects that "the state of being a subject under the influence of *māyā* is indeed non-existent because the knowledge of the true nature of Śiva has been forgotten,
appearing thus like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," there arises a state of wonder through the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of ever-new and unsurpassed excellence at every moment.
It rests upon the path of worldly experience; for upon its attainment, the agitation of the exertion of saṃsāra—which is bound to the limited notion of "I"—comes to rest. || 11 ||

Commentary: (p. 43) By the pronoun "that" (*tam*), the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) set forth in the ten verses is referred to. That very self-nature, characterized in such a way, [is present] as the presiding principle (*adhiṣṭhātṛbhāvena*) within all bodies, in all states, at all times, and everywhere.

Because he stands pervading everything as the mere experiencer, [the Lord] perceives himself in this form: "I alone am the independent Supreme Lord, the presiding subject who has nothing else to preside over"—
both by means of the aforementioned logical perspective and that which is about to be stated.

Beholding through the perspective of the teaching on perception, recognizing [the Self], and as if smiling at the recognition of the true nature of the Self— which had been forgotten as the supreme subject— he reflects upon the nature of the subject under the influence of *māyā*, which, though unreal, manifests in this manner.

For that yogin who, having attained a state of wonder as it were, experiences an undisturbed stability— such being his characteristic— this well-known crooked path, rooted merely in the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth, [ceases].

Because of the connection with the pairs of opposites such as birth, old age, and death, whence could there be a contemptible and censurable course— a wandering through various other wombs?— for there is an absence of that impurity which is the cause of the aforementioned agitation; the meaning is that, for one who is seated [in the Self], such a course does not exist at all, like the movement of one who is sitting still.
And this has been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the passage beginning with "Since this Self is indeed woven through all [beings]," and so forth. || 11 ||

Now, for the sake of awakening those who might think that because the reality of the Self— whose nature is devoid of all knowable attributes— is being presented as something to be attained, it must therefore be taught as a mere non-existence, he says:
Non-existence cannot be brought into being, nor is there any lack of delusion regarding it;
for, through contact with diligent application, there arises the certainty that "it existed. (12)
Commentary: (p. 11) However, non-existence is not to be cultivated in the manner taught by other yogis, namely: "One should cultivate non-existence until one attains identity with it.
This is not logical, because cultivation of non-existence is not appropriate for those who are deluded.
It is indeed that same [state], because at a later time, due to contact with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*)— [with variants reading *abhilāṣa* or "consisting of conjunction" (*saṃyogātmā*)]—
that state of emptiness is remembered as "mine," having passed away; and yet, this is not its own inherent nature (*ātmasvabhāva*).
For the nature of consciousness is not remembered as being like the state of delusion;
rather, its experience is ever-arisen because it is the experiencer at all times. || 12 ||
Note: Regarding the samādhi which consists in the cessation of the manifestation of both the object of knowledge and the knower, some consider it to be non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is not so, because [non-existence] cannot be cultivated [as an object], which would involve a contradiction.
Having attained firm establishment therein, the yogi, after emerging from the samādhi of non-existence, at a subsequent time...

By the reflection, "That state was experienced by me," that other state is brought to the condition of being remembered; that very remembrance at that time would reveal the existence of the experiencer as distinct [from the object],
such that the object being remembered is itself of the nature of non-existence (abhāva) to its own self.

It cannot exist [as an object], like pleasure and so forth, because it is that which makes [everything] knowable; therefore, the supreme nature, which is devoid of all the attributes of the knowable, is to be accepted. || 12 ||

Commentary: Non-existence (*abhāva*), which is the emptiness of entities (*vastuśūnyatā*), does not become, that is, does not attain the state of being an object of focus (*ālambanabhāva*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because there is a mutual contradiction between the cultivation of non-existence and the cultivation of existence. For existence... [p. 45] indeed...

An object capable of being the domain of consciousness is fit to become an objective support (*ālambana*) by way of being meditated upon; it is not, however, the case that "nothing" [is so]. As it has been taught in a certain place: "One should cultivate non-existence (*abhāva*) until one attains identity with it."

Thus it is said. Let it be that this state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consists in the cessation of the conceptual constructions of the meditator, the act of meditation, and the object of meditation—a state which those who have forgotten their true self consider to be "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Yet, in that particular state, there exists no lack of delusion (*amūḍhatā*), nor is there an absence of delusion (*mūḍhatvābhāva*).
Because of contact with the application [of memory], at the time of emergence,
through contact— that is, through the connection— with an expression arising at that very moment whose object is the recollection of such another state, that other state [is recalled].
"It was," "it existed in the past"— this would be a certainty, a firm conviction. What is meant by this?—
If a yogin who has attained stability in the samādhi of non-existence, having emerged from it, were not to reconnect with that state, how could he think, "I have attained stability"?

What would be its basis? And in the absence of that [basis], there would be no apprehension of the distinction between meditative absorption and emergence. Therefore, one necessarily remembers: "At that time, I experienced such a state. And this [remembrance] occurs precisely because it is remembered as something past.

The nature of the self is not impermanent, like pleasure and so forth; because that which is of the nature of consciousness exists at all times as the experiencer, it is impossible for it to be remembered by another rememberer. This has been explained in the Vṛtti.
"But non-existence is not to be cultivated," and so forth. || 12 ||
To clarify this, he says:
"Therefore, that [state] should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep;
however, that true reality (tattva) does not attain such a state of being remembered. (13)

Commentary: (p. 12) Even for one who has attained the stage through the cultivation of non-existence (*abhāva-bhāvanā*), that state is artificial and impermanent, as in the state of deep sleep; for the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*) is the very essence of the Self, eternally present, and it is precisely that which is to be constantly realized through the instruction of the Guru.
It is to be observed. || 13 ||

Commentary: Here it is said— just as the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is a dense mass of delusion consisting at that time in the non-apprehension of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, appears as if it were of the nature of non-existence, yet upon reaching the stage of awakening, it comes within the range of reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) and thus becomes an object of memory— so too [is the case here].

It is not impermanent. Likewise, even the state of the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*) is impermanent because it must be contemplated as having passed away at the time of awakening; such specific types of meditative absorptions are to be included within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and are not of such a nature as that which constitutes the very essence of the ultimate goal.

The reflective awareness that is pervaded by time is that which is to be remembered by another rememberer; for the supreme reality, being eternally arisen as the very nature of the cognizer, possesses a supreme existence that is constant and unchanging. || 13 ||

Commentary: (p. 46) Because it is designated as having been "existent" (*āsīt*) in the past, that entity known by the name "absorption in non-existence" (*abhāvasamādhi*) should be understood as artificial (*kṛtrima*), because it is associated with the states of both existence and non-existence; (p. 47) it should be recognized as impermanent (*anitya*), being produced by conceptual construction (*kalpanākṛta*).

There is never a single fraction of time (*kālakalā*) in which that state of meditative absorption (*samādhyavasthā*) does not abide eternally. How is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) to be understood as artificial? It is like the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*); "deep sleep" (*suṣupta*) itself is "pertaining to deep sleep" (*sauṣupta*), meaning the state of blissful slumber. That very [state]...
The "foot" (pada) is the substratum; it is similar to that. What is meant?

Just as the worldly state of deep sleep, because its nature consists of dense delusion, is as if non-existent even while the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower exists, since that distinction is not apprehended at that time.

Being brought within the scope of subsequent reflection that arises at the time of awakening, it is impermanent because it is remembered as something past; likewise, the state of absorption into non-existence is also impermanent, due to the commonality of being remembered as having occurred at the time of emergence from meditation. By this, all [other states] are [explained].

It has been established that meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of this kind are included within the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) alone; however, that reality— which is the very essence characterized by one's own true nature (*svasvabhāva*)— has not been taught here as something most worthy of being adopted in the manner described.

It attains the state of being remembered, for since it is eternally risen, it is always present. This is so even for one who has attained the stage of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the cultivation of non-existence.
This has been explained in detail in the Vṛtti by the words beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth). || 13 ||
Now, although that reality is thus always manifest because it is eternally emergent,
it is the cause of bondage because it is not recognized; therefore, by one who has received the instruction,
in all states—
In order to instruct him in that reality— that the entire manifold of the universe is comprised within the dual reality of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*),
and that one must internalize it by reflecting upon the aspect of the knower as "I," which indeed transcends the nature of all objects of knowledge—
[the following is said].
In order to demonstrate the dual nature manifested through the power of his own *māyā*, he says:
"And here, the pair of states is designated as 'the state of being the effect' and 'the state of being the agent';
therein, the state of being the effect is perishable, whereas the state of being the agent is imperishable. (14)

Commentary: (p. 13) Regarding the "pair of states" (*avasthāyugalama*): [The reading *avasthāyugalama iti vākyaṃ nāsti* is absent in manuscripts k and g. The two states themselves are designated as "the object of action" (*kārya*) and "the agent of action" (*kartṛ*), and are distinguished by the duality of the "enjoyed" (*bhogya*) and the "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*).
Among these, that distinction which takes the form of the enjoyed arises and perishes; however, the distinction of the enjoyer... (manuscript kh).
Furthermore, that which has the nature of the enjoyer, being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), is never born and never perishes; therefore, it is eternal.

Note: This is what is intended here by the word "state" (avasthā). In reality, there exists everywhere only one independent Supreme Lord. He alone, through the unfolding of the power of His own sovereignty as the unconditioned and unrestrained Self, [manifests].
Having manifested its own two-fold nature—which is devoid of any external substratum—it sports.

This duality consists of being both object and agent, by means of which the reality is grasped in its two distinct aspects as that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be accepted. Among these, the state of being the object is as follows:
Dependent on the light of another, it is incapable of remaining without a perceiver;
therefore, because it consists of the unfolding of power (*śāktollāsa*), it reveals its own nature as non-different from that [perceiver].
The limitation of being an object (*kāryatā*) is merely transitory and soon dissolves, whereas the persistence of the state of agency (*kartṛtā*) remains.

Because its essential nature is solely that of the ever-arisen and undeluded power of vision, it is indestructible. Thus, for those who meditate upon the Self—which is self-evident, transcendent beyond darkness, and preceded by the realization of the manifestation of the entire universe as projected by one's own *māyā*—there occurs, in all states of existence, the cessation of the cause of bondage. 14.

Commentary (p. 48): Here, in this supreme reality called the Self (*ātman*) which has been explained, two states (*avasthā*) are possible. By means of this, [one understands] the distinctions between the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, which have been established through the systems of various philosophical schools (*darśana*).

Even though the reality consisting of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted is infinite, it is presented as being comprised of only two [categories] due to its connection with the two characteristics; the meaning is that, despite the infinity of the world's diversity, there are only two principles.
However, the Supreme Lord alone—the Self—is ultimately real and peerless.

The term "state" (*avasthā*) is employed to demonstrate that [the Lord], by virtue of His own sovereign power and strength—which are unobstructed and free from grasping—sports while manifesting Himself as a duality; the meaning is that this single reality exists in a dual state. Of what nature is it?
What is the pair of states? That which is designated as "the state of being an agent and the state of being an effect.

One state is independent, characterized by agency, enjoyership, the state of being a knower, and the nature of consciousness, expressed as "I. The second, however, is its opposite: it consists of effects, is an object of enjoyment, is knowable, insentient, and dependent. By these two...

"Śabdita" means "designated. By the word "śabdita," it is established that there is only a difference in the mere designation (*saṃjñāmātra*) of these two, and not a real one. Therefore, this state which consists of the effect, because its very nature is obtained solely through being manifest, [is non-different] from the Self, the supreme cause.

It does not differ from that which is designated by the word "agent" (kartṛ), whose sole nature is luminosity; for this reality has already been established as the source of its own manifestation, which consists of the wheel of powers (śakticakra). In those two such states, the state of being an effect (kāryatā) is perishable.

The state of being in the form of an effect is subject to momentary destruction; whatever is determined as having the nature of an effect precisely because of its lack of reflection upon the true reality, all that is perishable at every moment due to its connection with arising and passing away— this is agency.

Furthermore, it is imperishable; its state as the agent is eternal because it possesses the sole attribute of being the perceiver that pervades all states which are eternally manifest. Thus, it is indeed one—the agent, the knower, and the constant presiding authority over all.
The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: for one who remains identifying [the world] as the Self, bondage is logically impossible. This very point constitutes the two states.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth). || 14 ||
( p. 51) Now, an objection is raised: "It has been stated that the reality which is the nature of the perceiver is imperishable;

however, that is not tenable at all, because in the states of non-existence and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the essential nature of the perceived object is absent. How, then, can it be imperishable?"—thus the objection.
He states the resolution previously promised:
"Only that effort which is directed toward an object is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, 'I am destroyed. (15)

Commentary: Only the capacity for accomplishing an effect, which consists in the activity of the external organs, is lost. When that capacity is lost in one whose senses are restrained, the ignorant person thinks, "My very nature (the word *me* is supplied from manuscript *gh*) has been lost."
One knows [this], but there is no destruction of the entity. || 15 ||

Note: That eagerness for outward expansion— the inclination to manifest externally by means of the innate power of upward-striving (*sahajodyamanaśakti*) through the very act of leaning toward the object of knowledge (*vedyonmukhatā*), thereby delineating the manifold variety of the universe— is nothing other than the sense organ (*indriya*).
At the stage when activity has ceased, [the self] is dissolved within itself due to its non-manifestation;

at that state of non-manifestation, the unawakened person has this reflection, "I am not," and thus he considers it his own nature; he does not realize that, on the contrary, this is merely the reflection of non-existence.

Because one stabilizes one's own self by means of its being the witness of that [state], therefore, even though it is temporarily unperceivable during states such as non-existence (abhāva) and meditative absorption (samādhi), one must never infer the perishability of the Self. || 15 ||

Commentary (p. 51): When directed toward an object that is to be produced, fashioned, or known, the effort (*prayatna*) which is inclined toward its accomplishment in that manner—that innate exertion (*utsāha*) consisting of agency (*kartṛtva*)—is alone, and nothing else, the supreme cause, the cause of the operation (*vyāpāra*), in that [activity].

Because of the absence of the gross form of the effect during the state of dissolution (*laya*), it is withdrawn; remaining unmanifested, it persists as if submerged within the Self itself. When that effort has been dissolved at that very moment, the ignorant person—devoid of the realization of reality—conceives: "I am annihilated."

Such a cognition arises precisely for one who delimits the object by way of its being distinct from the notion "I am"; if it indeed delimits [the object], then since it exists as an agent even prior to that, being already established, how could it be the object of negation? Thus, this follows:

For example, suppose Devadatta, staying at home or elsewhere, is called by someone, "O Devadatta! and, wishing to conceal himself, replies, "I am not here. When this is said, on the contrary, it is established that "I am present," and not that he is absent.

Therefore, since there is an absence of effects during states such as the meditative absorption on non-existence (*abhāva-samādhi*), the cognition of the self's non-existence— which arises merely from the cessation of the activity of the instruments— is nothing but an error.
This has been explained in the *Vṛtti*.
"By means of the capacity for accomplishing the task," and so forth. || 15 ||
To further clarify this very point, he says:
"But as for that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience, its loss could never occur, because nothing else is perceived. (16)
Commentary: However, there is never the destruction of that which is inward-turned, whose nature is mounted upon the inner wheel, and which is the locus of qualities such as omniscience;
therefore, because there is no second or other [entity], its very own nature, like space, consists of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
It experiences [the result] everywhere. || 16 ||
Note: The single power of the Supreme Lord, at the commencement of assuming limitation, manifests itself as twofold;
following the emergence of the dyad of knowledge and action, it reaches the state that is extremely proximate [to the individual soul].

Having withdrawn its own form— which has become manifold through the cultivation of states such as the contraction [of consciousness]— from its dependence on the nature of the internal and external organs, it [rests] within itself,
which is of expansive extent and resembles the stainless sky, in the fullness of its own self-experience.

One tastes the wonder [of that state]. In that state, because there is no object of knowledge with a distinct grammatical case-ending, the disappearance of the inward-turned reality—which is impossible to conceive for those deluded ones who perceive it as either grasping or not grasping external objects of knowledge—is [actually] occurring; or else, this refers to the fourth quarter [of the verse].

The application [of the argument] is by way of its being the cause, because if the essential nature of the perceiver were to vanish, the entire universe would become as if blind and mute, and even worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be cut off.
Commentary: But this is not so for that supreme reality (*tattva*), which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*). (p. 53)
At some time, within any fraction of time characterized by meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth,

there would follow a lapse— that is, the destruction of one's own nature— because no other impermanent object consisting of the knowable, distinct from that [nature], is perceived, as there is an absence of experience thereof. It is not [the case that such a lapse occurs].

Indeed, it can be said that there is no object of knowledge (*vedya*) and no knower (*vedaka*). Of what, then, would there not be a cessation (*lopa*)? That state called the Self (*ātman*), whose face—that is, whose power of cognition (*jña-śakti*)—is turned inward because of the absence of any external object of knowledge distinct from itself; such is that being.

The reality [of the self], because it is the locus of the quality of omniscience—the unique substratum for the attribute consisting in the state of being the knower of the entire range of knowable objects. This is the intended meaning here: of the self...
That power, which is twofold by way of the distinction between knowledge and action, remains in the state of the *puruṣa*— when the operations of the internal and external organs have ceased—
as nothing but the power of knowing directed solely toward its own pure self; therefore...
It has been stated that "the state is inward-facing" (*antarmukho bhāvaḥ*). Furthermore, the use of the word *mukha* for "power" (*śakti*) is observed, as in the *Pārameśvara*:
"The face of Śiva (*śaivīmukha*) is spoken of here."
In such passages as these, there exists, at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*),
the presence of a state that cannot otherwise be accounted for. That state,
characterized by the mere delusion of not perceiving external objects, is designated as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) by those yogins.

It does not undergo [cessation]; for how could the cessation of that state—which possesses an ever-unimpaired power of cognition—be possible, since no entity distinct from its own nature is perceived? For at that time, it is indeed its very nature, like the stainless expanse of the sky, which is entirely distinct and all-pervading.

One experiences [reality] as being of the nature of pure consciousness (*citmātra*), yet, due solely to being under the sway of delusion (*moha*), one does not realize it as such because one has forgotten the nature of the self that connects [all things]. However, the Awakened One realizes it exactly as it is; the means by which this is realized will be taught below. This has been explained.
But this is not so, as stated in the commentary [vṛtti] beginning with "he who is inward-turned, mounted upon the inner wheel," and so forth. || 16 ||
Thus ends the first outflow, titled "Instruction on the Proof of Differentiation," in the Spandakārikā-ṭīkā known as the Vivṛti, composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāma. || 1 ||
Commentary: Now,
as for what is called "the perception of a distinct nature":
The second is the outflow.

Thus, having established through reasoning based on one's own experience the reality of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, as was promised, it is now the occasion for the instruction on the means of perceiving that [Self].

Within the threefold worldly system—distinguished as the well-awakened, the awakened, and the unawakened—who, for now, is the fit recipient for this instruction? To establish the scope of the subject matter, he says:
"The perception of that [Reality] is constant and never deviates from the three states."
For one who is perfectly awakened, it is eternal; for another, however, it exists at the beginning and the end. (2.1 [17])

Commentary: The perception of that all-pervading nature, which is of the form of consciousness, occurs eternally for one who is perfectly awakened throughout the three states beginning with waking; likewise, it occurs at the beginning and end of those states for another who is awakened during dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth; [and] in the waking and the fourth state (*turya*).

Regarding the phrase "accessible through scripture alone" (*āgamamātragamye*): the reading is *svapnasuṣuptyādau jāgratturyayostvāgamamātragamyā* (in the states of dream, deep sleep, etc., waking and the fourth state are accessible through scripture alone). [The two states] are accessible through scripture alone. *Commentary:* [These refer respectively] to the object that is pure consciousness transcending all, and the object that is the wheel of powers consisting of the universe.

Since the two-fold teaching— consisting of that which is undertaken and that which is consummated— is generally useless for those who are not awakened, because for one who is well-awakened, the realization of one's own Self is accomplished without effort within the three stages; for indeed, in the case of the awakened one, [the goal] resides in two stages.
For one who reflects upon the nature of the witness during the state of waking,
there is the realization of the essential nature as pure consciousness— transcending the universe and free from all taints—
which is to be recollected in deep sleep and is also accessible through the dream state.

The effortless realization of one’s own Self— the abode of universal agency, independent of any other cause, and characterized by the radiance of the manifestation of the universe— is accomplished without strain. However, the unawakened person does not perceive the supreme reality being taught, even through thousands of logical arguments.

It is capable of making [the truth] reach the heart; therefore, regarding the remaining two stages, there is a need for instruction on the supreme reality (paratattva), which is difficult to understand due to its being remote and unfamiliar. Thus, the determination of the subject matter of instruction applies solely to the awakened one alone. || 17 ||

Commentary: The realization, experience, and non-conceptual apprehension of that very Self who has been described as the Supreme Lord is constant— at all times and in every state of experience— for one who is "well-awakened," meaning perfectly awakened.

For one who has realized the goal and possesses right vision, whose consciousness is not obstructed even slightly by the great sleep of delusion—which consists of the long, nightmare-like dream of the "I-notion" regarding the body and so forth—it is possible; that is, it is logically established. Of what nature is this [vision]? It is constant, uninterrupted, and never deviating from the three states.
In the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— these stages of consciousness—
it is unerring and non-contradictory, for it is never overwhelmed by any condition; thus, its presence is immediate for this one who is perfectly awakened.
For one who has attained the supreme perfection characterized by mastery over his own self, there is indeed no subject matter for instruction here,
because he has already accomplished all that was to be done. As for the other— the second type of awakened person—
his darkness of *māyā* is being dispelled by the light of dawn brought about by the descent of the supreme power (*para-śaktipāta*).
For those whose eye of clear discernment is opening and whose power of delusion is waning—
such that the abundance of the impulse toward delusion no longer expands—
the state that constitutes the beginning of those three stages, namely waking and the others, at their initial point.

The two stages included within that [waking state], namely those called dream and deep sleep, are of the nature of the waking state; therein, the realization of that reality of the Self (ātmatattva) may occur.
According to the intention of the author of the *Vṛtti*, the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound beginning and ending with "that" (*tad-ādi-tad-anta-pada*) has been made in this manner.
Since [this occurs] in states such as dreaming and deep sleep, this word has been explained by him; and here, by the word "etc. (ādi),...

The inclusion of states such as memory and delusion, which are subsumed under the states of dreaming and deep sleep, is intended here. And this is the underlying intention of the commentary: that in this context, a twofold instruction regarding the perception of the reality of the Self has been introduced and must be carried through to completion; one [is as follows].
One has as its object the true nature of pure consciousness alone, transcending everything;

the other has as its object that wheel of powers (śakticakra) which constitutes the soul of the universe. Even though this instruction is of both these forms, it is generally of no use to one who is awakened even in these two states of deep sleep and dreaming.
It is like the three steps of one who is perfectly awakened, because the realization of reality is accomplished without effort;

for, by the mere reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of consciousness abiding in these two states, the realization of the supreme reality as it has been explained occurs spontaneously for him. (p. 58)

For instance, when, upon awakening, one reflects upon the state of deep sleep— which is partless (*niṣkalā*) because all conceptualizations of objects of knowledge have dissolved— one then perceives that which is merely the eternal, undeluded cognizer resting solely within its own nature, free from all objective coloring (*uparāga*).
He perceives the self-nature, the reality of the Self, by himself alone; and when,

even in the absence of various distinct individual causes, he [perceives] that which consists of the manifestation of a wheel of diverse states— both sentient and insentient— which appear with extreme clarity.
Being awakened, he reflects upon his own state of dreaming;
then, by that very same analogy, through the power of awakening, [he perceives] the Supreme Lord, whose very nature is the ultimate cause.

One perceives that reality which consists in the state of being the agent of all things, independent of any cause other than one's own mere will. However, for one who is unawakened, even when this [reality] is offered with hundreds of efforts, it produces no internal contact, like the water-dissolved essence of a gourd. Thus it is.
It is established that for one who is awakened, perception occurs within these two states;
by implication, it is stated that such perception does not exist for him in the remaining two states called waking and the fourth (*turya*).
Therefore, in the waking state...

The supreme reality is obscured by the activities of the senses, which are preoccupied with grasping objects such as sound; furthermore, because it transcends the world, it is utterly unfamiliar in the fourth state (turyāvasthā) and difficult to perceive even for oneself.
Therefore, even one who is awakened to it requires instruction in order to apprehend it.
For this reason, the author of the Vṛtti said: "The waking state and the fourth state (turya), however, are accessible through scripture alone."
The author of the commentary has explained this by means of the passage beginning with "of that which is of the nature of consciousness and all-pervading. || 1 ||

Having thus established the scope of the instruction, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the differentiation within all four states— waking and the rest— of the supreme reality (pārameśvara-tattva), which exists in two modes: as being transcendent to everything and as possessing all forms.

Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the all-pervading Lord shines in two states; elsewhere, however, He is composed solely of consciousness. (2.2, 18)

Commentary: In the two states consisting of waking and dreaming, consciousness exists in a dual form through the distinction between the knower and the known; however, in the two states consisting of deep sleep and the fourth (turya), there is only the experience of the nature of pure consciousness, and not a second thing as something other.
It is perceived. || 18 ||

Note: The Supreme Lord Himself, manifesting through the power of His own *māyā-śakti* in the form of various individual subjects (*kṣetrajña*), [perceives] the supreme power distinct from Himself within the two states known as waking and dreaming, [as well as] the internal organs, pleasure, and so forth.
And by manifesting through external instruments such as blue and so forth, it brings about the linguistic usage corresponding to those respective states;

however, this alone constitutes the transcendence of power—that which flashes forth with infinite majesty without obstructing the light of Śiva. But in the states of deep sleep and the Fourth (turya), however—
Because there is no object of cognition that is differentiated or distinct from Him, it is the Lord alone who shines forth, His powers having become one in essence within His own self.
The distinction between the first two terms arises from the conceptual differentiation regarding whether entities are perceived as stable or unstable. In the other case...

The distinction in the four states arises from the presence or absence of the wonder of the perceiver within that which is pure consciousness; thus, there is the unfolding of light as both transcending all things and assuming all forms. 18.

Commentary (p. 60): The all-pervasive Lord, the Self whose form is pure consciousness, shines endowed with His own power—that is, accompanied by His capacity—which is supreme because it is of an exceedingly wondrous nature and surpasses all else, within the two states designated as waking and dreaming.
It shines; it manifests. By what kind of power? By that which has the nature of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known—namely, the external and internal circle of instruments consisting of grasping, or pure consciousness itself. The "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) is that which is to be grasped, such as sound and so forth.

And pleasure and so forth constitute a class of objects with infinite distinctions; she whose very nature consists of that is "tathā" (such), by her. What is meant?—the Supreme Lord himself, through the power of his own *māyā*, appearing in the form of various individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), [perceives] his own [nature], which is non-different from him.
Manifesting the supreme power (*parā śakti*) through the state of both knowledge and the object of knowledge,
it brings forth the worldly activity of the waking and dreaming states; and this indeed is the supremacy of this power— that which [manifests] its own nature as sovereign majesty.

Not obscuring its state of luminosity, it manifests as consisting of both knowledge and the object of knowledge through its infinite forms. However, within the darkness of *māyā*— which consists merely in the non-manifestation of non-duality—
the single ultimate reality shines forth, free from the delusion of the distinction between knower, knowledge, and the known.

Reality is held to be of the singular nature of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśaikarūpa*), characterized by the power of the attribute consisting solely in being the experiencer of such an innate nature; for it is said elsewhere: "But that [reality] consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Therefore, from that which has been described as such—

Apart from these two states, in the other two states designated as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the fourth (*turya*), the all-pervasive Lord shines as consciousness; He is the Self (*ātman*), the Lord (*īśvara*), whose nature is that of the perceiver (*upalabdhṛ-svabhāva*),
having that [consciousness] alone as His material cause (*prakṛti*), because there is no object of cognition distinct from those two states.
The meaning is that the Lord alone shines forth, his power resting solely within his own partless self-nature.

Now, an objection may be raised: since waking and dreaming consist of both cognition and the cognizable, while deep sleep and the fourth state (turya) shine forth as consisting of consciousness alone, there is no difference between them; thus, there would be only two states.

How, then, are there four stages? To this it is replied: there is a distinction between the waking and dreaming stages caused by the conceptualization of their respective objects as stable or unstable; thus, those two constitute a pair. This is because the creation imagined by the Lord appears with stability during the waking state. (p. 62)

One proceeds [in this way], but in a dream, because of its lack of firmness, it is merely imagined by the knower of the field (kṣetrajña); this is the cause of distinction between these two states. In the state of deep sleep, however, although the reality whose nature is pure consciousness exists, it appears as if non-existent due to the absence of the wonder of the perceiver—the sense of "I"—under the influence of delusion.
However, the perception of that very reality as the Self by way of ultimate existence occurs in the fourth state (*turyapada*);

this is the distinction between deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and the fourth state. Therefore, there are exactly four states, well-known in other scriptures under such designations as Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya.

This has been explained in the commentary [vṛtti] by the passage beginning with "it has two forms through the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge" (jñānajñeyabhedena dvirūpam). || 2 ||

Now, in order to further establish that only one who has awakened is fit to be instructed in the manner just described, and to exclude those who are unawakened from that status, he speaks these three verses.

The outflows of the vibration of qualities and so forth, by virtue of resting upon the general vibration, constantly attain their own existence and do not constitute obstacles for the Knower. (2/3, 19)

Commentary: (p. 17) Those outflows, which are the currents of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, even though they have issued forth by depending upon the general vibration, would—for the knower, the yogi who has known what is to be known—be constantly such that they do not become obstacles. They remain non-obstructive.
They do not conceal their own nature. || 19 ||
Note: For one who, through the power of the Lord’s grace,

has developed the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted in the present moment, and who, relying on non-conceptual stability, practices the desire to ascend to the highest state through the combined cultivation of right reasoning, scripture, logic, and personal effort.
The streams of cognitions— such as pleasure, pain, and delusion— of the knower,

presided over by Khecarī and the other powers, attain their own established state only by relying upon the vibration of the universe embraced within them, which is the manifestation of supreme power; this occurs through the emergence of the potency of one's own self.
The intended meaning is that those whose power of obscuration has dissolved would be unable to obstruct the perception of the supreme reality. || 19 ||
But these [beings] of unawakened intellect, striving to conceal their own true state, cast others onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross. (2/4, 20)

Commentary: But for those of very slight awakening— having caused the obstruction of their own stable state, which is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)— those qualities cast them down onto this difficult-to-cross,
treacherous path of saṃsāra, because they [mistakenly] perceive the Self, which is eternally of that very nature, as being [identical with] that [the qualities].
They see [it], but not as the pure nature of the Buddha. || 20 ||

Note: The unawakened person, not recognizing the reality of *spanda*—the locus of qualities such as omniscience—which constitutes his own existing sovereignty, identifies entirely with the body and other such things that are utterly dependent on others as being the Self. For this very reason, there is the outward expansion of the qualities of [limited] knowledge.

Having concealed the state of the Supreme Self, [avidyā] continues to whirl the unawakened one in the stream of birth and so forth until the attainment of awakening; therefore, the firm conviction that only the awakened person is fit for instruction is established, while regarding the unawakened, there are injunctions and prohibitions—this is the essential meaning. || 20 ||
Therefore, one who is constantly engaged in the discernment of the reality of *spanda* attains their own true nature before long, even while remaining awake. (2/5) *Note:
The reading "bhāvamacireṇa" has been corrected to "bhāvam acireṇa" according to the variant in manuscript gh.*
(* Vivṛti: "He attains the state of being [Bhāva] before long.

[Vṛtti: Therefore, he who constantly, at all times, exerts effort for the sake of manifesting the essential nature of the *spanda* principle, even while in the waking state alone, [realizes] his own innate...
One attains the nature known as the enjoyment of the fourth state (turyabhogākhya) in a very short time;
[this is] because of the reason indicated in the verse under discussion:
for one who is awakened, due to their own ultimate reality (paramārthasattā).
The meaning is that realization occurs without any delay whatsoever. || 21 ||

Commentary: (p. 63) Therefore, for the reason specified in the three verses of the present exposition, one who is already awake—that is, enlightened—attains his own state, his own ultimate reality, in a short time, that is, within a very brief period, through perfect realization.
He accepts [this]. By the word "only" (*eva*), he excludes the unawakened.

Being of what nature does he attain [it]?—one who is constantly striving for the discernment of the reality of *spanda*, that is, the supreme *śākta* reality, which, by virtue of its nature as a conventional unity of the universal and the particular...

For the sake of discerning— that is, for the sake of distinguishing and isolating— the reality (*tattva*) which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whose nature is determined respectively as that which is to be adopted and that which is to be abandoned,
this [work] is the most excellent means of adoption.

The general vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) is one's own innate nature (*nijo dharmaḥ*), consisting of the reflective awareness: "I am this very Self, which is the ultimate cause and the true reality; from this everything originates, and into this alone it dissolves. Likewise, these particular vibrations (*viśeṣaspandāḥ*) are to be utterly abandoned.

In those things such as the body which are not the self, those who manifest the conceit of "I" have as their objects the limited subjects of māyā who are mutually distinct; the resulting streams of cognition consisting of the qualities (guṇas)—such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth—are the causes of saṃsāra. Thus.
Constantly and without interruption, he is devoted to discernment in all circumstances;
because his own strength is augmented by the realization of the means for attaining the logical proofs already stated and those yet to be explained, he is possessed of unimpeded enthusiasm.

[Having resolved with unimpeded enthusiasm. By this, it is established that only one who is awakened and solely intent on the cultivation of the means attains his true nature before long, and no other.
For what reason does he alone attain it and not another? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the outflows of the vibration of the qualities, etc.," the grammatical connection is as follows: since the outflows of the vibration of the qualities and so forth would not be obstacles for the knower. Here, "vibrations" (*spandānām*) refers to the powers of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), such as knowledge and the rest; "outflows" (*niḥṣyandāḥ*) [refers to their manifestations].
The various streams of cognition, which have issued forth by being directed toward manifold objects, are diverse modifications that flow from vibration (*spanda*).
Those whose primary element is the *guṇas* and so forth are "the *guṇas* and so forth";
they consist of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, having pleasure and the rest as their nature. And these are the *guṇas* and so forth.

The outflows of vibration (*spanda-niṣyanda*)—such as the various cognitions "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I am deluded"—what is their nature? They have acquired their own existence by relying upon the universal vibration (*sāmānya-spanda*). Of that universal...

By virtue of taking refuge— meaning by resorting to and worshiping— the Supreme One, who is all-pervasive, whose infinite particular vibratory movements are withdrawn within, and who is the manifestation of power;
and because of having attained self-existence, meaning that [existence] has been acquired and reached through various distinct forms.

Those qualities and so forth, which are the outpourings of the vibration [of consciousness], are such because they possess the attainment and arising of one's own true nature; this refers to the knower whose state as a subject has arisen through the grace of the Supreme Lord, characterized by the discernment of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.

From the particular vibrations (*viśeṣaspanda*), which possess mutually distinct forms produced by the coloring of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as pleasure and so forth, [the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) alone] is established as the primary power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) through the realization of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) state arising from the grace of the Supreme Lord.
For one who has turned away from the conceit of their own power,
who desires victory through constant effort in the practice of the reasonings already stated and those yet to be stated,
there would be no adversaries due to the manifestation of their own strength.

Having their power to obscure the essential nature obstructed, they would become without opposition; that is to say, they would not be able to destroy the zeal for the realization of the supreme reality.
This is the intended meaning here: whatever [obstacles] belong to anyone whatsoever within the realm of Māyā...

Because the knower consists of pleasure and the rest, all those outpourings (*niḥṣyanda*) consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*), which are the continuations of mental impressions (*pratyaya-saṃdhāna*), proceed by depending upon that single universal vibration (*sāmānya-spanda*); they thus attain their respective individual natures. [This is] for one who is awakened.

However, he is a vessel for the wisdom that realizes their arising; therefore, while he remains constantly diligent, these [afflictions] are unable to become active practitioners [within him]. But for those whose intellects are unawakened, these [afflictions] have an irresistible flow; thus he says: "But for those of unawakened intellect," and so forth—"unawakened."

Those whose intellect (*dhī*)—that is, their wisdom (*prajñā*)—is such that the deep sleep of ignorance has not been dispelled due to the absence of the supreme grace of the Lord; furthermore, for them, these aforementioned outpourings of the vibration of the *guṇas* and so forth are "terrible" (*ghore*), because they are crowded with hundreds of terrifying apparitions. Therefore...

Thus, they cause one to fall upon the path of saṃsāra—which is difficult to cross and hard to traverse, a road consisting of a continuous succession of births and so forth—and they cause one to wander there incessantly. Being of what nature? They are intent on concealing their own abiding state within themselves, that is, within the Supreme Self (paramātman).

In that which has as its sole activity the mere vibration of the universal, there is a firm and stable foundation arising from non-conceptual realization; when that [foundation] is obstructed— that is, immediately covered—
efforts are exerted because of the absence of awakening, which is its opposite.
They are thus metaphorically designated precisely because they have obtained the opportunity for expansion. What is meant?

Just as certain kings and others, due to states such as negligence, do not perceive their own actual power—such as that of their armies—as being present, while those who watch for an opportunity [seek to exploit them].

The opposing factors, being intent on depriving [the Self] of its own state, cast it into great calamity until the realization of the actual existence of its own power occurs. Thus, for one who is unawakened, there is [attachment to] its own greatness— characterized by universal agency and so forth— which consists of the nature of the common vibration.

For one who, though possessing [the true Self], fails to awaken and perceives the very creation of the body and so forth— which is dependent on all causal factors— as the Self, these streams of cognitions such as "I am happy," which consist of primary and secondary qualities, gain their scope and find no stability in the real Self.
They continue to undergo transmigratory existence until the attainment of awakening;

thus, it is only those who are awakened who are the proper objects of this teaching, not those who are unawakened. For even if the words of the teaching are somehow grasped by the latter, [they do not comprehend its true meaning].
Because their wisdom is weakened by a practice that lacks definitive certainty, it does not find rest within; as it has been said by someone:
"Even when it has entered the heart, the state of being an object of knowledge does not take root."
Can words of instruction avail those whose minds are utterly deluded?
Do showers from the clouds, even when clinging closely and without interval, impart moisture to lotus petals that remain suspended in the sky?
Thus [it is said]. Regarding that,
the passage from the *Vṛtti* states "only in the waking state," whereas according to the context, it should be understood as "in the awakened state."
It should be understood as follows: if, by means of the term "constantly striving" (*satatodyukta*), the state of being awakened (*prabuddha*) is accepted,

then one who is constantly striving and awakened attains his own true nature through the sequence of instruction to be described, even while in the waking state— that is, during the very condition of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).

—thus it should be explained. This triad of verses has been explained in detail with its divisions in the *Vṛtti* by means of the passage beginning with "he who performs [it] constantly, at all times," and so forth. Likewise,
By the phrase "of the vibration of qualities (guṇaspanda) consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas," and so forth; likewise,
[it refers to] those of meager understanding.
By such passages as these [in the text]. 3, 4, 5.
Thus, having established that it is only for one who is awakened that the states of waking and the fourth (turya) are to be taught,
[the author] speaks in order to first instruct on the perception of the supreme reality, which is indeed merged within the intermediate waking state common to all embodied beings:
Whether one is extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or while reflecting "What shall I do?", or while running—wherever the foot goes, there vibration is established. (2/6, 22)

Commentary: And when that *spandatattva* is possessed by such thoughts as "What shall I do? while one is extremely angry, overjoyed, or running about, and there occurs the disappearance of [objective] power (*śakti*), then the emergence of the *spandatattva* must be clearly realized through the instruction of the Guru. || 22 ||

Note: Even when facing extremely intense calamities, the sight of poison, and so forth; or when experiencing the restoration of the dead to life, union with a beloved, and the like; or when confronted by powerful adversaries and engaged in deliberating upon the means of counteracting them—[in all these cases], it is because the mental fluctuations remain without any objective support (*nirālambana*).

The perception of the established vibration (*spanda*) of the emergent stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which arises even prior to the production of the specific material causes that manifest various forms of joy and so forth, occurs in this way;
likewise, there is an immersion into the nature of the Lord (*aiśvararūpasamāveśa*) even during the particular activities of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). || 22 ||

Commentary (p. 70): Since vibration (*spanda*) is twofold, being established or unestablished according to the distinction between the universal and the particular, the connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "the vibration that is to be accepted, which is established, is perceived in that state. As for which...

Established as the cause for the designation of mobility, yet characterized by an unshakable state because it is not an object of specific, impermanent fluctuations such as pleasure and so forth, the primary vibration is of a universal nature, supported solely by its own intrinsic essence.

He whose nature is that of the Supreme Self, in whom the entire cycle of specific powers has completely subsided, is to be characterized there—in that very state which is being pointed out right now. In what [state]?
That state which one who is intensely enraged might enter, [even when facing] immediate, fresh, and terrible calamities.

One who is seized by an extremely intense anger through the sight of an enemy and so forth— attaining, even before the state of physical transformation produced by that [anger] has arisen, that very state or stage (*pada*) which is reached or attained by the mind as soon as the anger is born; likewise, one who is exceedingly delighted, reaches that same state.
Delighted by the sight of women and others who have risen from death as if their life-breath had returned—
delighted with a supreme, most excellent, and extraordinary joy, overflowing with bliss—
