he should go to that state in which joy arises the very moment he reaches it, thinking, "What shall I do? (p.)

71) *mṛśan yat padaṃ gacchet*: When one is assailed by an angry king or a powerful enemy and finds no resolution for counteraction, being utterly bewildered as to what to do or what means to employ—thinking only, "What shall I do? What recourse shall I take here?"—that is the state of one who is lost in his course of action.
The meaning is that by touching and conceptualizing, one who has a mental state devoid of objective support (*nirālambana-cittavṛtti*) should abide in whichever stage (*bhūmikā*);

therein, there is the perception of the vibration (*spanda*) established [in that state]. By these three modes, the waking state—which consists of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of grasping objects characterized by suffering, pleasure, and delusion—[is explained].

It should be understood that other such varieties are included by means of the very scope of the states [of emotion]. Therefore, just as one who is extremely enraged, even one who is overcome with extreme grief due to causes such as hearing of the destruction of an unsuspected beloved person, [is to be represented] even before the physical transformations indicative of grief, such as the shedding of tears and loss of consciousness.

The state to which one would go as soon as grief merely begins to manifest; likewise, the state to which one would go as soon as fear suddenly arises due to a cause such as being unexpectedly seized by an enraged black serpent, a tiger, or the like, and becoming utterly terrified.

Thus, it is taught that even when one reaches a state where, due to causes such as seeing objects that are utterly loathsome, loathing arises immediately, there too the vibration of the established [Self] is perceived—
distinguished by the varieties of anger, sorrow, fear, and loathing.
Because he is characterized by the sound of "atikruddha" (extremely enraged) regarding the fourfold mass of suffering;

likewise, as if greatly delighted, through the cause of conceiving his own perfection of heroic power and strength, he is one who, exerting himself with non-conceptual resolve to accomplish even an extremely difficult task, [attains] that state instantaneously.

One should go there; likewise, one should go to that state which one reaches all at once, being overcome with extreme wonder by seeing objects such as those never before seen and supremely delightful; and likewise, one should go to that state where an excessive laugh arises merely through causes such as hypocrisy. In that case as well—

The perception of established vibration (*pratiṣṭhitaspanda*) is thus taught; for the mass of fourfold bliss—distinguished by joy, enthusiasm, wonder, and laughter—is characterized by the term "extremely delighted" (*atiprahṛṣṭa*).
Likewise, like one bewildered as to what should be done due to distance and so forth...

Because there is an absence of certainty and definitive determination regarding the perceived object, one may proceed to a state filled with doubt; even in that case, perception occurs as before—this is what has been taught.
For in states such as forgetfulness, there are many kinds [of experiences] characterized by the non-apprehension of reality.
This is indicated by the state of being bewildered as to what ought to be done, which characterizes the mass of delusion.
Thus, having described the means for perceiving the supreme reality based on the waking state, which consists of the activity of the internal organ, [the author proceeds].

Since it will be explained in the context of the passage, "For just as an object is seen indistinctly by this [consciousness] which rests in the waking state consisting of the operation of the intellect and the senses" (ŚP Kārikā 4.6), we shall now [discuss it].

In order to establish that state which is the locus of the waking condition, characterized by the activity of the organs of action, he says: "or whatever place one may go while running, there [is it]";
for even in that place, there is the perception of vibration established therein. Indeed, in that case:

Due to the non-apprehension of the distinctions between functions such as desire, effort, cognition, and action, there is the manifestation of the form of the non-dual Lord. For instance, this is observed in one who is running, regarding each successive step:
in the desire to lift the foot, the effort of raising it, the determination of the location, and the action of placing the foot down.

When specific modes of activity exist, yet their distinctions are not perceived, consciousness—as if they were non-existent—becomes established solely in its own supreme nature which is devoid of division; at that time, the person, being entirely dependent on that [consciousness], enters the state of the Lord. This too—

This should be understood as an illustration for the activity of the organs of action, such as speech and so forth. Therefore, just like one who is running, even when the function of one's speech is occupied with the rapid utterance of very melodious syllables and sounds, one may reach that state; likewise—

Even when one goes toward that state where the multitude of fingers on the hands is being employed with extreme speed in the sounding of the lute and flute, there too the perception of a steady vibration is found— this is what is taught;
for by the term "running," all the activities of the organs of action are indicated.
For, in the verse beginning with "Just as an object is seen indistinctly," he will demonstrate that this apprehension consists in the functioning of the intellect and the sense organs;
and although for every living being, in all states, the functions of all the senses do not [operate] without...

They are indeed capable of manifesting the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that vibrates with the light of eternally arisen and established *spanda*; nevertheless, they are obstructed by infinite particularities of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-viśeṣa*) which surge forth as a multiplicity through the power of the appearance of difference projected by the energy of *māyā*.

Since this vibration (*spanda*), though established [within him], cannot be brought within the range of perception even for one who is awakened, certain states such as extreme anger— which are suitable for its perception—
have been taught and gathered as means (*upāya*). And these, for the awakened one...

When reflected upon, these [states] immediately become means for attaining the perception of established vibration (*spanda*), but not when they are being experienced; for that state consists precisely of suffering and the like. However, one who has emerged from it is awakened by the power of instruction.
One who has developed an extraordinary discernment capable of analyzing the true nature of the self experiences the principle of *spanda*; through one-pointed cultivation of that,
having gradually ascended to the state of the fully awakened, he will experience it everywhere— this has been explained.
And regarding that *spandatattva*, [it is explained] by the words beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*). || 6 ||

Now, he states three verses as an instruction on the means for attaining the realization of one's own nature, which has entered the fourth state (*turya*) that is dissolved within the waking activity; therein, first, is a pair of verses:
"Whatever this [teacher] will tell me, having taken recourse to that state..."
Having formed the resolve, "I shall certainly do this," he remains [steadfast]. || 2/7 (23) ||

Commentary: Relying upon that state whose very nature is vibration (*spanda*), one forms the resolution: "Whatever this person says to me, I shall certainly do"—thus, by means of this determination (*adhyavasāya*).
[The text following *adhyavasāyena* is as follows: *kh, gh*: "it exists in such a manner of determination..."]
[Note: The reading "sāyena" is an additional one found in some manuscripts. He who exists presiding over the principle of vibration (spandatattva).

Note: Here, regarding the other action that precedes the act of taking hold of the *sāman*, the intention of the sentence established [by this] is as follows: just as all mental functions (*vṛtti*) have dissolved due to the state of having a mind fully attentive to the execution of the Lord’s command.

The state of being waveless arises. Thus, by completely abandoning all other duties and through the practice of intense reflective awareness focused on the state of vibration (spanda), there is the attainment of the Supreme Reality. || 23 ||
Relying upon that [central channel], both the Moon and the Sun set within the path of Suṣumnā by way of the upward path,
having abandoned the sphere of the Brahmāṇḍa. (2/8)
(* Vivṛti: Both the moon and the sun) Vṛtti: (p.
20) For that person, by resorting to that state, both the moon and the sun set upon the path of Suṣumnā, which is called the central channel.
Having abandoned the path of the body that extends to the limits of the universe, the yogins [proceed].

Note: This is the intended meaning of the phrase "the moon and the sun": for one who has resorted to the state of *spanda*, the mind (*manas*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) dissolve into the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). Consciousness itself, through the progressive assumption of contraction, becomes contracted; prior to attaining the state of the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-śakti* and *kriyā-śakti*), it becomes the mind.
It attains the state of being the expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Upon ascending to the pinnacle of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*),

both [powers], consisting of the energies of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*), having abandoned even the dualistic perception of objects to be rejected or accepted as well as the function consisting of the movement through the channels (*nāḍī-saṃcāraṇa*), become universal—
They return to their original form. || 24 ||

Commentary: Having resorted to—that is, having reached—that state or condition indicated by the sentence characterized by the word "tām" (that), both the moon and the sun—the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—of the person set simultaneously; that is, they dissolve. Having done what?
Precisely by virtue of resorting to such a state, having abandoned the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—
wherein "that which is within is without"— the body itself, which is the cosmic egg, becomes his sphere,
the locus for the expansion of his own [consciousness]; having abandoned that, having relinquished it.
The meaning is "having transcended" due to the absence of the state of being an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatā*). By what path has it set?
By the upward path, by the superlative, extraordinary way that transcends all.
And thus—the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), whose nature is the expansion of the mind and which is signified by the word "moon"—this...

"This is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted"— thus, while remaining within the sphere of transmigratory existence, once she has transcended her own objective domain as a support and attained a state of neutrality in that condition,
she sets within her own cause; likewise, that which is denoted by the word 'sun' and consists of the expansion of the vital breath [does the same].

The power of action (kriyāśakti), having rendered void all the crooked movements characterized by the circulation through various channels (nāḍīs) and having attained the state of the universal vital breath (sāmānyaprāṇa), comes to rest in its own station via the path that transcends the world. Therefore, he says: "It has set upon the path of Suṣumnā."
The channel named Suṣumṇā, which occupies the very center of the body— within its path,
the route of the supreme power of the Supreme Lord,
one becomes tranquil through the abandonment of the coloring [of consciousness] by objects of knowledge and by effects.
They attain the state of being the supreme power (paraśakti)—this is the meaning. Relying upon what state?

He says: "having resorted to that condition," meaning having fully relied upon that state in which all activity toward external objects has been completely abandoned, and all powers are rendered motionless.

At a certain occasion, a person stands leaning against something. Having done what? [The text] states another action prior to the act of "leaning," namely: "having resolved thus" (*iti saṃkalpya*), meaning having formed such a resolution. How so?
Thinking, "Whatever this person says to me, I shall certainly do," one for whom the transgression of his command immediately brings about calamities such as the loss of life—
this person, such as a king and so forth, is indicated here by the word "this" (ayam); he is the one who [says], "This object is my duty to perform."

"He will speak" means he will discourse; "therefore, with my whole being, having completely abandoned all other duties, I shall do it"—that is, I shall accomplish it—such is the syntactical connection of the pair of verses. This, however, is the intended meaning: for some reason...

When a man, impelled by a powerful person with words concerning what must necessarily be done and with the intention of communicating a matter that is to be performed, possesses such intense attention focused solely on listening to those words that all [ordinary] mental functions (*vṛtti*) completely subside, his consciousness enters the fourth state (*turyā daśā*).
It necessarily enters; through the repeated practice of reflecting upon that, there is the realization of the supreme reality.

Here, by the term "the sphere of the cosmic egg" (brahmāṇḍa), the space within the body is indicated, and by the terms "moon" and "sun," the expansions of the mind and the vital breath are respectively presented.

The purpose [of this work] is for the awakened one who, by means of this instruction, has ascended to the pinnacle of the practice of reflective awareness regarding the recognition of the fourth state.
"Having attained rest in the supreme state that transcends the entire external and internal paths"—
this has been explained separately by the author of the *Vṛtti* regarding that state whose nature is vibration (*spanda*).
By such passages as "of him" and "that state," and by the textual passage beginning with "ityādinā" [and so forth]. || 8 ||
Now, one might object: "Surely such a state arises somehow for anyone at all;
so what is the use of instruction? To this he says:
"Then, in that great void, wherein the moon and the sun have dissolved..."
Like one in the state of deep sleep, the deluded person becomes awakened and unobscured. (2/9, 25)

Commentary: In that great void where the moon and sun have completely set, he whose manifestation of his own true nature has not occurred properly would be deluded by dreams and the like, unawakened, and obstructed; the awakened one, however, remains entirely unobscured.
It comes to be. || 25 ||

Note: Because all objects of knowledge and their effects have almost entirely dissolved into the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*), the previously described state of *turya* (the fourth) for the ignorant is of the nature of a void, like the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*); however, for those whose vision of knowledge has arisen through the descent of the power of the Lord (*īśitṛśaktipāta*).
Furthermore, in that state, the wonder of the experienced fourth [state] shines forth unobscured; thus,
even when that state arises in some way for everyone, it is independent of instruction.
The undesirable consequence would be entering the state of darkness; therefore, instruction requires dependence [on something else] in order to avoid that.
Thus ends the first outflow, "The Vibration of One's Own Nature," in the Spandakārikāvṛtti composed by the venerable teacher Kallaṭa. || 1 ||

Commentary (p. 79): At that time, in that state—namely, in the Great Void (*mahāvyoman*), the supreme space (*paramākāśa*) denoted by the term *sauṣumnādhvan*—because its essential nature is distinct from all objects of cognition (*vedya*).

Furthermore, because it is distinct from the nature of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), which consists of the quality of sound, it is one's own essential nature as expressed by the term "Great Ether" (mahāvyoma); of what sort is it?
In that wherein the moon and the sun have dissolved.
In that state where the entire expansion of the manifold of cognitive and active functions has subsided, the deluded one—
due to the absence of contact with the rays of the supreme power of the Supreme Lord’s sun—
would be like one in the state of deep sleep, exhausted by the slumber of the waking perceptions of a bound soul (paśu).

It would be like the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Just as the state of deep sleep— though its entire manifold of objects of knowledge has dissolved— is, for one who is not awakened, as if consisting of delusion (*moha*) because of the absence of the capacity for experience at that time, so too is this fourth state (*turya*).

It is essentially of the nature of delusion. On the other hand, the awakened one— having become pre-eminently enlightened through the power of the descent of the Lord’s grace (*īśvara-śaktipāta*), possessing the vision of correct knowledge that has arisen anew, and having experienced the enjoyment of the Fourth State (*turya*) during the occasion of reflecting upon that state— is unobscured.
One would become, or attain, that which is free from the veil consisting of the notion of "I" delimited by the body and so forth;
this very state exists within that great void.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of this and other passages. || 9 ||

Thus, of this very Self, which is Śaṅkara, who has been established as having the single nature of being the mere perceiver persisting through all states by virtue of being distinct from the category of objects of perception such as the body, and for whom the means of realization has been demonstrated.

That very capacity is the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantras which serve as the means for performing the rites enjoined by the scriptures that must necessarily be done— this is understood precisely by one who has awakened and perceived such a nature of the self.
To provide instruction, he speaks this pair of verses:
"Now begins the second outflow, called the Arising of Innate Knowledge (sahajavidyodaya):
Having seized that power, the mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One."
They proceed for the sake of authority, like the sense organs of embodied beings. (2/10, 26)

Commentary: Abiding in that power, which is the nature of unobscured consciousness (*nirāvaraṇacidrūpa*), the mantras proceed in their respective domains of authority, such as bestowing grace, endowed with the glory of powers like omniscience. They do so by means of their instruments, just as [the senses function] for embodied beings, and not through any other specific form or characteristic.

Note: It is precisely because they have been seized by the power of Śakti that mantras—accompanied by the prescribed procedure (*itikartavyatā*) as their restrainer—are like the organs of living beings; they possess unimpeded power in the accomplishment of their respective, specific tasks to be performed, and not otherwise.

The meaning is that they are incapable of bending even a blade of grass; by the power of the force of destiny (niyati), they proceed toward various distinct functions, such that not all [causes] operate for all [effects]. || 26 ||
Right there they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless; together with the mind of the worshiper, they possess the nature of Śiva. (2/11)
(* Vivṛti: Therefore these...

Vṛtti: (p. 23) In that very sky of their own essential nature, having ceased their office, they dissolve—being of peaceful form and free from the turbidity of *māyā—together with the mind of the practitioner; by this...
Because their nature consists in being conjoined with Śiva, they are said to be "of the nature of Śiva" (śivātmaka). (Note:
Following the word *iti*, the word *te* [they] also appears in manuscript gh. || 27 ||

Commentary: This is the intended meaning here—Śiva-Śakti alone assumes forms such as the arrangement of mantras, because she possesses non-difference from Śiva during both the states of arising and subsiding; wherever there is non-difference from Śiva, there [is Śakti].
The state of being the nature of Śakti—just as in the case of imagined cities, dream-cities, and so forth—is firmly established through such pervasion (vyāpti) and other means.
For one who is ignorant of the potency of mantra (mantravīrya), this results in the delusion of duality, which culminates in fixed notions of means and ends;
however, for the awakened one, mantras [function differently].
They become authorized for the accomplishment of all aims; not only mantras,
but even mere worldly speech attains the status of an unfailing mantra—
by this, the knowledge of action (kriyājñāna) is the effect or the object to be known.
It is characterized as being solely the practice of the Śiva-dharma. || 27 ||

Commentary (p. 80): For this reason—that is, by virtue of the explanation just presented—these mantras, which consist of the arrangement of phonemes and so forth denoting the deity to be propitiated, possess the nature of Śiva;
that is, they share the qualities of the Supreme Lord Śiva, such as omniscience and the like, which are not common to any other.
Those for whom that Dharma exists are "tathā"; the meaning is that their essential nature is non-different from Śiva.
By what cause? Because they have ascended by means of the power—the capacity or efficacy—belonging to that Śiva whose nature was just explained.
In the state of desiring to utter [the mantra], having accepted it through the logical proof of its non-difference [from the Self],
they proceed toward their respective offices of authority while praising by means of the power (*bala*) or capacity (*śakti*) of Śiva, who possesses the strength of omniscience.
They proceed with their own capacity for accomplishing specific effects.

For these [phonemes], having not yet attained the state of non-difference from the Supreme Lord, consist merely of phonemes characterized by the properties of arising and perishing; they [cannot move] even a blade of grass.

They are unable to bend [the disciple]; however, by means of the previously mentioned forceful penetration (*balākramaṇa*), accompanied by the necessary procedures (*itikartavyatā*), their power becomes unimpeded in accomplishing their respective tasks—both immediate and ultimate—beginning with initiation (*dīkṣā*) and ending with the extraction of the poison of the scorpion. If this is so, [then...]
Since all mantras possess an equal vigor characterized by the power to overcome [obstacles] as previously described,
how can there be a difference in their respective jurisdictions? Why should they not all be authorized to accomplish every purpose?— to this [question]:

To establish the very reason—that [the mantras] are constrained by the necessity (niyati) fashioned by the Supreme Lord—he states an analogy: "How do these mantras proceed toward the restricted domain of practitioners? Just as, for example, the instruments of embodied beings [proceed toward their respective functions]. (p. 82)

For all embodied beings who possess the conceit of self-identity fixed upon impermanent things such as the body alone, the instruments— the sense organs— proceed from the Supreme Lord alone, according to the reasoning established here in the verse beginning with "this group of instruments."
Even though there is equality in their acquisition of activity, the cause for inducing consciousness, and so forth, the instruments (karaṇas),
by the power of that imagined capacity of necessity (niyati-śakti),
have their capacities restricted solely to the illumination of objects such as sound and the like, each according to its own [nature].

Do they not function for distinct, individual offices, rather than all [mantras] functioning for every [purpose]? In the same way, these mantras function for the practitioners who have accepted the realization of the "I-sense" (ahaṃbhāva) as the nature of the Supreme, according to their specifically assigned offices; therefore, they are like instruments (karaṇa).

Even mantras endowed with the power of omniscience possess only specific domains of authority. Consequently, those mantras characterized by the nature of Śiva, having been granted such authority, become stainless (*nirañjana*)— that is, free from *añjana*,
which consists either of the impurity (*mala*) in the form of the coloring of the denotable object, or of the contemplative state (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the phonemes and so forth.

They have emerged; for this very reason, they are of peaceful form (*śāntarūpa*). Because pure consciousness alone remains, their nature (*rūpa*) is peaceful, pure, and changeless (*nirvikāra*); being such, they abide right there in Śiva, the supreme cause, which is their own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*).

They completely dissolve and attain oneness with it; with what? Together with the mind of the worshipper—that is, together with the practitioner’s own consciousness. For in that state, due to the absence of the limiting condition of intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), there remains only the natural essence.

The practitioner’s mind is together with that [mantra]. What is established by this? It is this: there is non-difference between the mantra and the consciousness during their states of arising and subsiding, due to their ultimate cause, Śiva. Thus it is.
As the very Śiva-Śakti, assuming the form of phonemes, volitions, and so forth, by virtue of being the essence of mantra and the essence of the practitioner's mind, she has arisen; now,
for those practitioners who have not yet attained the realization of the touch of the power of their own true nature—
Producing the delusion of duality, it culminates in the authority for accomplishing fixed objects.

However, for one who possesses a very firm self-realization within their own nature exactly as it has been explained, and who knows its arising and passing away, all mantras possess the authority to accomplish all purposes.
They become so even without depending on the necessity of association with various specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*) and rules;

or let alone the *mantras*, whatever speech one utters with whatever intention, that very speech attains the status of an unfailing *mantra*— this occurs precisely through the force of its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

The essential meaning is this: the yogin must realize that the potency of mantras is established by its very nature through the force of its own inherent being (*svabhāvabala*). This should be understood as an illustrative indication; for, according to the reasoning already stated, it is not only mantras that possess the nature of Śiva.
As long as no action, cognition, effect, or object of knowledge exists that—having attained its nature through non-difference from the supreme reality—is not essentially Śiva;
this he will state immediately hereafter. This has been explained in the Vṛtti.
"By the power of which [it is] the nature of unobscured consciousness," and so forth. (11)
Thus ends the second outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), titled "The Perception of a Distinct Nature," in the *Spandavivṛti* composed by Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. 2.
Now begins the third outflow, titled "The Establishment of the Power of the Universal Nature."

Now, by way of presenting an alternative position, it is the occasion to address the nature of Śiva himself— whose own essence is the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) consisting of the entire universe— as promised in the second half of the opening verse of this treatise.
He speaks three verses in order to establish [the doctrine] through both logical reasoning and scriptural authority:

"Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being; because it takes on the form of their perception, and because of its realization of identity with them. (3/1, 28)
Commentary: This very Self is indeed of the nature of all things by way of being the source of the arising of all existents. [The phrase "this" (*ayam*) is supplied from manuscript *gh*.
Because there is cognition only of that which is being experienced, it is precisely while experiencing an external object that—
One perceives it as a body, but not as a single body characterized by the head, hands, and so forth. || 28 ||

Note: Every object being perceived is, in reality, like one's own limb to the conscious individual soul (jīva); thus, his body consists not only of the elements (bhūta), but also of objective existents (bhāva). For the perception of an existent such as a jar or pleasure—
Origination is simply the state of being experienced;

for that which is not being experienced cannot attain self-establishment. Therefore, the origination of all things occurs even from the individual soul (*jīva*). Consequently, that too is composed of the universe. [The limited "I"—]

The term "product" (kṛti) refers to a body possessed of a head, hands, and so forth, which consists of the elements; however, that which consists of dispositions (bhāva) is that which is cognized through objects such as sound and the rest. || 28 ||
Therefore, among all reflections upon the meaning of words, there is no state that is not Śiva;
for the enjoyer alone is eternally established everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment. (3/2, 29)
(* Vivṛti: [The commentary] says:
By means of that such-like, all-pervading nature, there is no state in the reflections upon word and meaning that does not manifest the nature of Śiva (or: that does not manifest Śiva).
Because it manifests [itself], the enjoyer alone indeed exists everywhere in the form of the object of enjoyment; there is no other object of enjoyment whatsoever. || 29 ||

Note: Through the realization that all things consist of the universe as previously described, whatever stream of consciousness exists within the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) comprising both the denoted and the denoter is nothing other than identical with Śiva, whose nature is supreme light; therefore, the subject is the Supreme Lord.
Through the dispatching of the wheels of will (*icchā*) and the rest,
one is intent upon the wonder of the objects to be ruled, the self, the knowable, and the effects; by attaining identity with that [reality],
there is a state of universal, ever-arisen presence— thus, the very nature of the Self is the unfolding of the universe.
The nature of the manifestation of power has been fully accomplished. || 29 ||
Or, he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as a play—constantly seeing thus and remaining disciplined, he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. (3/3, 30)

Commentary: He whose mind has such a nature—for example, that "the entire world is composed of Me alone"—perceiving everything as play, is liberated even while living like a Lord because he is eternally disciplined; his body and so forth do not function as bonds for him. || 30 ||
Note: According to the principle indicated in the immediately preceding verse, for the yogin who has cultivated uninterrupted attention and discernment,
there arises the realization of the full state of "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva) as the independent, conscious Bhairava, the Lord of All.
Having perceived this entire universe as nothing more than a mere plaything fashioned for His own sport,
He is not tainted in the slightest by the constraints of doubt, fear, or the stain of anxiety— even though He experiences the coloring of joy, sorrow, and the like produced by His own pastimes.
The meaning is that liberation occurs even while one is still alive, due to being a knower of reality as it truly is. || 30 ||
Commentary (p. 86): The connection is that he who possesses such consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
Thus, according to the manner just explained, for whichever supreme practitioner there is consciousness—that is, perfect knowledge—he [remains] constantly, without interruption, in all states.

Being disciplined and composed, with a mind that is vigilant, one-pointed, and devoted to the cultivation of the power of its own nature according to the perspective of the teachings already spoken and those yet to be spoken— he is liberated even while living, while still maintaining the vital breaths whose locus is the fixed body.

Through the firm realization of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as all-pervasive, the self of all, the Lord of all, and autonomous, one has emerged beyond birth and other such states; that one has become the Supreme Lord himself— of this there is no doubt and no delusion.
Because this matter is unshakable due to its being self-evident, logical, and perceived through direct experience,

what does the one liberated while living do? He regards the entire, complete universe— the world variegated by the manifestation of infinite entities— as a mere play, consisting solely of the sport fashioned from the toys of the moving and unmoving beings he himself has created.
Beholding and contemplating [this]: for every person,
lacking the vision of pure consciousness capable of perceiving their own true nature— which has not yet been awakened—
regards this entire collection of phenomena as distinct from themselves and from one another.
Constantly imagining that [pleasure] has arisen from some other cause,

and experiencing the transformations of joy, sorrow, fear, and so forth produced by that state of being, he repeatedly becomes a vessel for the bonds of birth and so on upon the path of existence. But he who...
The manifestation of the supreme consciousness that has arisen occurs by way of the mode of what is to be established; it is, for example,
like someone intent on play who plays with imitations of objects that serve as causes for fear, anger, and so forth, which he himself has imagined.
Because he knows things as they truly are (*tadyāthātmyaveditvāt*), he does not undergo even the slightest turbidity of transformation such as fear;

likewise, knowing that all phenomena are merely the manifestation of their own inherent nature and power, one who knows them as they truly are does not undergo even the slightest distortion. Thus, everything...

Seeing [all things] as nothing but play, one is liberated even while living. To the question, "How is his consciousness [such]?"—he explains this with the verse beginning with "by that" (*tena*); by that reason which is about to be stated, among the reflections upon words and their meanings, there is no state whatsoever that is not Śiva—for him.
"He who possesses such consciousness is liberated while living. A word (*śabda*) is a collection of syllables that conveys meaning;

meaning (*artha*) is the multitude of entities to be expressed, which is manifold due to distinctions such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Reflection upon these two consists of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpanā*) corresponding to each [object], arising from the coloring by infinite objects of thought.
Regarding these cognitions, which constitute worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) within these reflections on word and meaning—
there is no such state or condition whatsoever, whether in the form of reflection on words or reflection on meanings,
that does not directly become Śiva himself. Since this is so, at that time, the enjoyer is indeed the experiencer alone.

The Lord is eternally and always present everywhere in all states as the object of experience, in the form of the very substance that is to be experienced; there is no such thing as an "object of experience" existing separately.
This distinction between the experiencer and the experienced is merely a manifestation of the failure to discern the true reality.

"For what reason is there no state that is not auspicious? To this he says: because the living soul (*jīva*), which is the Self (*ātman*), consists of all things and is the form of the universe (*viśvarūpa*), its cognition is such that [subject and object] are not perceived as mutually distinct; even the worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) of the living soul is established only on the basis of the non-difference between the known (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).

This is the meaning. Why is this so? Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, due to the emergence of all things through the realization of identity with the nature of their cognition. Regarding that which is cognized by someone—such as a jar or pleasure—there is a cognition, which is knowledge; the "nature" (*rūpa*) of that [cognition] is...
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); by that cause, the realization of identity (*tādātmyapratipatti*), which is the consciousness of non-difference;
from that cause, there arises the emergence of all entities, the production of all things; therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything. What is meant by this?

When this empirical usage of the individual soul (*jīva*) is investigated, it establishes the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmya*). For instance, it is only while cognizing its own object that the soul brings it forth and creates it; for an object exists only as it is being cognized.
It attains its own nature, but not while remaining unperceived; and being perceived is nothing other than manifesting itself in this or that form.
Furthermore, the state of manifesting is non-different from manifestation itself; it is nothing else at all. As the proponent of Nyāya has said:
"And because it is experienced through volition, and because that which does not possess its form is not experienced.
Thus, whatever this living being perceives, each of those things becomes his very body;
it is not restricted solely to the specific arrangement of parts such as the head and hands.

For even that [the body] becomes his body only during the state of being perceived; at other times, however, it is merely an external object. And thus, because of the commonality of being perceived, two kinds of bodies are taught for him by those who know reality: the elemental (bhūtātmaka) and the existential (bhāvātmaka).
In this regard, because the true nature [of the self] has been made forgettable by the power of *māyā*,
at the moment of perceiving an object, this individual soul (*jīva*)— its capacity being contracted due to a lack of awareness of its own essential nature—
identifies itself as a body possessing a head, hands, and so forth, by virtue of being the locus of a limited ego-sense.
That which he perceives as consisting of the elements—because it is composed of creation and so forth—is said to be of the nature of the *bhūta* (the elemental);
however, that which he perceives as distinct by way of objects such as sound and so forth is of the nature of *bhāva* (existence).
But when the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is investigated, both of these constitute his body.
Because there is no distinction in the fact that it is being experienced. Thus,
in the state of association with existence characterized by being experienced, the individual soul (jīva),
although remaining as the all-pervading universal form because it is non-different from the object of experience, is nonetheless [perceived as such].

Thus, due to the non-emergence of the reflective awareness of the reality of the perception of objects, one differentiates all this as being distinct from oneself and from one another, on the grounds that it has acquired its own nature through other causes external to the self; and [one likewise differentiates] the self...
One who identifies with the ego-sense toward impermanent states such as the body, and thus partakes in the bondage of birth and so forth,
is designated as a transmigrating *jīva*. However,
when one possesses clear vision awakened by the dawn of enlightenment produced by the falling rays of the power of the sun that is Śiva—

Being firmly established in the realization of the "I" whose true nature is the real Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth that appear as clearly manifest, he becomes manifest through the powers of reflective awareness that perceive objects exactly as they exist.

Then that very Śiva becomes the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), consisting of the manifestation of the manifold universe drawn forth by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*). Therefore it has been said: "That realization of identity which occurs through the power of the nature of the cognition of each respective object, arising from the consciousness of non-difference from the object being experienced..."

He is the source of the arising of all entities; therefore, the living soul (*jīva*) consists of everything. By that reason—namely, the realization that he consists of everything—there is no state whatsoever that does not consist of Śiva; and thus, the enjoyer himself exists as the Lord (*īśvara*) in the form of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*).

"Always and everywhere established in the form of the object to be ruled over"— this has been stated again for the purpose of synthesizing the meaning of the sequence of statements that "he who possesses such consciousness is liberated while living. By these three verses, the existence of the Self alone as the universal form is established.
It has been established that the manifold world cannot have any other cause, as it has been said by the knower of Brahman:
"The divine Self, by its own power of illusion (*māyā*), fashions itself out of itself."
"That very [Self] perceives through differentiation"—this is the definitive conclusion of the Vedānta.
Thus it is said. Likewise, by another [author] also, through the medium of praise, it was stated:
"Though You abide externally with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), Your manifoldness is described as being like that of crystal and other such substances."
If they were ever, in any way, or anywhere capable of existing apart from your manifestation, [then they would be other than you].
Or rather, let the universe be accepted as a manifestation (*vivarta*) arising from the delusion of the transformation through the cooking of atoms;
for if that were the conceptualization here, it would be [accepted] by the best of the wise.
Praise alone would not be able to bring it about in such a manner.
And so here too, though at every moment the circles of rays of various conceptual constructions flash forth as they open and close,
it nevertheless possesses an exceedingly pure body and is the wondrous sole ground.
O Śiva, you alone shine forth as the jewel consisting of pure consciousness.
This has been explained individually in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the passage beginning with "this very self consists of all things," and so forth.
By the phrase "by such [a person]" and so forth,
[it refers to] one who has such a nature.
And by such passages as this [in the] text. || 1 || 2 || 3 ||

Thus ends the third outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), titled "The Demonstration that the Universe is Merely the Power of One's Own Essential Nature," in the *Spandavivṛti* composed by the venerable Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. || 3 ||
(p. 94) Now,
[the section] called "The Perception of Non-difference."
The fourth [point] is the outflow (*niḥṣyanda*). Now,
in order to demonstrate that this very realization, when properly grasped, is the means for perceiving non-duality,
[the text establishes] its nature as the purifier through all ritual procedures, such as the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth.
To demonstrate this, he says:
"This very arising of that object of meditation in the mind of the meditator is the attainment of identity with it for the practitioner who so desires. (4/1, 31)

Commentary: Through the medium of the cognition of that [mantra], the grasping of its self—which consists of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra—is itself the "arising" (*udaya*) of that object of meditation, which is the mantra-self, within the mind of the practitioner.
"Identity" (*tādātmya*) is the attainment of its own nature by means of the deity of the mantra.
It was brought about by the desire of the practitioner to recite the mantra together with the deity (kh, g: "by the desire for the recitation of the mantra"). || 31 ||

Commentary: This is what must be established here: that state in which the mind of the practitioner, while desiring to utter the mantra, effortlessly achieves identity with the object of meditation—that very [state] is the [nature] of that which is denoted by the mantra.

Through the aforementioned well-established reasoning, the perception of non-difference is accepted; for the object of meditation arises as a visible manifestation through a form that possesses the unerring power to perform the various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) of the deity to be meditated upon, and not as a separate, conceptualized form. || 31 ||

Commentary: The "arising" (*udaya*) of that certain object of meditation—that specific deity who is to be remembered in various forms and expressed by mantras—is its manifestation in those various forms of the object of worship, which possess unfailing power capable of accomplishing their respective purposeful actions. In what locus?—

In the meditating mind— that is, in the mind or intention belonging to the meditator, the rememberer— what is this "arising"? It is [the arising] established by the power of the reality itself for the diligent practitioner who, while in the state of desire, wishes to utter the mantra.

"Attainment of identity with that" (*tadātmatā-samāpatti*) means: the self (*ātman*) of that object of meditation is its essential nature (*svarūpa*); the state of being that is "identity with that" (*tadātmatā*); and "attainment" (*samāpatti*) is becoming one with it. The intended meaning here is as follows:
at the stage when there is the desire to utter the mantra for the sake of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth—

The state of non-differentiation, which is spontaneously accomplished by the mind of the practitioner within the form of the deity constrained by mantra (or the form of another deity constrained by mantra), is precisely the primary [state] for the meditator whose consciousness is capable of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

The emergence [of the deity] consists in the direct perception of the worshipped divinity, and not in a form to be conceptualized through exclusion; it is by this very consciousness that the attainment of the state of Śiva occurs.
"...having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva"—
this is the fulfillment of that injunction.
This very [injunction] is realized through the medium of that realization.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by such passages as "ityādi" (and so forth). || 1 ||
He states that this very consciousness is what purifies through other rites:
"This alone is the attainment of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva. (4.2 [32])

Commentary: This very thing is the unobstructed self-realization of the practitioner who is devoid of false knowledge; it is the attainment of immortality. It is not, however, that the attainment of immortality is said to be the tasting of the gross "essence of the elements" (dhātusāra) in the form of the relish of nectar (*rasa*). That which is precisely this...

By the mere utterance of the mantra, one attains the state of abiding in the very nature of the mantra; that itself is said to be the "grasping of the self. For this reason, at the time of initiation, the Guru should effect the grasping of the self through his intellect.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, unlike a clod of earth or similar objects, there is no grasping of this formless [reality] with the hand;
for this very reason, this alone is the initiation of nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva and manifests the essential nature of Paramaśiva. || 32 ||

Note: Consciousness (*saṃvit*), as previously described, possesses the nature of the unsurpassed nectar (*anuttarāmṛta*)—distinctly superior even to initiation (*dīkṣā*) dependent on external means and the like, which consists of impermanent and insentient entities—and it serves as the cause for the purificatory refinement (*saṃskaraṇa*) through the supreme ritual procedure. || 32 ||
Thus ends the second outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), titled "The Arising of Innate Knowledge," in the commentary on the *Spandakārikās* composed by the venerable teacher Kallaṭa. || 2 ||

Commentary: This very [cognition], as previously explained, has as its object perishable things such as the body; it consists of the perception of an object of knowledge distinct from self-luminosity, taking the form of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), and is thus false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

Consciousness (*saṃvit*), which consists in the perception of the single reality that is the mere nature of uninterrupted, pure, and spontaneous freedom due to the cessation [of duality], is right knowledge; it is indeed the attainment of the immortal—
the attainment and perception of the self whose nature is Śiva, which is imperishable.

The attainment of immortality consists in the acquisition of the nectar that follows from the true meaning; it is not the acquisition of any particular material object, which is insentient and impermanent. For that [attainment] is metaphorically described as such because it serves as the cause for the soul's possession of a body that endures for a long duration.

Likewise, this very apprehension of the self— that consciousness which arises for a moment at the time of the desire to utter such a mantra— is precisely this apprehension, that is, the grasping of the self, of the individual soul (jīva),
within those various specific rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) and the like.
In the scriptures, the grasping of either one's own self or that which pertains to the disciple is taught; as it is stated in the Vṛtti:
"At the time of initiation, the Guru should perform the grasping of the self through his intellect."
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing such an injunction (*vidhi*), there arises a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in which the self— conceived as having a specific form—

is non-different from its own nature that constitutes the supreme cause; when this absorption is reflected upon, it brings about the fulfillment of the injunction consisting of the grasping of the self, and not otherwise.

Otherwise, the apprehension of that formless [reality] would be impossible, because it is non-different from the grasper— the Supreme Self— which is all-pervasive and consists of consciousness. Likewise,
this very [state] is the initiation of liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā), which is liberation itself.

Nirvṛti is the ultimate tranquility of consciousness resulting from the complete exhaustion of the agitation characterized by dualistic cognition; it is the establishment of consciousness in its own essential nature. Initiation (dīkṣā) has that as its purpose, consisting of the bestowal of awakening to one's true self-nature and characterized by the destruction of the bondage consisting of duality.

It is a specific transformation (*saṃskāraviśeṣa*); and this very initiation into Nirvāṇa is of such a nature, for it is precisely this consciousness (*saṃvit*) that has been taught, since she is the cause of that [initiation]. For this consciousness bestows the true being of Śiva—that which belongs to the Supreme Lord, who is one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*).

Existence (*sadbhāva*) is being (*sattā*); it is that which bestows and establishes the uncontradicted realization—"I am indeed this"—which is possible in the state of perfection. For that is the unsurpassed *saṃskāra*, the domain of a perfectly awakened Guru.
It consists solely in the attainment of one's own nature as Paramaśiva, and not in the nature of specific ritual procedures to be accomplished through external means; this has already been explained.
This very [attainment] belongs to one who is devoid of false knowledge.
Thus [it is stated] in the commentary on verse 2.

Having thus established that this consciousness is the cause for the performance of the supreme rites, he now speaks two verses to demonstrate its status as the cause of other accomplishments by means of an illustration from the worldly conduct of transmigrating beings.
Now begins the third outflow, called the vibration of manifestation:
"Just as the Creator, when requested by desire, brings about for embodied beings the emergence of the moon and sun so that they may attain the objects situated within their hearts while awake. (4.3)

Commentary: (p. 28) Just as for this yogin whose own essential nature is unmanifest, whatever desire arises during the waking state, in that very manner, even when many objects are present, there occurs the perception of only that specific object which is intended.
In the case of watching actors, wrestlers, and the like, [the perception] occurs by fixing the attention on the eyes and other faculties after performing the rising of the moon and the sun. || 33 ||

Note: For one who desires to see an object, the attainment of the desired object occurs only by entering into a state characterized by concentration upon the ascertainment of that desired object while in the stage of the desire to see; therefore, that stage is metaphorically designated as "prayer" (*prārthanā*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, it says "of the two eyes."

This is an illustration by means of another sense-faculty; by this, the state of desiring to hear (*śuśrūṣā*) and even the state of touching (*spraṣṭu-kāmatā*) are likewise metaphorically designated, because the manifestation of all objects occurs only through the mediation of desire. || 33 ||
Likewise, because it never fails to fulfill desired objects even in dreams, that which abides in the center must necessarily manifest most clearly and constantly. (4/4) (*Commentary:
"must necessarily abide")

Commentary: Likewise, even in a dream, one perceives only those objects that are desired, because of the non-transgression of affection—that is, because of the non-transgression of the request of one's will. And that heart which is constantly manifested most clearly within that [dream] is this very sovereignty of dreaming.
Thus it is said; the meaning is that this itself is the breaking through of the veil of darkness. || 34 ||

Note: Since, in the manner described, there is no transgression of the affection (*praṇaya*) consisting of the realization of identity throughout all states involving the relationship between the grasped and the grasper,
even regarding the objects of the creation known by the mind, the desired things are indeed most clearly manifest.

"Expansion" means that dream-objects would not be able to manifest independently; therefore, because there is no distinction between the two aforementioned states for the yogin, the piercing of the veil of darkness occurs, through which the production of other supernatural powers (*siddhi*) takes place. || 34 ||

Commentary (p. 99): Just as for every transmigrating being who, while awake, has come to regard the mere body as the self and experiences the waking state—characterized by the activity of the sense-faculties being occupied with grasping their respective objects—so too [is it for one who regards the intellect as the self].

Requested by his own desire— that is, requested by the desire consisting of the wish to see— he desires to see those beloved objects situated in the heart and established in his latent impressions (*āśaya*);
for, by the power of the nature of that state, through the attainment of identity (*tādātmya-samāpatti*), those objects are realized.

Like a creator who has been entreated, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, the maker of all, brings about and manifests according to one's intention. Having done what?— having brought about the rising of the two eyes, the Moon and the Sun, which consists of the mere discernment and the focused attention upon the intended object.
"Having brought about the manifestation of its own nature"—this is the sentence of comparison. The intended meaning here is as follows:
whatever transmigrating being arises with the desire to see any particular object, at that very moment of desiring to see it, he necessarily and instantaneously [perceives] the Supreme Self.

One enters into the Creator non-differently; that state of his is metaphorically designated as "longing," because the attainment of the desired object is preceded by it. Thus entreated by her, the Creator, through the attention of his eyes directed toward the manifestation of that very object, [perceives it].

Having brought about the emergence characterized by the manifestation of its own nature, even when many other visible objects are present, it reveals only that object which has been requested through the very desire to see it,
and nothing else. This statement, "having brought about the emergence of the eyes," should be understood as a mere illustration.

Thus, when requested by the desire to hear, the Creator bestows upon the embodied soul the arising [of consciousness] within the two ears, causing that very object which was desired to be heard to be heard even amidst other things worthy of hearing; this should be applied to all the senses as well. And with regard to the eyes, by the words "Soma" and "Sūrya," [the same principle applies].

The purpose of demonstrating the actual non-difference of the element (*dhātu*) from the individual soul (*jīva*) through this exposition [of their identity] is established; and this has been explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) itself as being for the sake of illustration.

Because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "by means of attention toward the eyes and so forth," the manifestation of all objects for all living beings occurs preceded by will; and that state is the state of will.

Transmigrating beings are of a nature non-different from the Supreme Cause; thus, it is the Supreme Lord alone who, being autonomous, manifests this entire universe according to His will. This is the ultimate truth, yet transmigrating beings—due to the limitations of the body and so forth produced by His power of *māyā*—do not realize it.

But he who is awakened, whose sword of wisdom has been sharpened on the whetstone of the excellence of practicing the aforementioned instruction, who has severed the coarse knots of egoism regarding the body and so forth, and in whom the unobscured realization of the true Self has arisen— he alone, when being remembered, [removes] that...

"It is sufficient to recognize [the Self]"— this is taught by means of a sentence providing a comparison (upameya) to the yogin who has attained the samādhi of non-difference. Or rather, just as He, being entreated by the will, manifests all objects according to the reasoning established by those very [authorities], so too in that same manner.

It is because [the Lord] never, at any time, and in all states involving the relationship between the knower and the known, transgresses or disregards the state of longing— that is, the prayer consisting of the realization of identity— by remaining attentive through constant self-reflection.

Even in a dream, during the state of sleep—where the eyes and other senses have ceased their own functions and the objects are one's own creations perceivable by the mind alone—one perceives very clearly those very objects that are desired and agreeable to the practitioner. (p. 102)

Having made it exceedingly manifest, he who dwells in the center, seated eternally in the heart, must necessarily and by rule reveal and spread it—this is the meaning of the sentence concerning the object of comparison beginning with "tathā" (thus). Furthermore, the intended sense is this: he who...

At all times, in all experiences, the subject— the Lord of All— does not transcend that state of devotion characterized by absorption into his own essential nature, which is established through his own power, because he remains attentive through moment-to-moment self-reflection; thus, he is the Creator (dhātā) of that [nature].
Just as in the waking state, [the Lord] manifests only those objects desired even in the dream state; for the objects of his dream do not, by acting independently,
manifest any obstruction to his own power characterized as universal agency, because he is beyond saṃsāra.

However, being independent, he creates them as he pleases by his own power. As Bhartṛhari said: "Having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of entities, the Lord of All, possessing all powers, becomes the enjoyer within a dream."

Thus, for this very reason, it has been said that this is the sovereignty of dream. There is no difference between that [state] and waking; therefore, it is precisely the piercing of the veil of darkness (*tamas*) that has been described. Darkness is the obstruction of one's own unconditioned majesty produced by the egoity (*ahaṃtā*) directed toward the body and so forth. (p. 103)
By that [means], *varaṇa* is concealment, the obscuration of one's own nature;
its *nirbheda* is its destruction through the manifestation of one's own infinite majesty, for that [destruction] indeed manifests in that state. This has been explained separately in the *Vṛtti*.
Just as [he sees things] through the passage beginning with "of this [consciousness] whose own nature is unmanifest," so too in a dream he perceives only those objects that are desired.
By means of the textual passage beginning with these words. || 3 || 4 ||

Now, demonstrating that the yogin is equal to those in the cycle of existence merely by emerging from such a state of samādhi, [the author] says the following in order to strengthen the notion of his constant union:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent, because it would possess that nature."
Constantly, as in the case of the worldly person, in both the states of waking and dreaming. (4/5, 35)

Commentary: Otherwise, in the absence of abiding in one's own essential nature, the creation appearing in a dream—such as the sight of a cat—would be independent. This is because that very reality has the nature of creation, owing to its quality of procreation; just as [it occurs] constantly.

For all the world, during the state of waking and the state of dreaming, there are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding connection and non-connection [with objects]. (Note: An alternative reading, *svapnāvasthāyāṃ ca saṃbaddhā vikalpāḥ*, is also observed.)

Commentary: Within the expansion of Śakti, which consists of two aspects and unfolds through the relationship of knower and known, for one who is eternally united— due to the non-departure of intense and continuous cultivation established in the absorption of self-awareness— the two aspects, whose nature is emission, become liberated and constitute a restraint upon Śakti.

He is not at all capable of ordaining [otherwise]; rather, occurring otherwise like worldly beings, he is rendered subject to others by his own creation of states (*bhāva-sṛṣṭi*). The meaning is that one must remain intent on what is beneficial. || 35 ||
Commentary: Otherwise, however—by a manner other than the one previously stated—this world is the effect belonging to me alone, the single, independent Supreme Lord who is the creator of all;
[this is said] regarding the state of the yogin who exists in the absence of such realization during the two stages of waking and dreaming.
Because it possesses those attributes in both the states of waking and sleep, and because its nature consists of the qualities of emanation,
creation— the manifestation of various entities— would be independent in a real sense, due to the constant absence [or, rather, the arising] of the consciousness of the reality of the Self.
Being unreflected upon as the independent agency of one's own self alone, it would become a free-willed bestower of manifold delusions, with the expansion of such power being difficult to restrain.
Of what is it like? It is like that of the worldly person, the transmigrating world; this is the intended meaning here.

The two stages characterized by waking and sleeping constitute the nature of emanation (*sarga*); for it is therein that the abiding of the Supreme Lord’s power is established through the relationship of knower and known.
Regarding such a pair of stages consisting of these two, the yogin who—
Even if one should arise from the non-abandonment of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the aforementioned consciousness,

for him who is firmly established in his own self— the independent creator of all— that pair of words, which by nature belong to the process of emanation, is not capable of obstructing his power; however, this is not the case for one who is otherwise.

The meaning is that one must remain constantly disciplined as a yogi, for one is rendered subject to the power of others by the very creation of objective phenomena (*bhāva-sṛṣṭi*), which resembles the world;
otherwise, there is an absence of abiding in one's true nature (*svarūpa*).
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by such statements as "ityādi" (and so forth). || 5 ||
Now, the cognition of objects that are past, future, concealed, remote, and so forth, is easily obtained through this very consciousness; thus he says in a pair of verses:
"For just as an object is seen indistinctly even when the mind is attentive..."
Cultivated through the exertion of one's own power, it shines forth even more clearly. (4.6 [36])

Commentary: Just as, for instance, a certain object situated at a distance is not perceived by a person even when he is previously attentive, yet that very same object becomes clear to one who remains in that very place while examining it with a specific effort; [so too is the case here]. || 36 ||

Note: At the very commencement of the expansion of the eyes by one desiring to see, the object is perceived indistinctly; yet in the next moment, there is a much clearer manifestation, because for the observer, there exists no means of perception whatsoever other than the act of seeing itself.

Or rather, it is brought forth without entering into the actual nature [of things], because the manifestation of reality as it is occurs precisely through not grasping that [nature]. Thus, although this manifestation of the object is common to all,
it reveals the aforementioned power of reflective awareness only for the yogi, and not for anyone else.
"Of one blinded by the darkness of illusion. || 36 ||
Thus, having mastered that power which exists in its ultimate sense, at whatever time, in whatever place, and in whatever manner it abides, it proceeds accordingly before long. (4.7 [37])
(* Vivṛti: Thus, that which exists in its ultimate sense, in a certain place, by means of something, and in a certain manner.
Vṛtti (p. 31): In that same way, by that very same specific effort, whatever object, in whatever form (*k, kh:
in its own form*), at whatever time, in whatever place, and in whatever manner or configuration.

That object, being thus established, manifests to one who relies upon his own power and his own essential nature in a very short time, because its nature is free from obscuration; therefore, it is not at all surprising that knowledge of the past and future has a limited scope. || 37 ||

Note: By the very power of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) thus described, the cognition of objects—whether past, future, concealed, or remote—is indeed easily attained, owing to its non-contradiction regarding their respective states, forms, locations, times, and so forth; this was stated previously.
The intended meaning is that this is further corroborated by means of a verse and an illustrative example. || 37 ||

Commentary: For instance, even when someone’s mind is attentive and possesses an intense effort born of the desire to see that object, the object—merely upon being seen—suddenly appears and manifests unclearly and unmanifestly; immediately thereafter, [it becomes clear].

"Perfumed by the exertion of one's own power" means: by that power or capacity characterized by omniscience and so forth, which belongs to one's own self; and by "exertion," meaning effort or the enthusiasm for vision through extremely intense concentration—one who has been perfumed, that is, characterized, by that.

"It shines forth more clearly, manifesting through recognition all its specific qualities without exception as 'this is that'—such is the statement regarding analogy (upamāna). Its intended meaning is this:
for any object desired to be seen, [the form] does not appear correctly to one whose eyes have merely been opened instantaneously."

It becomes an object of sight; yet again, in another moment, for that very same person who has gone to that place and whose eyes are fixed upon it in the same manner, it appears with even greater clarity. What is the cause of this? For he does not bring forth any means for perceiving specific qualities other than his own visual faculty. Therefore...
Only the penetration into the ultimate nature (*tāttvikasvabhāva*) arises for him, by the touch of whose power that object manifests according to its true reality (*yāthātmyena*); therefore,
for all embodied beings, the mere exertion of one's own power is the means for the manifestation of all objects.

Nothing else at all. Although the manifestation of such an object is common to all living beings, it shines forth in that way only when it is reflected upon by an awakened yogi; it does not shine for anyone else whose right vision is obscured by the darkness of *māyā*. Thus, it is the yogi alone who—by this [means]...
It is reminded by means of the instruction expressed in the sentence concerning the object of comparison (*upameya*), beginning with "in this way" (*evam*).
For just as an object that was previously unclear becomes more clearly manifest once its own power is harnessed,
so too is the power [of the meaning] [manifested] by this very manner expressed in the sentence concerning the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Having overcome the capacity of each thing's own intrinsic nature at the moment of the desire to see, and having presided over it non-differently, for the yogi who exists in that state, [he perceives] in that very manner,
which is non-contradictory with respect to those respective states, forms, places, times, and so forth.

It proceeds correctly, it attains correct manifestation, and it becomes directly present as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). What is that entity?— that entity which, in its ultimate sense and according to reality,
such as a cow or the like, exists in whatever state, by whatever mode, and in whatever manner.
"By means of a specific form characterized by the dewlap and so forth, that which exists in a place—whether obstructed or remote—or at a time such as the past, proceeds in that very manner.
This is the essential meaning here: when an object is perceived indistinctly, [this process occurs] for the sake of its manifestation in a much clearer way.

The non-difference from the very nature of omniscience arises effortlessly for anyone at all; once awakened through the practice of reflecting upon that [nature], one knows objects as they truly are—even those separated by space, time, and so forth—exactly as desired. This is an unrefuted logical principle.
This very [nature] is the cause for the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience when they are present. For this reason it has been said:
"Knowledge of limited objects, whether past or future, is not at all wonderful, because its own nature is free from obscuration."

Thus, for in that state, the power of its own intrinsic nature, unimpeded by space, time, and so forth, becomes manifest. This should be understood as an illustrative indication— that an object is seen indistinctly— since the same principle should be applied to what is heard and so on.

And by this [process], through the entry into the established vibration (*pratiṣṭhitaspanda*) which is being accomplished during a particular state of effort for the sake of the clearer perception of the object of sight and so forth;

It should be understood that, as a secondary consequence, the waking state— which consists of the operation of all the faculties of cognition and serves as the means for perceiving the supreme reality—
has been established; these two verses have been explained by the author of the commentary individually.
Just as [it was explained] by the passage beginning with "as if situated at a distance," so too by that very same specific effort.
By such a passage as this. || 6 || 7 ||
Now, by this very same reasoning, he speaks in order to demonstrate the conquest of hunger, thirst, and so forth:
"Since even one who is weak, having overcome that [hunger], proceeds to his task;
likewise, one who is excessively hungry should suppress his hunger. (4.8) (38)
Commentary: Even one whose constituent elements (*dhātu*) have diminished proceeds toward their task by resorting to that strength characterized by enthusiasm;
and just as someone, though initially incapable, attains great power through the practice of exercise by means of the force of exertion, so it is with this [strength].
By cultivating the awareness of one's own nature, even one who is extremely hungry can suppress that hunger;
for everywhere, the capacity of the self-nature to accomplish cause and effect is immediate. (p. 32) || 38 ||

Note: Even the cessation of hunger and so forth is accomplished solely through the manifestation of one's own innate power, which is eternally satisfied; thus, another expansion of accomplishments (siddhi-prapañca), indicated by such [examples], is also brought to light only through the attainment of the aforementioned reality. || 38 ||

Commentary: Because, for this reason— that is, having seized his own power characterized by the sovereignty of being the creator of all— and by remaining inseparable from it through the reasoning previously stated, even one who is weak— meaning one who is incapable due to the diminished constituents of the body— [is empowered].

"Someone, in an action such as the labor of carrying a burden, engages in activity and becomes focused on the performance of the act"—this is the illustrative statement. Its intended meaning is as follows: one who, because his body is extremely emaciated, is indeed incapable yet still attempts to undertake activities such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).

Through the power of practice, one becomes capable of performing physical exercises and other such actions even when they are more difficult than other objects; in the arising of such capacity, there is no cause whatsoever other than the overcoming of its own inherent nature through the reasoning previously explained. And that—
The power (*bala*) of the reality of the Self is characterized by the capacity to perform all actions according to one's will; whereas the illusory agent (*māyīya-kartṛ*),
because his powers are obstructed by *māyā*,
considers his ability to accomplish specific effects to depend upon specific, restricted causes.

Even he, thinking "I am able to do this," relying upon that very power in a state of unimpeded enthusiasm, becomes capable of accomplishing that task; thus, this principle becomes the object of realization for the yogin alone—taking this as an illustration... (p.)

111) This very point is taught by means of the following illustrative statement: just as even a weak person becomes capable of accomplishing a task that requires strength only by resorting to the power of his own inherent nature, so too does it occur in that same manner.
Having mastered his own power— which is independent in accomplishing all tasks— and having presided over it by means of his own capacity,
he who is exceedingly hungry, being possessed by an intense desire for food,
should cover, conceal, and suppress that hunger.
Since the manifestation of the power of one’s own unconditioned nature is eternal satisfaction,
the very act of consuming food and drink results in effects such as the cessation of hunger; therefore,
once the obstruction of the power of *niyati* (destiny/limitation) has been shattered, one should completely cause that [power] to disappear, being eternally satisfied.
The meaning is that it should be exactly so.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words "the weak one," "one whose constituent elements (*dhātu*) are diminished," and so forth. || 8 ||

Having thus established the individual logical proofs for the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience and omnipotence, he speaks again in order to demonstrate them by means of a single illustrative proof: "Just as omniscience and the other qualities [reside] in this body presided over by Him..."
Likewise, through presiding over its own self, it will be so everywhere. (4/9) Commentary:

Because the body is presided over—that is, pervaded—by this nature of the Self, [the yogi] possesses omniscience and other qualities; for that reason, he knows even the eating of a tiny louse therein immediately, and likewise [everything else].
For one who is concentrated within one's own self, omniscience will arise everywhere. || 39 ||

Note: Through the destruction of the obstruction caused by the notion of the imagined ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*), all objects and qualities such as perfect knowership manifest without impediment in the Supreme Knower, who is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and possesses the full ego-sense (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*). And herein [resides] universal agency...
The means for the manifestation of qualities such as knowledge and so forth is now set forth with illustrative examples. || 39 ||

Commentary (p. 112): In this body, presided over by this self as the thinker and occupied by the notion of "I," there exist omniscience and so forth—all objects of knowledge and effects that have the body as their locus. Among these, those whose beginning is "knowing" (jñatā)—that is, the state of being a knower (jñātṛtva)—are precisely what is meant.
"The attributes such as agency and so forth reside in everyone"—this is the illustrative statement (*dṛṣṭāntavākya*).

Its intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as follows: whatever this Self presides over through the realization "I am," that becomes its body; and everything dependent upon that, whether gross or subtle, belongs to it.
"By this illustration— that one knows what is to be known and performs what is to be done—
it is shown that in exactly that same manner, within one's own self (svātman), which is one's own essential nature (svasvabhāva) and which, like the body being the locus of the 'I'-sense,
is characterized as being where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, and so forth."

Because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) through the sense of "I" upon that which is the substratum— the pure, non-dual, and purely conscious essence distinct from the body and so forth— likewise, for the yogin, all objects of knowledge and effects residing in the body, such as the state of being a knower and so on, [manifest] everywhere throughout all the worlds.
