Omniscience and the other [perfections] will necessarily come into being and attain manifestation; for the yogin whose egoity is established in the self that is non-dual pure consciousness, these [perfections] are free from obstacles due to the destruction of the impediment characterized by the sense of "I" limited to the body alone, which is distinct from [the true Self].
The meaning is that omniscience and the other qualities are indeed manifested everywhere.
This has been explained in the commentary by the passage beginning with "by this nature of the self" (ātmasvabhāvena). || 9 ||
Thus, he states the reasoning for the eradication of disease, wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth:
"Sickness is a plunderer in the body, and its course proceeds from ignorance; if it is destroyed by the unfolding of that [knowledge], how could it exist without a cause? (4/10) [40]
(* Vivṛti: "Languor is a plunderer. Commentary (p.
33): Languor, it is said, is the destroyer of the body, and that languor arises from ignorance;
if that ignorance is eternally abandoned by the unfolding of one's own essential nature (*ātmasvabhāva*), [then...]
[The word] *padaṃ*; [the letter] *gh*: presented based on the manuscript. Then, from where could that [aging] arise, being devoid of a cause?
For this very reason, there is an absence of wrinkles and grey hair, as well as firmness of the body, for yogins. || 40 ||

Note: Since it is precisely through ignorance that the ultimate nature is obscured, there are modifications such as the increase and decrease of the body; [these cease] through the recognition of the reality that is a mass of consciousness-bliss devoid of such [modifications].
Furthermore, the absence of illness and so forth is precisely the recognition of reality; this alone is the means for the eradication of disease, wrinkles, gray hair, and the like. || 40 ||

Commentary: *Glāni* is the loss of joy produced by lethargy and the like; it is a ravager within the body (*deha*), forcibly seizing the constituents (*dhātu*), strength, complexion, luster, power, and so forth.
Its "path" (*sṛti*) arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*), due to the absence of comprehension of the reality as it has been explained. (p. 114)
The flow [of worldly existence] is its movement; if that ignorance is "destroyed by the unfolding"— that is,

if it is cut off and reduced to rootlessness by the "unfolding" (unmeṣa) which will be described later, namely the expansion of the light of one's own nature— then from what source could that exhaustion possibly arise, being as it is causeless and devoid of any reason?
It would neither exist nor not exist, because that which is signless lacks origination; for what is called "ignorance" is simply birth—
the failure to recognize one's own eternal and changeless nature, which is devoid of modifications consisting of transformation, growth, decay, and destruction.

In the context of the modifications such as birth and so forth, there is the identification of the self with the body and its like; and while this exists, the unawakened person, superimposing those modifications—birth and the rest—upon the self, is dragged down by exhaustion.
But he who, through the cultivation of the unfolding [of consciousness] to be described hereafter...

For one in whom the realization of the true Self has become manifest, whence could there be exhaustion? Thus, the primary fruit is the absence of exhaustion, which consists in the loss of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); while the secondary fruit is the absence of wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth, because at that time, how could such exhaustion exist when it is devoid of its cause?
Having explained it thus— "it would be so"— the author of the commentary further explained:
"For this very reason, there is the absence of wrinkles and gray hair, as well as firmness of body, for yogins."
Thus [ends the tenth verse].
Then, in order to demonstrate the true nature of *unmeṣa* (the upward opening), which is the cause for destroying the ignorance that serves as the reason for exhaustion, he says:
"Because for one who is intent upon a single thought, there arises another."
That, however, should be known as the opening [of the eyes]; one should perceive it for oneself. (4/11) (41)
Commentary: When the mind is occupied with a single object, that nature from which another thought suddenly arises must be known as the cause of that thought—the "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*).
This, moreover, should be characterized by the yogi himself through experience, by virtue of its pervading the interval between two thoughts.
Pride (is pervasive at the end of the two).

Note: Since the Self—the pure consciousness alone that pervades the two objects to be investigated and is the cause of all—is designated by the term *unmeṣa* (awakening/expansion), the meaning is that the investigation, attentiveness, and so forth directed toward that [Self] constitute the destruction of the aforementioned ignorance. || 41 ||

Commentary (p. 115): That, moreover, is to be known—that is, it must be understood and characterized—as that unfolding (*unmeṣa*), which is the expansion of the manifestation of one’s own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*). What is it? It is [the state] of one who is intent upon a single thought (*ekacintāprasakta*), [a state] colored by various objects currently being perceived or being remembered within that single thought.

For one who is intent upon knowledge, one-pointed, and engaged in reflection— from that very cause which is the self-nature of knowledge appearing as the object of thought, due to the manifestation of its own intrinsic nature—
there arises another reflection, characterized by a graspable object.

There would be the arising, that is, the production, of another cognition; and the yogi himself, by his own self, would perceive it—realizing: "I am this very Supreme Lord, the ultimate reality, distinct from all things, the supreme cause, the Supreme Self. For there is no [other] for him.
Its essential nature cannot be characterized as "this" in the same way that sound and other objects can,
because its nature is known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Nevertheless, although it is eternally manifest,
it is designated by the term "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*) because it is revealed at that very moment to the one being instructed.
This designation has been made. However, one who thinks thus— that when a certain thought exists,
the arising of another thought is caused by that very thought itself, and there is no other intervening entity existing apart from the nature of the two thoughts— [is mistaken].
If it were argued that the second act of reflection would consist of the nature of the object to be observed (*upalakṣaṇīya*),

then this relationship between the two acts of reflection— the former and the latter— which are intended as cause and effect, would not be established, because there would be no third [factor] to synthesize them.
Without a prior cause and without a subsequent thought that has become an effect— thus,
he who synthesizes [them], and who is this undeniable synthesizer,
is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, which pervades the two thoughts to be synthesized.

The Self alone is said to be the cause of all, which is the unfolding [unmeṣa]. For this very reason, the author of the commentary has explained it with the words: "experienced as pervasive at the end of the two types of thought," and so forth. 11.

Now, in order to demonstrate the power of the practice of *unmeṣa*, he says that for yogins who are generally intent upon specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), those very *siddhis* which they desire as their attainable fruits become nothing but a succession of obstacles for those practicing this [method of] worship.
(34) Therefore, from the *bindu* arises the *nāda*, from that the *rūpa*, and from that the *rasa*; these manifest very swiftly as the agitators of embodied beings. (4/12 [42])
Commentary: Therefore, from this unfolding being cultivated, there arises the *bindu*, which is of the nature of light;
the *nāda*, which is the sound known as the *praṇava*; and form, which is vision in the darkness (*gh* reads *prāṇākhya* [the vital breath], while the phrase "vision in the darkness" remains).
It has been clearly perceived and set forth: the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is like the taste of nectar in the mouth; these [flavors] function as agitators in a short period of time. || 42 ||

Note: For those who meditate on the element of earth (dharātattva), the *bindu* is a particular manifestation of light appearing in regions such as the space between the eyebrows. For those who practice the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on space (*vyoman*), the *nāda* is a particular resonance that arises spontaneously.
For those practicing the concentration on fire (*tejodhāraṇā*), the perception of visible objects even in total darkness is *rūpa* (form);
for those meditating on the essence of water, the relish of its taste even in the absence of a flavorful object is *rasa* (flavor).
All such collections of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are obstacles for one who practices the unfolding of consciousness (*unmeṣābhyāsī*).
The meaning is that it shines forth intensely. || 42 ||
Commentary: Therefore, from this unfolding (*unmeṣa*) whose nature has been explained,
by means of an undistracted attentiveness during the states of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth occurring in conditions such as waking,
[one perceives] that which is moment-by-moment perishable, manifold, dependent, and insubstantial in form.

By meditating upon the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the object to be known— which serves as the cause for all— these signs of accomplishment (*siddhicihna*) will appear before long, in a short time; for they cause the embodied being’s mind to arise from its state of composure through agitation, such as contentment, pride, and arrogance.

For the yogi whose notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth has not been completely uprooted, certain things proceed—that is, they manifest. What are they? They are: *bindu*, which is a particular radiance consisting of an ever-increasing serenity resulting from the excellence of practice in meditation upon a location such as the space between the eyebrows; and...
Through the practice of piercing the *bindu*, it becomes manifest to those who meditate on the *dharātattva* (the earth principle). Thus:

the *nāda* begins with a sound like the deep roar of a swift river or a thundercloud, and as it gradually becomes more subtle, it manifests as a resonance following the humming of bees intoxicated by honey.
The agent is the specific sound uttered by oneself, which those practicing the *vyoma*-tattva hear.

Likewise, form is the perception of the shapes of various visible objects even when there is an obscuration such as deep darkness, [perceived] by those whose minds are fixed upon the *tejas*-tattva. (p. 119)
They behold it thus: even in the absence of a flavorful substance, there is the taste of nectar in the mouth;
that which is experienced by those intent on the meditation of the water-element (*aptattva*), such as those practicing the *lolāgra* or *lambikā* dhāraṇās;
and even that specific touch which is manifested for those meditating on the air-element (*pavanatattva*) arises from this [source].
"—it should be understood that [the state] proceeds. This is the essential meaning here:

one who practices the yoga of *unmeṣa* (expansion) should not be content with these attainments, even though they are acquired through the practice of various *dhāraṇās* and other means, and are thus easily obtained after a long time.
Because these [powers] constitute obstacles to the ascent to the unsurpassed state, they occur sequentially even for other yogis;

however, for those who practice the yoga of *unmeṣa* (the upward opening), due to the absence of such intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), they also proceed non-sequentially. Thus they have been described accordingly. This has already been explained.
Therefore, [the phrase] "from this unfolding" (*unmeṣāt*) and so forth is [explained] in the commentary (*vṛtti*). || 12 ||

(p. 120) Thus, having briefly demonstrated through this teaching on *unmeṣa* that the nature of the Self is distinct from the body and other objects of cognition— a point already established previously in many ways— he now [establishes] that very same [nature] for it in the same manner.

Having illustrated the worldly transaction established by the direct experience of all people, and demonstrating the nature of the universe in brief, he states the essential purport of the entire treatise:
When he remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? He will understand by himself. (4/120)
Commentary: *Didṛkṣā* is the desire to see. When one abides pervading all phenomena (*bhāva*) as if situated in that state, then what need is there for much speaking?
One will understand the very nature of reality (*tattvasvabhāva*) by oneself. (Note: Variant *k* reads *tattvasvabhāvo 'vagamyate*; variant *g* reads *avabhotsyate*).
"He understands the intrinsic nature"; [alternatively,] "the intrinsic nature will be understood," meaning he will know it. || 43 ||

Commentary: Just as there is no difference in the objects of desire when those who possess field-knowledge (kṣetrajña) perceive their own consciousness, so too there is no distinction between the entities pervading the universe and the reality of the Supreme Self; thus, having established that all entities are merged within the essence of consciousness.

Through the practice of reflecting upon the supreme reality as it has been taught, the fruit of that state— which is independent of other means— is to be personally realized by the yogi alone; however,
for one whose vision is impaired by the darkness of conceptual construction, even an object within the fettered creation appears as non-different from oneself.
How could there be any capacity for the realization of the non-difference between the world and its underlying being?
Indeed, this vessel of wisdom alone is fit for such a realization. 43.

Commentary (p. 120): When, at which time, the practitioner—as if with the desire to see (*didṛkṣayā*), that is, with the wish to perceive—having pervaded all objects (*sarvārthān*), meaning all entities that have entered the domain of the knowable (*prameyapadavījuṣo bhāvān*), and having covered them with the light of his own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitprakāśena*), has caused them to be absorbed within himself; [at that time...]
It remains steady, resting upon the single reality through the cessation of the delusion of perceiving multiplicity;
what is the use of a lengthy description of the fruit experienced in that state? [This is] because of the desire to explain it.

Even thousands of books, when spoken, become meaningless because that [reality] transcends the sphere of speech; therefore, it is said that "one will realize it by oneself. That is such a fruit which one will attain by oneself—that is, by one's own self—independently of any external means.
It is directly experienced, because it is self-evident. This is the intended meaning here:

a yogi who desires to know that all things are non-different from their own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*) must take the state of desiring to see what has been personally experienced as his point of reference; for it is thus—

When desired objects abide without distinction from one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), because the cognition of "this-ness" (*idantā-pratyaya*)— which is the cause for the differentiation of objects— has not yet arisen, then, just as in the state of desiring to see, there is non-difference from the essential nature of the knower (*kṣetrajña*) regarding those things one wishes to see.

Since all phenomena of the entire universe are non-different from the nature of the Supreme Self, one whose eye of discernment has been awakened— capable of perceiving the very moment of the desire to see through the practice of reflecting upon the realization of the nature of the Self as distinct from that previously taught— [attains this state].
This instruction is intended specifically for the yogin; for one whose vision of right knowledge is obscured by the cataract of conceptual construction produced by the power of *māyā*,
the reality of the Self— which is in truth a single, undivided essence of pure consciousness— appears as distinct subjects.

Perceiving them as having various forms according to the distinction of their objects of cognition, they conceptually construct the divisions of states such as "about to be seen," "being seen," and "already seen" for entities; yet, they [also] maintain that even those things about to be seen are non-different from the nature of the soul (*jīva*).

Being unable to grasp even that which is substantially real, how could they realize the non-difference of the entities of the world from the nature of the Supreme Self? This is understood through the direction of the yogi’s own reflection upon the moment of his desire to see, which serves as the illustrative example.
One must contemplate the non-difference of the intrinsic natures of all appearances of the entities of the entire world,
becoming one who illuminates the piercing away of the darkness of duality;
this has been explained as being like one situated in the state of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), which is the wish to see.
Thus [it is stated] in the Vṛtti, verse 13.
To strengthen this very instruction, he says:
"The awakened one should always remain, having discerned the field of experience through knowledge;
he should unify everything in one place, and thereby he is not afflicted by anything else. (4/14 [44])

Commentary: One who is awakened, whose power is uncontracted, should remain at all times, having perceived the field of experience through knowledge and having discerned the object of knowledge; thus, in the true nature of reality (an alternative reading, *tattvasvabhāve*, is also seen).
One should project everything onto that which consists of knowledge; then one is not afflicted by the collection of kalās, which will be described later as something other than that. || 44 ||

Note: Any given object, by way of ascending through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), partakes in the penetration of the supreme subject; otherwise, because it would not have ascended to the path of manifestation (*prakāśa*), its existence as a real entity would be untenable.

Thus, those who are attentive to this connection do not suffer at all from the conceit of being knowers—which ranges from the creative arts (*kalā*) down to the earth (*kṣiti*), as if it were overflowing; in this way, the firmness of the instruction already taught is established.
Commentary (p. 123): At all times, in all states of experience, one should remain awakened;

because of being intent on the practice of the taught instructions, one should stay as if waking, with the vision of right knowledge unblinking. How so?—by means of *jñāna*, that is, by means of conscious awareness, [one perceives] the *gocara*, the object.

Having observed and discerned, and having ascertained it as being of such a nature, one should project and deposit everything that is to be discerned upon the single knower, which is one's own self; the meaning is that one should realize it as non-different from that [self]. And therefore:

One is not afflicted by the objects of knowledge— which appear as distinct from [consciousness]— that is, by the multitude of entities consisting of *kalā* and so forth which will be described hereafter, because of the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) that consists in the realization of the non-difference of all entities from the nature of the single cognizer.

One is not tormented by being bound within the wheel of saṃsāra through the fetter of the realization of an ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) characterized by perishable states. This is the intended meaning here:
whatever object, such as form and so forth, the cognizer perceives and determines through the cognition of the eyes and other senses, that very [object]...

In the state of ascertainment, it is indeed non-different from the nature of the cognizer; for what is called "ascertainedness" is simply the manifestness of the object, and that manifestness is non-different [from the subject], as it cannot be anything else.
Because its manifestation would be impossible if it were of a nature distinct from light; thus,
in the state of certainty, the non-difference of all entities from the subject whose nature is pure light is established by their very essence, and for that very reason, such [a state]...
The relationship between the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping, though ever-present,

binds all living beings through the web of delusion regarding multiplicity when it is not reflected upon; therefore, one should maintain uninterrupted reflection in all states, by which the ultimate reality of the single subject is realized.

Having realized the true nature of worldly phenomena, one would no longer be a transmigrating being; thus it is said that the awakened one should remain forever in that state. The awakened one is one whose power is uncontracted.
This has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of these and other [verses]. || 14 ||

(p. 125) Now, in this way, the Supreme Lord, being the one single reality who has established himself as his own self, plays by manifesting himself through his own power of *māyā* as distinct for every individual soul (*paśu*). Such is the case from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*).

Establishing precisely the non-existence of a second category of objects, he speaks in order to demonstrate his play with the expansion of power (*śaktiprasarakrīḍā*) by means of explaining the true nature of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*).

Having fallen into the state of being an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds, he whose sovereign power has been eclipsed by *kalā* is known as a bound soul (*paśu*). (4/15)
Commentary: The "mass of sounds" (*śabdarāśi*) consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

The Person (*puruṣa*), having become an object of enjoyment for the collection of powers beginning with Brāhmī—which are composed of the groups of consonants starting with *ka*—has had his power eclipsed by the digits (*kalā*) of Brāhmī and the others, namely the letters beginning with *ka*.
One who has fallen away from their own true nature is called a bound soul (paśu). || 45 ||

Note: The meaning is that because the expansion of duality is incessantly manifested by the Śaktis such as Bhūcarī and others, [the individual soul], whose entire activity is dependent on another and whose sovereignty has been stolen away, is brought under control. || 45 ||

Commentary: (p. 125) By this much of the treatise, it has been established that the Self (*ātman*) itself is the Lord (*īśvara*). However, by the reason about to be stated—namely, because all its functions are dependent on another and its true nature is not manifest—it is traditionally known as a "bound soul" (*paśu*), which is for the most part like an animal, owing to its beginninglessness.

He remains as one who is constantly mindful of the worldly play and activities of saṃsāra. Being of what nature?— having his power eclipsed by the *kalās* of the group of powers (*śakti-varga*) arising from the mass of sounds (*śabda-rāśi*), he has become an object of enjoyment for the supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*).

With the intention of explaining the expansion of the nature of speech that is about to be described, [there is] that which consists of the collection of phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*; its opposite is...
[the opposite follows immediately after this].

The remaining portion of the commentary on this verse is missing, having been lost from all extant manuscript copies of the original root text. Therefore, this explanation is inserted and presented here from the *Spandapradīpikā* for the sake of understanding the meaning of the verse:

The "mass of sounds" (*śabdarāśi*) is a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*), namely the *mātṛkā* consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*. Because it consists of phonemes, it is the mother (*jananī*) of sounds;

[it is also the source] of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) beginning with Brāhmī, which arises from that [mātṛkā] and consists of the groups of consonants starting with *ka*, by means of its constituent parts (*kalābhiḥ*).

With his power eclipsed by the letters beginning with *ka*, his great pervasiveness stolen away, and fallen from his own true nature, the *puruṣa* has consequently become an object of enjoyment; thus, due to his ignorance, he is called a *paśu*. And it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
The subject is called the Lord (pati) when [the objects] appear as his own limbs;
through Māyā, he becomes the bound soul (paśu), differentiated and defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth.
Thus it is said: "In other cases as well, upon the dissolution of the knot of duality, one attains the identity of the soul with the action (Karma).
When unawakened, he is called a bound soul (paśu); when awakened, he is indeed the Lord (pati)."
The loss of the supreme nectar-essence for him arises from that [perceptual] cognition;
through that, he falls into a state of lack of autonomy, and that [cognition] has only those [limited objects] as its domain. 4/16 (46).

Commentary: From the supreme nectar-like essence of one’s own nature (*svarūpa*), there occurs a falling away, which is a displacement; from that arises the causal condition—the manifestation of perception toward objects and the emergence of memory (the reading *viṣayadarśanasmaraṇa* is taken as a compound). By means of this, the person (*puruṣa*) attains a lack of autonomy and a state of non-omnipresence.
And that condition has as its object only that [object], consisting of the desire for form and so forth. (46)
Note: The meaning is that the bound soul’s (paśu) lack of autonomy is rooted solely in innate impurity (sahaja-mala).

By means of its substratum, there is an obstruction consisting of an extremely dense, difficult-to-pierce, and very firm covering—the māyīya and prākṛtika veils—which function as specific [obstructive] states; this constitutes an endless expansion of misfortune. || 46 ||
[(1 footnote) The initial portion of the commentary on this verse, ending with the words "parāmṛta" and "asvatantra," is present in all extant manuscript copies of the root text.]

Like the portion of the commentary on the preceding verse, this one has been lost due to the destruction of its manuscript existence. Therefore, the commentary that explains the meaning of this verse is also inserted and presented here, having been extracted from the *Spandapradīpikā* text itself:

And that arising of cognition in the bound soul (paśu)— the production of memory and other forms of knowledge upon the perception of objects through the doors of the ears and other senses— is itself the "fall" or "deprivation" resulting from the supreme nectar, that is, from the emergence of one's true nature; for by means of that [cognition], the person experiences lack of autonomy, which is dependence on another.

It attains—that is, reaches—the state of being non-omnipresent and so forth; and that [state] arises from conditions, has only those [objects] as its domain, has sound and other sense objects as its sphere, and consists of desire for them—this is the meaning.
[16] The person (puruṣa) is not independent; he requires a collection of external means for all his desired ends.

The meaning is that he attains that state; being joined with the threefold division known as *sakala*, *vijñānākala*, and *pralayakevala*—which are comparable to the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—and being veiled by the three innate impurities (*mala*s), he becomes a bound soul (*paśu*). For his...

The very arising from conditions is the departure from the supreme nectar-essence; that is, the departure from one's own nature—which is called Śiva, consisting of non-dual consciousness, imperishable, supreme, and unsurpassed nectar—from its essence, which is an experience consisting of such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). From that [arising], there is a falling away.

"Separateness" (*pṛthagbhāva*) is a different mode of being, consisting of conceptual constructions such as "this" and so forth. This is what is implied here in the sentence: of the one supreme reality alone—which, though its nature is devoid of the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*anugrāhya-anugrāhaka*) imagined by its own will—the beneficiary...

Likewise, for the sake of instruction, that fivefold nature which is established in the *Prakriyā* treatises as the appearance of divisions consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidya, conceived according to one's own will— [that is what is meant here].
This has been stated concisely by means of the terms *parāmṛta* and *rasa*. And thus,
the term *parāmṛta* denotes the very "I" (*aham*) as the essential nature known as Supreme Śiva, which is entirely devoid of contact with any absolute duality.
Furthermore, the word *rasa*, employed as a denoter of the *tattva* of power (*śakti*) whose nature consists in that very reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*),

has already been explained previously for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of those who maintain that the *śiva-tattva* is utterly quiescent, devoid of reflective awareness, and almost equivalent to a void (*śūnya*). Thus it is.

The two principles known as Śiva and Śakti, though non-different, are distinguished and elucidated by those who know reality because it would otherwise be impossible to explain their essential nature. And so it has been stated by the Gurus in the *Tattvagarbhastotra*:
The Śiva-tattva was thus praised with the intention of establishing the primacy of that power whose own essential nature consists of the characteristic of being an eternal, undeluded perceiver—
she who, in her form as unconditioned light, is designated by the name Śiva.
We perpetually worship you, that supreme Mother, under this very designation.

Thus, the principle of Śakti (Power), which is designated by those who have realized the supreme reality through such names as "self-nature," "reflective awareness," "universal vibration" (sāmānyaspanda), and so forth,
is expressed by synonymous terms such as "unfolding" (unmeṣa) and the like.
It has been explained:

"O Mother Śivā, when your state of being a power (*śaktitā*) manifests within you, O Auspicious One, then designations such as 'unmesha' (expansion) and so forth arise due to the occurrence of a slight swelling [of consciousness]."

Thus [it is said]. Nor should it be thought that this state of power sometimes exists and sometimes does not exist due to a delusion regarding the hearing of the word "when" (*yadā*); for it has been stated that *dharma*—which consists of the self-awareness of its own nature—is eternal and is precisely the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) itself, characterized as a certain degree of swelling (*ucchūnatā*). (p. 130)

Beyond that, even the triad of principles known as Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā is indeed denoted by the term *parāmṛta*; for although the Supreme Lord is in reality one, by virtue of his most wondrous sovereign power (*vīrya*) and his nature as pure consciousness alone, [he manifests these levels].
Furthermore, regarding the twofold nature consisting of the internal and external that exists by virtue of being the self of the universe (*viśvātmaka*):

since the external form, which is the self of the universe, has acquired its own nature through its status as both the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the effect (*kārya*), that single power also appears as a duality in the form of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*).

It is so designated because that nature consisting of knowledge and action remains internally in a state of equilibrium, without the outward expansion [of manifestation] being grasped externally— just as the three *guṇas* remain in the unmanifest (*avyakta*) state—
even though it possesses the form of knowledge and action which constitute the enjoyment of the Supreme Lord, due to its inward-turned nature.

The state of Sadāśiva consists of *nimeṣa* (closing). On the other hand, that state of Īśvara is where there is repose in the supreme *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness) of the power (*śakti*) which has externally grasped *unmeṣa* (opening) through the predominance of its creative activity (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, in that [state], its outward orientation is due to the surging of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

Because it culminates in the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the internal and external forms, that state of knowledge (*vidyā-daśā*) consists precisely in resting within one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-viśrānti*). In all three of these states, the power of *māyā*, although having attained its own being, is rooted in the perception of duality.

Because the supreme consciousness rests within its very own nature, characterized by the all-encompassing and perfectly full *ahaṃkāra*, it has set; thus, it is no longer capable of concealing the form of Śiva, which is replete with supreme bliss.

These three words are indeed the supreme nectar. As it has been said in the *Tattvagarbha*: "O Śivā, regarding you who have proceeded in the form of knowledge and action, those who know the principles have declared your state of Sadāśiva to be called 'enjoyment' (*bhoga*)."
When you, whose power of knowledge has become subordinate and whose nature as action has become manifest,
then the Lordly Principle (aiśvara-tattva) attains manifestation through its functional activity.
When you become intent upon manifestation within the Supreme,
you are then celebrated as the noble Vidya, the power of knowledge.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

"In this way, action, which functions internally and externally and follows the sequence of time, as well as cognition and activity—which are inseparable from one another—belong to the subject alone."
However, due to the predominance of the internal state, the reality called Sādākhya arises first;
but when there is a predominance of external existence, the Pārameśvara follows after.
Īśvara is the external unfolding (unmeṣa), and Sadāśiva is the internal closing (nimeṣa);
the identity (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the cognitions of "I" and "this" is Sadvidyā.
For those things endowed with the state of "thisness" that have entered the ground of the knowable,
because their essence is consciousness, they are perceived exactly as they are.
Beyond that, however,
because one relies on objects perceived as distinct— characterized by the notion of "I" which exists through mutual exclusion—
and because one possesses a self-conceit fixed upon various differences, one remains ignorant of one's own true sovereignty.

In the reality of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), it is solely the power of Māyā belonging to the Lord that unfolds as the locus for the manifestation of His sovereignty in universal forms. As it has been stated in the *Tattvagarbha* itself:
But when, in this state, the bound soul (paśu) possesses such innate ignorance regarding its own experience of enjoyment, then You are sung as Māyā by nature, the locus of sovereign power.
Thus [it is said]. Even in the case of recognition (pratyabhijñā),
when difference shines forth as being of a single essence, and the non-self is not perceived through the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā)—
In the void of either consciousness or the body, the power of illusion unfolds.

Thus, she is designated here by the term "arising from cognition" (*pratyayodbhava*), because the perfect knowledge consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of one's own nature as Śiva is precisely the thought "I," and [this knowledge pertains] to that very nature appearing in the form of the universe through the delineation of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

The power called *māyā* is described as the capacity for manifesting differentiation, but it is not some separate entity whatsoever. Furthermore, since an object being referred to as "this" cannot exist otherwise by transcending its state of manifestation, therefore—

Although this Māyā has the form of differentiation, because it does not transcend the nature of the Supreme Lord, which consists of Light, it is indeed the power (śakti) of the Blessed One; for it is most wonderful that He Himself established His own very nature in such a way.
For this divine illusion of mine, composed of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion.

Thus it is said. For this is the meaning here: "This is my divine *māyā*, belonging to me as the Lord (*īśvara*), who consists solely of the delight of such divine play; as a power (*śakti*), it is related to me as its possessor. Of what nature is it? It is composed of the *guṇas*; the *guṇas* consist of pleasure and the rest."

The designations such as "being" (*sattva*) and so forth have that [consciousness] as their nature; for it has the manifestation of difference as its intrinsic nature. And the differentiated object consists of the sense-objects such as sound; and the object, in turn, culminates in the experience of pleasure and so forth. Thus.

Māyā, which manifests in the form of perceivable objects such as pleasure and so forth, is said to consist of the *guṇas*. Likewise, she is "difficult to transcend" (*duratyayā*), meaning she cannot be easily surpassed; for even by the awakened ones who exert themselves to go beyond her, the immediate eradication of all worldly existence is impossible.
Because the conventional usage of differentiation is difficult to transcend; rather, those who take refuge in Me alone—

those who are well-awakened, whose consciousness is established in the state where duality is severed— they recognize Me alone as the one Reality through non-difference as their own Self, and having attained My state, they become one with Me.
They transcend this [state]. For in that state, which shines like the radiance of day, this [state]—like a night whose very nature has been utterly destroyed—is transcended by them.
As it is said in the *Stotra*:
The mountain of duality, which cannot be split even by the vajra of meditative concentration or by other means,
is both grasped and destroyed by those endowed with the power of devotion to you.
Thus, illusion (māyā) consists merely in the arising of such cognitions, and its root— the principle of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)—

is here explained by the term "dependent" (asvatantra), which is a synonym for "bound soul" (paśu). For, by means of this illusion in the form of the arising of cognitions, he is displaced from his true nature.

The state of being a *paśu* (bound soul), characterized by dependence, is manifested in one who is bound by the fivefold fetters (*pāśapañcaka*)—such as time and the rest—which are easily produced and contrary to those [liberating] qualities. And thus:
this [soul], deluded by these [fetters], does not reflect upon its own nature, which consists of being undivided and so forth.
By means of its opposite, the delimiting factor consisting of time— which is divided by conceptual constructions such as past, future, and so forth— and likewise,
due to the forgetting of the attribute of being the self of all, everywhere.

By means of that which is called *niyati*, consisting of the fixed relationship between cause and effect; likewise, by means of those termed *kalā* and *vidyā*, which consist of limited agency and limited knowledge due to the indifference toward the two attributes characterized by omniscience and omnipotence; and likewise—

Due to the absence of the desired object, and because he does not attend to his own nature characterized by eternal desirelessness, he is bound by the noose called *rāga* (attachment), which consists of the longing for objects; thus, with his functioning dependent on another, he is bound as a *paśu* (bound soul). And this [bonding] is due to the power of *māyā*.

The fivefold birth, which exists by veiling the essential nature of the entire continuum of bound souls (paśus) without distinction, further obscures that [nature] which undergoes transformation into the form of diverse cognitions and so forth for each individual living being. Of that [birth],...

He explains the expansion of that which is called the primary cause (pradhāna), namely the manifestation (prasava), by means of demonstrating the objects of the arising of cognition, stating: "And that has the subtle elements (tanmātra) as its domain. That arising of cognition, which is the cause of the state of being a bound soul (paśu), has the subtle elements as its domain; [that is,] the subtle elements.
That whose range or object consists of universals such as sound and so forth is thus [described]; for this cognition arises in dependence upon a distinct object to be cognized (*pratyeya*),
and the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is possible only when there exists a triad consisting of the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable.
Furthermore, even that triad would not exist without a common cause for its manifestation;

thus, this fourfold set is implied by this statement. Among these, the perceiver is the conscious individual soul (*paśu*), and the objects of perception are primarily sound, touch, taste, form, and smell.

The qualities (*guṇas*), which consist of specific [manifestations], have as their substratum the gross elements beginning with space; for it is through their nature that all objects are perceived. And since their inclusion here is established, all specific [qualities] are contained within the general; thus, by the word *tanmātra*, which denotes the general, [all particulars are implied].

They are appropriated. By those [subtle elements], such as sound and the rest, the gross primary elements (bhūtas) beginning with space—which serve as their substratum—are projected, for they cannot exist without a substratum. This constitutes the tenfold effect. And that [individual] is a bound soul (paśu), characterized by conditions and dependent on another.
Being a subject, it requires an instrument for the activity of rejecting or accepting objects that are desired or undesired.
In that process, the instrument called *buddhi*, which consists primarily of illumination, is that by which one determines the object;
and [the instrument] by which one regards as the self that which is not the self, such as the body and so forth—
That which consists of the opposite [of the intellect] and is characterized by determination is called *ahaṃkāra* (ego);

and that which, being characterized by activity, conceptualizes objects and consists of doubt is designated as *manas* (mind). Thus, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is threefold, in successive order.

It is described as being an effect. That by which one perceives sound and the other objects is the pentad of the sensory organs (buddhīndriya), such as the ear; that by which one performs actions such as speaking is the pentad of the organs of action (karmendriya), such as speech—thus, there are ten kinds of external instruments (bahiṣkaraṇa). And that...
It has been stated precisely because it is an effect of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Thus, this internal and external instrument [is established].
In this way, the group of twenty-three effects and instruments is implied here by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the existence of subjects. Likewise, that which impels [to action]...
Since the engagement with objects cannot occur in the absence of a cause, objectivity itself is not tenable;

thus, the cause here is implied to be the Pradhāna, whose nature consists of pleasure and the rest. For instance, pleasure is the satisfaction resulting from each individual’s attainment of desired objects in accordance with their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and it is impermanent.

Ānanda, being impelled by that [pleasure], proceeds toward the acquisition of desired objects; its opposite is pain (duḥkha), which is non-contentment, and from that [pain] one proceeds toward the avoidance of undesired objects; while the neutralization of both is delusion (moha), and when that exists, one remains stationary—thus [the world] consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

For the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint, that which consists of the three qualities designated as *sattva* and so forth—though existing in a state of transformation—is, because they are mutually inseparable, a single principle called *pradhāna* for all living beings. (p. 139)

It is the common cause of activity, consisting of its own transformation into a manifold of effects in various forms according to diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it is composed of the expansion of the impurity of *māyā* known as attachment (*rāga*). It is with this very intention that [it is said]:

The author of the *Vṛtti* has employed the synonym "consisting of desire for form and so forth" (*rūpādyabhilāṣātmaka*) for the phrase "having that alone as its object" (*tanmātragocara*). This is because [the latter] is caused by that desire (*abhilāṣa*), which is attachment (*rāga*), directed toward form and the other [sensory objects].

That which arises from cognition is of the nature of that [object]; therefore, the primary cause consisting of pleasure and so forth is nothing but the proliferation of desire (*abhilāṣa-prapañca*). This is the twenty-fourfold principle of the Pradhāna school, and it is implied by the statement "that has the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as its object. And previously:
Twelve principles have been determined, namely: the five beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā; Māyā; the pentad beginning with Kāla; and the principle of Paśu.
Thus, the supreme power of the Lord alone unfolds as the nature of the thirty-six principles.
This has been largely explained in the commentary (p.
140) by the passage beginning with "falling away from one's own nature, which is the essence of supreme nectar," and so forth. || 16 ||
Thus, having established that for one who arises from conditions, the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) constitutes the cause [of bondage],

he says the following in order to resolve the previously mentioned contradiction: "The bound soul is traditionally defined as one who has become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers (*śakti*)."
And its powers for veiling its own nature are perpetually active, because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words. (4/17 [47])
Commentary: Regarding the obscuration of its own nature (svarūpa) or essential being (svabhāva), those powers of this Puruṣa—namely the Brāhmī and others previously mentioned—are constantly active;
for there is no arising whatsoever of cognition (pratyaya), that is, knowledge, devoid of sound (śabda). || 47 ||
Note: Only those categories [of phonemes] produced from the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) and so forth constitute the suffixes (*pratyaya*);

the presiding deities of these, the *Pīṭheśvarīs* such as Māheśī and the others, are constantly intent upon veiling the true nature of the bound soul (*paśu*). For this very reason, for the individual souls (*aṇu*) who are increasingly attached to the enjoyment of sense objects—
Samsara is a continuous flow. || 47 ||

Commentary (p. 140): For this very Self, whose state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) has been brought about by such a cognition, there is an obscuration of its own nature—that is, an obscuration of its essential nature which consists of Śiva—and thus, by the mere absence of such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), there occurs an intervention or concealment.

For that reason, the powers previously mentioned are "constantly arisen" (*satatotthitāḥ*); because the transaction between the Lord (*pati*) and the bound soul (*paśu*) never ceases, they are perpetually and eternally arisen and manifest.
This is because [the power] has been established as the cause for the loss of the nectar-essence, by way of bringing about a state of lack of autonomy.

That which arises from conditions (*pratyayodbhava*) cannot occur without the interpenetration of sound, that is, without the commingling of sound—this is the remainder [of the statement]. If it is asked, "Why is this so?", it is said in response: sound, indeed, consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśātman*), whereas the object consists of manifestation (*avabhāsātman*); [the former] is distinct from the latter.

Because it is distinct from insentient objects—such as a sword, water, or a mirror—which internally encompass a multitude of various things, [the light] is indeed its own inherent nature. And thus, the Pratyabhijñā school knows that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the manifestation is its very nature; otherwise, it would not be so.
Even when colored by an object, light remains like an insentient substance such as a crystal.
Thus it is said elsewhere as well:
"There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by speech."
Thus, that [cognition], being grounded in the primary sense which consists of the pure light of consciousness devoid of all limitations,

is called *pratyavamarśa* (reflective awareness). However, when it is grounded in the manifestation of the universe— which is of a diverse nature differentiated by various specific attributes such as genus, quality, action, and denotation— [it is not so called].

Because its nature consists of various conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*), it is called "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*). That alone is the primary form of the word; established as its conventional designation (*saṃketa*), the object itself—which consists of a specific sound (*dhvani*) perceivable by the ear—is generally designated as "word. (p. 142)

Therefore, the powers themselves—which have attained the form of sound and whose very life-breath is the arising of cognition—are ever intent on veiling His true nature; thus, having become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers, he is known as a *paśu* (bound soul). Consequently, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously.
This has been established;
this was explained in the commentary by the passage beginning with "in the obscuration of its own form, its own nature," and so forth. || 17 ||
Now, having first established the non-difference between this expansion culminating in sound and the supreme power,
[it is shown that] bondage and liberation are based solely on the non-recognition of its true nature.
To explain this, he says:

"This power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing in the bound soul (paśu), is a binder when it remains on its own path; but when known, it is the giver of perfection and other [attainments]. (4/18) (48)
Commentary: And this very power of the Blessed One, which has the nature of action, resides within bound souls (*paśu*).
As it has been said (p. 38):
"There is no such portion of the individual soul (*jīva-kalā*) that exists within both lineages."
"The pervasive power of Śiva (śivakalā) is that in which no presiding deity is found.
And that very [power], when unknown, is the cause of bondage; yet when known, it bestows both supreme (parā) and intermediate (apara) accomplishments upon men. 48.

Note: The meaning is that the conceptualization of bondage and liberation is based solely on the perception of difference and non-difference, which arises precisely from the power of action (kriyā-śakti) of the Supreme Lord that extends outwards as far as external existence. || 48 ||

Commentary: That power (*śakti*) of Śiva—the Supreme Lord who is one's own essential nature—is of the nature of action; its body consists of the activity characterized by the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of His own nature. It is an unfailing attribute in the form of capacity (*samarthatā*), and it takes the form of the expansion (*prasara*) that has been explained.

That very power which consists of the reflective awareness of the non-dual nature of pure consciousness—the supreme power (parā śakti) of the Supreme Lord—is this [power] itself that manifests by thus expanding outward; the meaning is that in reality there is no difference between her and him. As it has been stated in the Vṛtti:
There is no portion of the individual soul existing within the two continua in which the all-pervading portion of Śiva is not found as its presiding authority.

Thus [it is said]. For this is the meaning of the verse: for the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a bound person (*puruṣa*) like a beast, there is a twofold continuum of the *kalās*—consisting of the nature of knowledge and the nature of action. Among these, that which consists of knowledge is of the nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and is threefold; that which consists of action is...
The elevenfold [group] consists of the nature of the external organs together with the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) abiding in its own state;
thus, the fourteenfold continuum of the constituent parts (kalā) of the individual soul (jīva), when summarized, is indeed twofold.
There exists no such thing as a "part" (kalā) of the living self that could reside within both of these two continua.

The "Residue" (*śeṣa*) is that [power] in which the *śivakalā*—the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose nature has been described—resides as the pervasive presiding principle. Because its majesty is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it pervades everything by way of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) and the like; having rendered all things dependent upon itself, it exists therein.
It does not exist apart from being; rather, it is that very [Being] which manifests in this manner—this is the meaning.

Even amidst manifold diversity (*vaiśvarūpya*), because the pervasive attribute of Śiva, characterized as manifestation and consisting of the universal form, is never obscured, that very Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) appears in this way as the Non-Supreme (*aparā*).

"Having the form of gross action"—thus, the ultimate non-difference between the two powers, the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā), has been made known through recognition. This very point is also stated in the *Jñānagarbha-stotra*:
"Residing in the external organs, the intellect, the ego, the mind, and the *suṣumnā*..."
O Caṇḍikā, O Mother, wherever one may travel among the fourteen paths,
there you manifest as a digit of Śiva’s abode—
a digit that is indeed difficult to attain in this world even for the gods.
The intended meaning of this verse is as follows: the five beginning with the ear and the five beginning with speech constitute the tenfold external instruments (bahiṣkaraṇa);
the intellect, ego, and mind constitute the threefold internal instrument (antaḥkaraṇa).

And the *madhyamaprāṇa*— these are the fourteen divisions of the power (*kalā*) whose essence is consciousness (*cidātmikā*). Among their corresponding paths or channels of expansion, by whichever single one among them this *kalā* [proceeds] to the abode of Śiva.

"He should go"—that is, Śiva, the Supreme Self, He alone is the *niketana* (abode) or *mālaya* (refuge); he should go there, where the tenfold state (*daśā*) arises—this is the connection. "He should go to the abode of Śiva" means taking refuge in one's own state called Śiva, which is distinct from the cognition of duality belonging to Māyā.

The ultimate operation of *kalā* is treated as if it were already established. For this *kalā* arises from its own locus, which is of the nature of Śiva and characterized by such [scriptural] definitions as "neither suffering nor pleasure," and having accomplished its purpose, it finally enters back into that very [locus].
It becomes of one taste, like a river in the ocean; even in its midst,

although it appears as a multiplicity through the nature of the various expansions of intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest which are mutually distinct, it does not deviate from its common nature as the essence of consciousness (*cidātmatva*), just as [the river] does not deviate from its nature as water— thus it is not [otherwise].

Sometimes it departs from the nature of Śiva; however, those who are deluded by the power of *māyā* do not recognize it as such. Thus, by whichever path this *kalā* proceeds toward the abode of Śiva, there it remains of such a nature that, because it is self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*), it cannot be designated [in words].
A certain awakened one alone experiences and manifests a state that is difficult even for the gods, such as Brahmā and others, to attain;
for they do not transcend the animal-like conceit delimited by Brahminhood and other identities produced by the arising of mental constructs.
"How might they gradually attain the state of the Lord, whose nature is Śiva?"—

this is now explained in its proper context: however, although this supreme power of the Supreme Lord, consisting of action, is of such a nature, it remains within the bound soul (paśu) as its binder.

Residing in the *puruṣa*, whose dependence is brought about by the arising of the cognition of difference, she is the agent of bondage— that is, of *saṃsāra*, which consists of the continuous revolution of the stream of births and so forth. For the bound soul (*paśu*), indeed, determines her as his own property, while [in reality] the self is entirely distinct from her.

Because its own cognitive activity (*jñānakriyā*)— which consists merely in the experience of pleasure and so forth produced by the acquisition of desired objects and the avoidance of undesired ones— is in motion, it excludes [the object] without having touched upon that ultimate reality (*tatparamārtha*). And that [activity], being grasped as thus excluded, [excludes] him...

"By the emergence of awakening, she binds through the state of being a *paśu*"; thus it is said that she abides in the *paśu* as its binder. Now, one might object: since this [power] is his very nature (*svabhāvatvāt*), does it not follow that there can be no destruction of the *paśu*'s bondage? To this he says: "The knower, the known."
When recognized as being of the nature of the activity of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one's own essential nature which is Śiva,
it brings about accomplishment (*siddhi*). This refers to the supreme accomplishment characterized by the attainment of the Lord’s sovereignty,
as well as the secondary accomplishment consisting in the manifestation of various supernatural powers (*vibhūti*).

The Aparā [power] is the one who brings about birth, accomplishing it through the power of the essential nature of things; for she stands upon her own path— that is, she abides on her own path which consists of the nature of Śiva— meaning that her movement has ceased from other objects distinct from that.
However, with respect to the distinctions manifested through the power of illusion (*māyā*) arising from conditions (*pratyaya*),

that portion of the living soul (*jīvakalā*) residing in the state of the bound (*paśu*) is so designated; yet for one whose awakening has arisen, when recognized as it truly is, it brings about all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

Having thus explained the meaning of the verse, it is now set forth in detail how she abides in her own path. For she is indeed the supreme power (*parā śakti*), whose nature consists solely in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the manifestation of the essential form of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

"Having emanated in the form of speech"— thus, by demonstrating this repeatedly in the scriptures, the Supreme Lord has established that she is always situated on his own path. And so it is said in the *Śrī Mālinīvijaya*:
O Goddess, that power of the Creator of the universe which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) becomes His will when He desires to emanate.
Listen to how even a single entity comes to possess multiplicity:
it should be understood with absolute certainty that "it is thus" and not otherwise.
When she makes known [the will] here in this world, saying, "Let all this be so," and becomes intent upon action, she is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
At that very moment of arising, the action is considered to be performing its respective functions;
thus, while being essentially of two forms, it again attains multiplicity through its various divisions.
Under the influence of the limiting adjuncts of objects, the Sovereign Goddess becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem;
having first entered therein into the state of the Mother, she then manifests in differentiated forms.

This meaning has been elucidated by such statements as: "Mālinī is twofold, ninefold through its divisions, and fiftyfold. Likewise, even those who maintain the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvayavādin*), while demonstrating its expansion through the terminology of *vivṛtti* (manifestation), remain situated precisely on their own path.
This has been demonstrated. As they say:
"If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, manifestation itself would not manifest, for it is that which possesses self-reflective awareness."

Thus, this is the state of absolute non-difference, in which its own abiding within its own path is perfectly manifest. However, when the entire universe— which has internally vibrated in various forms as "this," characterized by differentiation and succession— is withdrawn through a lack of reflective awareness (avimarśa), [it becomes manifest].

When [consciousness] rests in its own majesty, which is devoid of the sequence of division, within the sky of its own nature (*svabhāvavyoman*), it remains as nothing but the residual manifestation of its own essence; at that time, there occurs an unfolding of the inner, supreme knower in the form of speech designated as *paśyantī*. As they say:
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all sequential order withdrawn;
she is the light of her own nature within, the subtle and imperishable speech.

Thus it is said. Here too, she remains established in her own path; for, apart from the effort of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), she follows—within each individual—the sequence of time and the division of phonemes and so forth, which consist of the specific sounds that have arisen within the body since beginningless time and are without end.
When it assumes expansion, it is then designated as the manifestation in the form of speech called the "Middle" (madhyamā);
even then, not transcending its nature as pure consciousness, this [speech] remains established on its own path.
As it has been said:
Taking up the intellect as its substrate and following the sequence of forms,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).

Thus it is said. But when the wind called *prāṇa*, impelled by an effort that conforms to the will of the person who utters [the speech], undergoes a collision within the regions of the body such as the chest and so forth,
that very [wind] takes on the form of the universal sound (*sāmānyadhvani*), which is differentiated into the shapes of vowels, consonants, and so on.

When [the manifestation] proceeds without deviation even when there is a difference among speakers, maintaining a fixed color and form, then that expansion is called *vaikharī*—a form of speech whose nature consists of the manifesting vital breath (*prāṇa*) and which is based on the distinctions of phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth; thus it has been said. As it was stated:
When the vital air (vāyu) strikes the various locations [of articulation],
the Vaikharī speech— assuming the specific phonemes and dependent upon the activity of the breath— is produced by speakers.

Thus, even then, this [speech] remains eternally so, not abandoning its nature as a collection of phonemes that are unchangeable and fixed, despite the diversity of place, time, substratum, speaker, and so forth, and while its manifestation depends upon the will of persons; this is true even of its nature as consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpatva*).

The middle state (*madhyamā*) follows her exactly even in this [state]; thus, her own status as abiding on her own path (*svamārgasthatva*) is not contradicted. In this way, although she has attained the form of *vaikharī*, she possesses an infinite expansion through the distinctions of the groups of letters, individual phonemes, words, and sentence-meanings within the *mātṛkā*.

It grasps. And just as this [power] has an infinite expansion in the form of *varṇavaikharī*, so too it has an infinite expansion in the form of *svaravaikharī* through the distinctions of the scales (*svaragrāma*), melodic patterns (*mūrcchanā*), musical sequences (*tāna*), and the resulting melodies (*rāga*) and so forth. Thus, this is the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of the Supreme Lord.

Although it has expanded by its own infinite majesty— beginning with the act of reflecting upon its own nature and extending to conventional words— it is such that for the entire collection of objects,
whose acquisition of self-nature is impossible apart from the light of universal consciousness, [this expansion occurs].
Being reflective, it never deviates from its own path; and therefore,

even though it becomes connected with various forms of conceptualization— obscuring veils produced by the power of *māyā* manifested by Īśvara for the sake of the world’s play— [it remains unchanged].

For those subjects whose vision of pure consciousness is skilled in grasping that true nature— which has been made manifest by the touch of the power of grace— it is absolutely impossible for [the world] to be concealed or hidden from them.
As it has been said:
"Though this [nature] is constantly being overspread by adventitious impurities,
it is not utterly overwhelmed, just as the final digit of the moon."
Thus, it is established that the Supreme Cause itself has thus issued forth even in the form of differentiated sound.
It is real, supreme, subtle, faultless, and unsurpassed.
Then the supreme Brahman, which is absolute peace, attained the state of being the primordial phoneme.

And so forth. Thus, in the doctrine of the non-duality of word and meaning (*śabdādvayavāda*), he has employed the expression "evolution" (*vivarta*) to refer to that expansion of the Lord’s power (*śaktiprasara*), which consists generally of both the word and its object and possesses limitless internal subdivisions. As he said:
Then this internal knower, abiding in the subtle self of speech,
undergoes a transformation into the form of sound for the manifestation of its own nature.
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of sound, the imperishable syllable;
from it proceeds the evolution of the world, as it manifests in the form of objects.

Thus, here, by virtue of being the reality of the word that is synonymous with Brahman, it is the very form of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara) that is indicated. That is to say: this supreme power (parā śakti), when she abides in her own path, is known; and thus, having correctly realized her own nature, she brings about complete accomplishment (siddhi).

Thus it has been said. This very [power], having attained the form of *vaikharī*, is called the "gross" power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) because its manifestation is dependent upon the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the person; and prior to that is the *madhyamā* speech, which is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and prior to that...
And thus, as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), she perceives.

Therefore, while being a power (*śakti*), she depends upon a possessor of power (*śaktimat*); consequently, her divine form (*aiśvaro vigrahaḥ*) consists of the undivided *mātṛkā*, primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) in the form of the totality of sound (*śabdarāśi*).

The common substratum (*samāśraya*) is that wherein this [Power] unfolds through its various expansions, beginning with the *vargas* and ending with sentences. Furthermore, her expansion in the form of sentences is twofold, distinguished by being eternal (*nitya*) or non-eternal (*anitya*); therein, it consists of both the nature of mantra and the nature of scripture (*śāstra*).

It is eternal, yet that which consists of worldly sentences—the objects of worldly transaction—is non-eternal. Thus, this manifestation consisting of speech, when recognized as the power of the Supreme Lord, bestows supreme accomplishment; however, when delimited by its connection with various bound souls (paśus), it remains limited.

"It becomes the cause of bondage"— this has been explained in the commentary by the passage beginning with "and this [activity] consists of action, having the nature of action," and so forth. || 18 ||

Having thus established that the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is manifested by one's own *māyā* within the very nature of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is [in fact] the Lord (*pati*), this supreme power (*parā śaktiḥ*)— which was previously unrecognised— is now known as being situated on its own path due to the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) in one who is a bound soul.

Having fallen [into this state], it brings about manifestation; as it becomes the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra, so, first explaining the causes of saṃsāra, he speaks two verses while promising to state the reason.

Constrained by the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), which consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arising in the form of mind, ego, and intellect, [the soul experiences] that which arises from the resulting cognitions. (4/19) (49)

(* Vivṛti: by the functions of mind, ego, and intellect) The emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); that is, by means of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*)—consisting of the mind, ego, and intellect—which perceives the subtle elements such as sound and so forth in the form of experience.
Bound; at that time, there arises from that [bondage] the experience of pleasure and pain produced from it. || 49 ||
Note: Precisely because this bound soul (paśu) is enclosed within the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), it experiences the rotation of the wheel of karma. || 49 ||
Under the power of another, he experiences enjoyment; because of that state, he transmigrates.
Therefore, we shall explain the cause of this transmigration—or rather, as the corrected reading appears: "the condition for transmigration. (4.20)
(* Vivṛti: "Because of its existence, it wanders through transmigratory existence.
Vṛtti: It experiences—that is, it consumes—enjoyment, which consists of the perception of pleasure and pain;
because of the existence of that *puryaṣṭaka*, it wanders through the body of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-śarīra*). (p. 39)

Therefore, we shall explain— that is, we shall speak of— the cause of the destruction of *saṃsāra*, which consists of the continuous flow of birth and death, and is the dissolution of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*). [50]
Note: Therefore, the means for the destruction of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), which is about to be described, is logically established. || 50 ||

Commentary (p. 155): For this reason, we shall fully and thoroughly explain—in the verse following this pair—the cause, that is, the means for the dissolution of transmigration, the destruction of saṃsāra, of this bound soul (*paśu*) whose nature has been described and will be described hereafter.
And we say this: here, the two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhī*) should be explained as having different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*). For what reason?

Because this bound soul (*paśu*), being confined by the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), experiences enjoyment within that city—the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*)—which consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*) and the three qualities (*guṇa-traya*).

The group of eight that constitutes the cause of the gross body, which is situated there, is primarily the *puryaṣṭaka*. Because the gross body is its effect, it too is here referred to by the term *puryaṣṭaka*; [the soul] is constricted by that.
Identifying with only that much as his self, he is bound by virtue of having forgotten his own power— such as being the Self of all— and for this very reason,
he is subject to another's control.

Because he depends on other causes distinct from his own nature of all-pervasive power (*sarvaśakti-svabhāva*) for the accomplishment of all desired objects, he is not independent; thus, while experiencing enjoyment,
he undergoes pleasure and so forth in accordance with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) accumulated by his own beginningless karma, which are manifested through *māyā*.
Having culminated in the nature of pure consciousness, it experiences—that is, perceives—only its own object.
Of what kind? "Arisen from that," meaning emerged from that *puryaṣṭaka*; for only when there is a bond with a body is the accomplishment of experience possible. Whom?
What is that enjoyment?
It is the arising of a cognition whose nature was previously explained as being restricted to its own specific object;
it is precisely the arising of a cognition whose form consists in the conceit of being the enjoyer of that very object alone.
The meaning is "enjoyment. By what kind of *puryaṣṭaka* is he obstructed?
It is by that which consists of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
These subtle elements, which serve as the causes of the gross elements, are manifested solely by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*).

Sound and the other [tanmātras]; their emergence (*udaya*) is their manifestation in the form of ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest, which have undergone transformation into the state of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*).
And thus—it is here that whatever cavity there is, such as the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth, that is ether, the emergence of the sound-tanmātra; and whatever...
That which is active, such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, is *vāyu* (air), arising from the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*).

Whatever has the nature of heat and luminosity, such as fire and the like, is *tejas* (fire), arising from the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*). Whatever has a liquid form, such as blood and the like, is *āpas* (water), arising from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*). Whatever is solid...

Flesh, bone, sinew, and so forth—that is earth, which is the manifestation (*udaya*) of the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). Thus, "having that as its form" means having that manifestation of the subtle elements as its nature or configuration; by that [it is so described].
Having thus explained the state of having the manifestation of the subtle elements as its form, [the author] proceeds to show the state of having the manifestation of the *guṇas* as its form.
He states another qualification: "by the functions of mind, ego, and intellect.
The acquisition of its own nature and the experience of that which is being experienced reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Thus, when the quality of *rajas* arises in the mind (*manas*), the quality of *tamas* arises in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and [the quality of *sattva*] in the intellect (*buddhi*)...

By one whose mode of being (*vṛtti*)— that is, whose activity or abiding— is of the nature of the arising of the qualities of *sattva*; and who, being thus obstructed by such a "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), is a bound soul (*paśu*) because of that state—
that is, due to the existence of that city of eight, both gross and subtle.

Because it exists, as long as there is no awakening, due to its non-cessation, one would transmigrate incessantly, experiencing the whirling of the wheel of karma consisting of various bodies, enjoyments, and latent impressions, until the dawning of awakening. This is the intended meaning here: for the person confined within a body...

The conceit of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvābhimāna*) within the experience (*bhoga*) whose nature is the perception of specific pleasure and so forth is the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, we declare that the mere abiding in one’s own state, free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇasvarūpasthitimātra*), is the cause for the destruction of transmigratory existence. This has been explained.
By the author of the commentary [it was stated] with the words "the arising of that alone," and so forth.
And by [the passage] beginning with "he eats and consumes under the control of another," etc., [it is shown]. 19 || 20 ||

Now, immediately following this, while teaching another means (*upāya*) that was previously promised— which reveals the state of being the Lord (*patitva*), the nature of whose sovereignty over Śiva himself is as described— he concludes the treatise:
But when he is firmly established in one [state], then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, he attains the status of the enjoyer; from that, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel. (4.21)
(* Vivṛti: dissolution and emergence) When, moreover, one's mind is firmly established and dissolved in a single object— whether gross or subtle— then,
while restraining the emergence and dissolution, that is, the destruction and manifestation, of that cognitive state;
By performing [this], one attains the state of being an enjoyer; from that, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), the sovereign of all.

*Tippanī*: Thus, through the practice of intense reflection upon the Self—which has been previously established as having the singular nature of pure perception—by means of the functioning of methods such as the abandonment of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*).

Because one attains the nature of non-conceptual consciousness within either of the two bodies— the body of the elements or the body of existence— and because the wheel of powers such as *gocaryā* functions independently, one becomes the Lord (*pati*) through the mere realization of the unfolding of one's own sovereignty.
By the illustrious Pratāpasiṃha, the lords of Kaśmīra, who were devoted to the work of restoring ancient sciences, and by Mukundarāma and others who were appointed to that task;

In the Śaka year measured by fire (3), the sky (0), the quarters (10), and the moon (1)—that is, 1043—this *Saṃkṣiptārthaprakāśa* on the commentary to the *Spanda-kārikās* has been completed in its entirety for the welfare of fortunate beings. || 51 ||

Commentary (p. 159): But when, at a certain time, from between these two bodies—designated by the name *puryaṣṭaka* and having as their sole root the arising of cognitive impressions—one [of them], that is, either one or the other... or else—
Since it has been established through previously demonstrated reasoning that the object of cognition alone constitutes the body,

[the inquiry concerns] one of the two bodies— the gross or the subtle— distinguished as being composed of the elements (*bhūta*) or composed of existence (*bhāva*), or else, between the two objects to be taken as supports (*ālambana*) by virtue of being meditated upon (*dhyeya*).
