When the practitioner has become firmly established in one of the two states— the gross or the subtle— having properly and without delay ascended [to it], and when his consciousness has been transformed into non-duality through the excellence of one-pointedness, then, at that moment, for him, by way of non-duality...

Restraining the dissolution and emergence— meaning the destruction and arising in the form of relinquishment and grasping— of the aforementioned body of one who has entered [the path], and determining that the true agent to be described by the term "experiencer" (bhoktṛ) is indeed the Self (ātman) as the subject of action, [one realizes]: "I alone..."

Establishing through non-conceptualization that "the agent of these two is the nature of pure consciousness, eternally unobscured and independent," one attains the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*).
The state of being an enjoyer is the condition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), whose essential nature is that of a mere perceiver (*upalabdhr-mātra-svabhāva*).
One attains that [state] and, even while it is present, recognizes it at that very moment through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); therefore,
by the cause characterized as the recognition of the true nature of the Self, one becomes the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*),
[presiding over] the wheel [of existence] consisting of the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) down to all moving and non-moving beings, according to the condition previously explained.

The Lord is the presiding controller of the expanded multitude of powers arising from the mass of sounds, which is understood as being nothing more than the unfolding of His own sovereignty; thus, He becomes the disposer of them according to His will. At that very moment—

When the notion of being a bound soul (*paśu*) has been destroyed through the manifestation of innate sovereignty, and having abandoned the state of being an object of enjoyment for the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), one should attain the lordship (*aiśvarya*) that consists in the state of being their enjoyer; therefore, one should restrain both dissolution and emergence within that Self who is the enjoyer. Thus it is said.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the intended purport here is this— that just as every embodied being, whose self-conceit is established solely in the body, exercises the acts of abandoning and grasping toward external objects such as jars, which are perceived only as objects of apprehension, [so too does he exercise them] toward his own such self.

Deciding "I alone am the agent of these two," he considers himself to be an independent agent who is not situated within the state of having a body; likewise, the acts of abandoning and grasping performed by bringing that very body onto the plane of the object of knowledge are always distinct from him.

Although [the two] are subject to a necessary restriction by the power of reality— since one's own true Self possesses the nature of agency that is not shared with anything else and cannot tolerate contact with the state of being an object—
[the agent] does not realize this due to a lack of awakening; therefore:
This instruction is intended only for one whose intellect has been awakened to the discernment of the distinction between the body and the embodied soul;
for it is only such a person that the Supreme Lord’s power of grace can shatter the knots of doubt.
He is a fit recipient for such specific instruction. As it is said:
"Thinking that He is the source of all and that everything proceeds from Him, the wise, filled with devotion, worship Me."
With their minds fixed on me and their lives dedicated to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they find contentment and take delight.
To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love,
I give that yoga of discernment by which they attain Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
Thus, because of this instruction being practiced, immediately after [the state] of this body— which has been established as "in one place," which exists as appearing without division,
and which is being made an object of knowledge— there occur dissolution and emergence, consisting of abandonment and grasping, within that which possesses contrary properties.

When these two [the senses and the vital breath] are brought under control as effects by the enjoyer—the self which is the Lord of all—through its own sovereignty, they bring about the recognition of the other nature of the Controller and lead to the attainment of universal sovereignty; therefore, one should restrain them there. This is the meaning of the sentence. That...
By this, it is established that the dissolution and emergence of the universe depend solely on the mere will of Śiva himself;
and since the universe is non-different from his own nature, it is his manifestation consisting of the wheel of his powers (*svaśakticakra*).
Thus, by fulfilling the meaning as it was introduced, there is only one single reality (*tattva*).

It has been established that the ultimately real is characterized by the non-deviation from the mere self-reflection of its own nature; therefore, nothing whatsoever exists apart from this. As it has been said:
"In the ultimate sense, however, oneness does not have a characteristic distinct from separateness."
Reality shines as a single essence in the form of both difference and unity.
That which is undoubtedly distinct does not differ from unity;
that which is undoubtedly one does not differ from distinctness.
The sky, the earth, the wind, the sun, the oceans, the rivers,
and the directions are the external manifestations of the reality of the internal organ.

Thus, this very same meaning has been set forth by us in our own hymn (*Svastotra*) through another mode of expression: "Dancing in many ways outside of her own body, yet not divided within it, she displays various forms marked by ever-new ornaments fashioned from the conceptualizations of diverse perceptions; yet again,"
Victorious alone is Śambhu, whose perpetual delight is ever-new as he gazes upon his own beloved power, and whose greatness of joy is unbroken and incomparable.

Thus, in this verse which has just been explained, the subject matter— the non-dual sovereignty of the Self characterized as being knowable through self-awareness— which was promised in the opening verse of the treatise, has been fully established. This has been explained by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*).
Furthermore, as stated in the passage beginning with "when, however, [the mind is] fixed upon one thing, whether gross or subtle," etc. (21).

Thus ends the fourth outflow (*niḥṣyanda*), titled "The Realization of the Non-difference of the Universe from the Nature of Power," along with its miscellaneous sections, in the *Spandavivṛti* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Śrī Rāma. 4.

Commentary: Now, the sole cause for the non-manifestation of even the mere doubt regarding the single reality that is the Self is that it cannot be uprooted except through the instruction of a true guru.
For the Supreme Lord, having entered the form of the Guru, awakens those to be graced by means of causing them to recognize Him; thus, by way of praising his own Guru as Sarasvatī, he says:
"She who is the boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt... (K.)
"From the ocean of doubt"; [this refers to] *saṃśayāmbhodhau*.
I pay homage to that wondrous speech of the Guru, which possesses marvelous meanings and words. (5/1, 52)
For it is unfathomable, without foundation, and infinite. || 52 ||
Thus ends the third outflow, "The Vibration of Supernatural Powers," in the commentary on the Spandakārikās composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. || 3 ||
The *Spandasarvasva*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa—who was eager for the joy of embracing the single reality of consciousness that is self-luminous—is hereby completed. (1)

From the ocean of the Śiva-sūtras, as taught in a dream by Maheśa on Mount Mahādeva, the nectar of Spanda was extracted; that [nectar] which had been woven together by the venerable Vasuguptapāda, the illustrious Kallaṭa has now made manifest.
(In the *Cittattvaprakāśa*: "in the embrace within the principle of consciousness").
For me, whose lineage of gurus extends from Ātapaṇa down to Moṭaka,
there is no poverty of instruction for me, who am a disciple of all.
This *Spandavṛtti* is complete;
it is the work of the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa, the most excellent teacher among the great Mahāmaheśvaras.

Commentary: I pay homage to the venerable speech of my Guru, named Vasugupta, which, though its true nature is impossible to fully express, flashes forth within the heart— that speech which is the Spanda-tattva, the very essence of all secret Upaniṣads, transmitted directly from the mouth of a perfected being (siddha).
I praise the speech of Bhārati, which is the outflow of the deceased [sages]. Of what sort is she? She is characterized by the half-verse beginning with "agādha" (p.
166): that doubt, which is a delusion consisting in the non-comprehension of reality, wherein no "gādha"—that is, no ground for rest—is found; such is she. That very [doubt]...

Because it is crowded with a network of waves of difficult-to-overcome conceptual constructions, it is like an ocean; for crossing—that is, for completely traversing—that ocean, she is a boat (*tāriṇī*). Likewise, her words and meanings are diverse: "diverse" means that their subject matter (*abhidheya*) or essential reality is exceedingly wonderful.

That [composition] in which there are such words; likewise, she [the composition] is "wondrous" (*citrā*) because it possesses a particular arrangement that inspires amazement. By these two adjectives, he praised both the excellence residing in the meaning and the excellence residing in the word, since in this case—

The meaning of the words is manifold: it is beyond the reach of the minds of all ordinary people, yet it resonates with the hearts of a few who are awakened to the supramundane; and the composition of words and sentences is variegated, being endowed with the capacity to convey such a meaning—thus [it is]. This has been explained in the *Vṛtti*.
For [it is described] by such passages as "indeed, it is unfathomable, without support, and without end," and so forth. || 1 ||
This treasure called Spanda has been revealed here, with the fear of the serpent of doubt dispelled; it contains within it the ruby of unsurpassed knowledge that bestows all perfections.
Having bestowed [its wealth] upon all seekers, it itself attains the experience of innate bliss.
May the supreme grace of Śaṃkara make the attainment of this [work] fruitful for those who are worthy. || 1 ||

This which has been sung by me— sweet with incomparable joy— has been composed for Rāma, who is attentive, by one whose mind is like a vast, noble blue lotus adorning the lake of the six sciences, and who is a bee of fully ripened awakening rising upward.
To what conscious listener does it not extend supreme inner tranquility? (2)
When the mind is agitated by some base object, one should turn away from it and remain silent; then, having gently turned back toward one's own beloved consciousness and appeased it with affection,
one should kiss her— [the consciousness] who shines with a fresh embrace, dense and devoid of any intervening space, as the [external] kissing ceases.
May you, whose dispositions are auspicious, remain forever with eyes closed in the blissful vibration [of the Self]. || 3 ||

Whatever has been stated here in excess, or whatever has been left unsaid, or even whatever has been poorly expressed— let that be disregarded by the wise whose intellects are solely intent on discerning subtle nuances.
For those who are eager to taste the drops of the essence of nectar within the flowers wander through the forest.
Do bees experience the pain of contact with the tips of harsh thorns? (4)
That darkness which, having rendered the entire world motionless, could indeed not be quelled by the moon, the stars, lamps, and the like—
now that it has reached its destruction, struck down by the arrival of the stainless sun.
May the eyes of people, their purpose fulfilled, abandon their contraction and become sleepless [with joy]. || 5 ||
Victorious is Bhavānī, who delivers people from misfortune;
victorious is the Enemy of Smara, by whose own splendor the universe is pervaded;
and victorious is that Elephant-faced One, by whose grace—
The entire host of obstacles and calamities is pacified. || 6 ||
This *Spandavivṛti*, following the commentary, is complete.
It is the work of the venerable Rājānaka Śrī Rāmakaṇṭha, who lived at the lotus feet of the illustrious Rājānaka Utpaladeva— the crest-jewel of the great Mahāmaheśvara teachers.
Thus may there be auspiciousness.
